Netflix will premiere Rockstar's next GTA 6 look on August 27, six hours before YouTube
ScaleAnalysts put GTA 6 at $3.3 billion to $5.2 billion in its first week, three times Spider-Man: Brand New Day's first week. Netflix announced the deal through its unscripted chief, not its gaming chief.
CEO Summary
Rockstar Games gave Netflix an exclusive six-hour window on an "extended look" at "Grand Theft Auto 6," premiering Aug. 27 at 3 p.m. ET before going wide on YouTube and social at 9 p.m. ET. Netflix did not develop, publish, or invest in the game, and neither company disclosed terms. The same day, Take-Two reported $1.39 billion in first-quarter net bookings, down 3% year over year with a widened $34.1 million loss, and CEO Strauss Zelnick called GTA 6 pre-orders "unprecedented and astonishing" while declining to translate them into a sales forecast.
Key Takeaways
  • Scale: The largest single entertainment launch of the year is a video game, and the gap is not close enough to argue about.
  • Distribution: A platform with enough scale will pay for premiere rights to a cultural event it has no ownership in, because attention has become an inventory category separate from IP.
  • Forecasting: When a publisher calls demand unprecedented and still refuses to forecast, the honest read is that the category has outgrown its own comps.
Why It's Happening
Rockstar did not need the reach. Trailer one has 288 million YouTube views since December 2023 and trailer two has 176 million since May 2025, so a third would have found its audience unassisted. What Netflix supplies is placement: it moves GTA 6 out of the games press and into the entertainment-industry conversation eight weeks before a Nov. 19 launch. Zelnick agreed when Variety put that motive to him directly.

On Netflix's side, sources say the pursuit came from the same logic as its move into sports, wanting to be present at "big cultural moments." The tell is who spoke for it: the announcement quote came from Brandon Riegg, VP of nonfiction series, not from head of gaming Alain Tascan. This is being run as event programming, not as a gaming initiative.
The Facts
  • "Extended look" premieres on Netflix Aug. 27, 3 p.m. ET; YouTube and social six hours later at 9 p.m. ET.
  • Prior trailers: 288 million YouTube views (Dec. 2023), 176 million (May 2025).
  • Analyst projection: $3.3 billion to $5.2 billion in global GTA 6 sales in week one, at least three times "Spider-Man: Brand New Day's" first-week box office.
  • Netflix quote came from VP of nonfiction series Brandon Riegg. Terms undisclosed by both parties.
  • Take-Two Q1 FY27 (Apr. 1 to Jun. 30): net bookings $1.39 billion, down 3%; revenue $1.53 billion; net loss $34.1 million versus $11.9 million a year earlier; $43.4 million write-down on an abandoned third-party title. FY27 net bookings guidance reiterated at $8.0 billion to $8.2 billion.
  • GTA 6 launches Nov. 19 at $79.99 standard and $99.99 ultimate. Pre-orders opened June 25.
  • Existing Netflix and Take-Two business: prior GTA mobile license, current "WWE 2K" pact.

The Odyssey crossed $1 billion in three weeks, with $257 million of it from IMAX
Format EconomicsA quarter of the gross, $257 million, came from IMAX, making it IMAX's biggest release ever. The film has not opened in China yet; it arrives Aug. 14 on nearly 800 IMAX screens.
CEO Summary
Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey," a three-hour adult drama adapted from Homer and starring Matt Damon, has grossed $1.008 billion worldwide in three weeks for Universal, $429.65 million domestic and $578.8 million international. IMAX supplied $257 million of that, and the film will be IMAX's highest-grossing title ever by the end of the weekend. It is the fifth film of 2026 to cross $1 billion, the most in any year since 2019, and it hit the mark before opening in China.
Key Takeaways
  • Format Economics: Premium large format is now a pricing tier with its own demand curve, not a surcharge attached to a normal release.
  • Greenlight Risk: An adult drama with no franchise and no sequel can carry a studio's year, which means the constraint on that category was distribution willingness rather than audience appetite.
  • Talent Value: A filmmaker who can reliably fill premium screens holds leverage that does not show up in a standard star or director comp.
Why It's Happening
The $257 million IMAX line is roughly a quarter of the worldwide total, and it arrived without China, the second-largest theatrical market, which opens Aug. 14 on nearly 800 IMAX screens. That sequencing matters: the billion was reached on the strength of premium capacity in markets already exhausted, with the largest premium market still ahead.

The concentration cuts both ways. Hollywood is counting on "The Odyssey" and "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" to push domestic ticket sales past $4 billion for only the second time since 2020. The first time was 2023, carried by Nolan's "Oppenheimer" and "Barbie." Two titles clearing a market is a recovery at the top, not across the middle.
The Facts
  • Worldwide $1.008 billion after three weeks: $429.65 million domestic, $578.8 million international.
  • IMAX contribution: $257 million; will be IMAX's highest-grossing release ever by the end of the weekend.
  • Nolan's first $1 billion film since "The Dark Knight Rises" (2012); will pass "The Dark Knight Rises" ($1.08 billion) and "The Dark Knight" ($1.008 billion) within days.
  • Runtime roughly three hours; adult-skewing; adapted from a nearly 3,000-year-old poem.
  • China opens Aug. 14 on nearly 800 IMAX screens plus thousands of standard auditoriums.
  • Fifth $1 billion film of 2026, after "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" ($1.18 billion), "Toy Story 5" ($1.067 billion), "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie" ($1.001 billion), "Michael" ($1.001 billion).
  • Nine films crossed $1 billion in 2019, a record; no year since had more than three.

Seventy Percent of This Century's Top 100 Films Had a Creative With Family Already in the Business
AccessThose creatives reach a first feature at 33 rather than 35 and a top-100 film in eight years rather than ten, and Follows found their films earn the same and rate the same.
CEO Summary
Film industry data analyst Stephen Follows opened Locarno Pro on Aug. 6 with new research on the top 100 films of 2000 to 2025. Counting any film where a director, writer, or one of the top three actors had a family member already working in the industry, the figure was 70 percent. Follows also found that three out of four directors never make a second feature within five years of their first, and that the strongest predictor among those who do is whether an experienced producer worked on the debut.
Key Takeaways
  • Access: Family connections in the business buy entry and career longevity, not better films.
  • Packaging: For a first-time director, the producer attached is a stronger predictor of a second film than the quality of the debut.
  • Distribution: In independent film, reaching theaters separates a profitable title from a write-off more reliably than anything about the film itself.
Why It's Happening
The profitability numbers explain the third point. On data through 2018, 3.4 percent of independent films generate a profit. Among the roughly 10 percent that reach cinemas, about 33 percent do. Studio films come in at 51 percent. The gap between 3.4 and 33 is the gap between made and released, which is a distribution outcome, not a creative one.

Follows framed all of it as a power law: "A small number gets really all of the riches." His argument against the industry's risk tools follows from that. Stars, test screenings, franchises, formulas and algorithms are what he called an "illusion of control," and he compared buying them to installing window bars on a house exposed to earthquakes and tornadoes. Film school fits the same access pattern as family: graduates' films outgross the rest while quality ratings are identical.
The Facts
  • Presentation: "Fear, Lies, and the Illusion of Control," StepIn: Out of the Box, Locarno Pro 2026, Aug. 6.
  • Method: top 100 films 2000-2025; counted when a director, writer, or one of the top three actors had at least one family member already working in the industry. Result: 70 percent.
  • Follows: "It's not always nepotism in a terrible way. It might be that they grew up around the industry. ... I'm not saying they have no merit."
  • Family ties correlate with a first feature at 33 rather than 35, eight years rather than ten to a top-100 film, more second features and more films per career. "But the films themselves are no bigger and no better," citing the same box office and the same ratings.
  • Three of four directors do not make a second feature within five years. Among those who do, working with an experienced producer on the first is "one of the biggest predictors." "Even a brilliant debut loses to an ordinary one with a better producer." The correlation disappears after the first film.
  • Film school graduates' films outgross the rest; quality ratings identical.
  • Indie profitability through 2018: 3.4 percent overall; about 33 percent of the roughly 10 percent that reached cinemas; 51 percent for studio films.
  • Locarno Pro runs Aug. 6-11 alongside the 79th Locarno Film Festival, with roughly 2,000 accredited guests expected including about 800 producers, 350 buyers, 100 sales agents and 300 festival programmers.

E.W. Scripps cut 432 jobs and called itself an AI-powered broadcast journalism company
LaborRevenue fell 9% to $490.4 million and Scripps posted a net loss of 34 cents a share. The stock rose more than 20% the same day, on $100 million in annualized savings from 432 eliminated positions.
CEO Summary
E.W. Scripps has eliminated 432 positions and 126 open roles this year, 12% of its workforce, and CEO Adam Symson told analysts the station group is becoming a "technology-forward, AI-powered broadcast journalism company." Most of the 268 layoffs disclosed this week hit local television stations. The restructuring targets $100 million in annualized savings and a $125 million to $150 million EBITDA increase by 2028, against Q2 revenue of $490.4 million, down 9%, and a net loss of 34 cents per share.
Key Takeaways
  • Labor: AI substitution has moved from a tool inside an operating model to the operating model itself, and the first mover published the per-head math for every peer to copy.
  • Valuation: A content company can now be rewarded for a quarter of falling revenue and a net loss if the accompanying story is automated cost takeout.
  • Consolidation: A demonstrated cost structure is a takeover defense, because it lets a target argue a valuation an acquirer's synergy case was supposed to supply.
Why It's Happening
Local television is absorbing cord-cutting and advertising migration at the same time, and Scripps reported a 9% revenue decline in the quarter it announced the plan. The savings are specific and dated: $100 million annualized now, $125 million to $150 million in EBITDA by 2028, alongside a shift to a 24-hour streaming news model.

The market's reaction is the part that will be studied. Shares rose more than 20% in midday trading on a loss-making quarter. Investors priced the cost line, not the product, and that reaction is legible to every board facing the same pressure.

Scripps' board separately rejected a $622 million takeover bid from Sinclair, unanimously.
The Facts
  • 432 positions eliminated plus 126 open roles cut since the start of the year, 12% of the workforce; includes 268 layoffs disclosed this week, mostly at local stations.
  • Symson: "We're leaning into AI, automation, technology and the centralization of some roles"; called it a "revolution" in how Scripps produces local news; "We are not wavering on our commitment to quality journalism."
  • Target: $100 million annualized savings; $125 million to $150 million EBITDA increase by 2028.
  • Q2 revenue $490.4 million, down 9% year over year; net loss 34 cents per share.
  • Shares up more than 20% in midday trading Friday.
  • Moving toward a 24-hour streaming news model. Scripps also owns the ION broadcast network.
  • Scripps' board unanimously rejected Sinclair's $622 million takeover bid.

Starz Took a $147 Million Charge to Get Out of Its Universal Output Deal
Output DealsStarz had not aired the Universal titles in about eighteen months and says they carried almost zero engagement, while paying pay-2 prices for them. It also licensed four Power seasons to Netflix.
CEO Summary
Starz reported Q2 revenue of $307.9 million, down 4 percent year over year, with net losses widening to $189.4 million including a $147.2 million charge for ending its output deal with Universal. CEO Jeff Hirsch said total subscribers rose during the quarter despite a June price increase to $11.99 a month, though the company no longer discloses the figure. Separately, Starz licensed the first four Power series to Netflix globally while retaining exclusive rights to all sequels, prequels and spinoffs.
Key Takeaways
  • Output Deals: A subscale premium service will now pay cash to escape a volume commitment, because engagement per dollar has replaced volume as the metric that matters.
  • Rights Retention: Licensing mature seasons to a larger rival while keeping every derivative turns a competitor into an audience-acquisition channel for a franchise you still own.
  • Production Costs: A network that produces in-house rather than buying from a former corporate parent can hold output constant and cut the bill materially.
Why It's Happening
Hirsch's account of the Universal deal is the mechanism. The titles sat off air for roughly eighteen months at the supplier's request to keep them fresh, and when they did air, "we were paying pay-2 prices for library performance." A $147.2 million write-off is cheaper than continuing to pay premium rates for inventory the audience does not watch, and the savings are being redirected into library that does drive engagement.

The Netflix arrangement runs on the same logic from the other direction. Alison Hoffman called it syndication: put the mature seasons where the audience is, keep the derivative rights where the value compounds. Fightland, the in-house replacement for Lionsgate-sourced originals, costs about $2.5 million per episode and posted the second-best debut of any Starz original. Hirsch's summary of the swap: "It's the same amount of content, just much cheaper cost."
The Facts
  • Q2 revenue $307.9 million, ahead of Wall Street, down 4 percent from $319.7 million. Net losses widened to $189.4 million, including the $147.2 million Universal output-deal charge.
  • Price increase to $11.99 a month took effect in June. Hirsch said subscribers rose in the same period and called that "very rare": "So, there's real strength of the business on both sides of the revenue equation." Starz ended 2025 with 17.6 million subscribers and has since stopped reporting the metric.
  • On the Universal titles: not aired in almost a year and a half at Universal's request; "absolutely almost zero viewership or engagement tied to those titles"; "we were paying, pay-2 prices for library performance."
  • Netflix deal covers the first four Power series globally. Hoffman: it "creates an opportunity for us. It's a way for us to introduce the franchise to new audiences." Starz retains exclusive sequel, prequel and spinoff rights. "We think that syndication model actually works for us."
  • Q2 engagement was the second-highest in Starz history.
  • Fightland, released last week, had the second-best debut of any Starz original, at about $2.5 million per episode. Power Book III: Raising Kanan wrapped its fifth and final season.
  • Michael, the billion-dollar Lionsgate release, debuts on Starz next week.
  • Starz shares have more than doubled in 2026 and drifted down 2 percent pre-market. The company completed its separation from Lionsgate in 2025.

Ryan Murphy Has Not Charted a Nielsen Top 10 Show for Disney Since He Came Back
Overall DealsNeither Love Story nor All's Fair nor The Beauty made Nielsen's top 20 for the first half of 2026. Taylor Sheridan, Shonda Rhimes and Dan Fogelman each placed a show.
CEO Summary
Ryan Murphy's work has made 35 all-time appearances in the Nielsen streaming top 10, but the only series to chart since he returned to Disney in summer 2023 were installments of Monster, made for Netflix. Disney's direct-to-consumer revenue rose 11 percent to $5.53 billion in the quarter reported Wednesday with operating income more than doubling to $712 million, gains Belloni attributes to price increases, tech and interface work, and bundling rather than programming. Disney placed one show, Paradise at No. 14, in Nielsen's first-half top 20 original series list, fewer than Peacock.
Key Takeaways
  • Overall Deals: A top-of-market producer deal is priced on brand and volume, and a buyer will keep funding it through a multi-year performance drought.
  • Slate Contraction: A studio cutting its series count in half does not cut its committed relationships proportionally, so the reduction lands entirely on everyone without a standing deal.
  • Platform Economics: Streaming profitability and content performance have decoupled, which means a strong platform quarter is no longer evidence that the slate is working.
Why It's Happening
Disney reduced the number of shows on its platforms by almost 50 percent between 2022 and 2025, per Ampere Analysis as cited by Bloomberg, while continuing to fund Murphy's output at volume. All's Fair was renewed for a second season on U.S. numbers comparable to The Beauty, which was canceled. Murphy is described as far more likely than a peer on a comparable Disney deal to hit his productivity bonuses, which is what a volume-triggered structure is designed to do when hit rate is unreliable.

The perception gap is the other half. When All's Fair opened to some of the worst reviews in years, the response was a release calling it "Hulu Originals' Biggest Scripted Series Premiere in Three Years." Belloni's own line is the tell: "some might assume the Murphy shows were performing better. I certainly did."
The Facts
  • 35 all-time Nielsen streaming top 10 appearances for Murphy's work; since his summer 2023 Disney return, only Netflix's Monster installments have charted. Caveat: Love Story and many Murphy shows also air on FX linear, classifying them as "acquired" titles needing more viewing minutes to chart.
  • Nielsen's top 20 shows for the first half of 2026 excluded Love Story, All's Fair and The Beauty. Sheridan, Rhimes and Fogelman each placed one.
  • Nielsen total-viewership data supplied to Belloni shows Murphy still delivers above-average ratings. Disney says Love Story delivered 5.4 billion minutes streamed worldwide and was a top Disney+ subscriber-acquisition driver globally this year.
  • Doctor Odyssey was canceled after one season. Paradise and Alien: Earth were both far bigger on Hulu than Love Story.
  • Disney DTC revenue $5.53 billion, up 11 percent; operating income more than doubled to $712 million.
  • Disney's share of total TV viewing has risen from the mid-4 percent range in 2023 to around 5 percent, but streaming viewership has been flat for two years, per Nielsen.
  • Series count on Disney platforms down almost 50 percent 2022-2025 (Ampere Analysis via Bloomberg).
  • Disney un-renewed the Marvel series Wonder Man last week after renewing it in March. Co-creator Destin Daniel Cretton, director of Spider-Man: Brand New Day: "I know this sounds weird — but if it were up to Kevin, we would be doing that show."
  • Dana Walden said last week she feels "great about what we've accomplished" and plans to raise content spend, especially internationally, "while significantly expanding our creative output over the next several years."
  • Love Story drew seven Emmy nominations. The People v. O.J. Simpson drew 22 nominations and nine wins a decade ago. Murphy, 60, declined to comment.

'Michael' Crossed $1 Billion and Lionsgate Still Posted a $29 Million Loss
Franchise ValueMotion picture revenue more than doubled to $587 million and segment profit hit a first-quarter record $105 million, while the stock has run from under $6 to near $17 on takeover speculation.
CEO Summary
Lionsgate Studios reported June-quarter revenue of $777 million, up nearly 50 percent and ahead of forecasts, with motion picture revenue of $587 million more than doubling and segment profit reaching a Q1 record $105 million. The drivers were Michael, now at $1.013 billion worldwide and the highest-grossing biopic ever, and ancillary performance from The Housemaid. Net loss narrowed to $29 million from $107 million; television production revenue fell to $189 million on delivery timing.
Key Takeaways
  • Franchise Value: Music-catalogue and life-rights material is now being underwritten at tentpole scale, and a studio without a streaming service can carry it.
  • Participation: A billion-dollar gross producing a net loss shows how far segment profit sits from corporate profit at a distributor that shares territory economics with partners.
  • Valuation: A content-only company with a deep library and no linear or streaming attachment is the shape acquirers are paying up for in this cycle.
Why It's Happening
Trailing twelve-month library revenue was $987 million against $777 million of total revenue in the quarter, which is the reason the takeover story exists. The library is the stable asset and the slate is the option on top of it, and that separation became legible only after the Starz split turned the company into a pure content play. The stock has moved from a 52-week low under $6 to a high near $17, including a 9 percent single-day move last month on reports it was courting European buyers.

The sequel pipeline is already dated. A second Michael is targeting production at the end of this year or early next, with release at the end of calendar 2027 or in the first half of 2028. A Housemaid sequel is in development, Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens in November, and Mel Gibson's The Resurrection of the Christ Part One arrives in 2027.
The Facts
  • Fiscal Q1 total revenue $777 million, up nearly 50 percent, ahead of Wall Street. Adjusted net income from continuing operations $18.9 million, or $0.06 per share. Net loss $29 million, narrowed from $107 million.
  • Motion picture revenue $587 million, more than double the prior year; segment profit $105 million, a Q1 record.
  • Television production revenue $189 million and profit $10.2 million, both down on episodic delivery timing. Scripted deliveries expected to double in fiscal 2028 from fiscal 2027.
  • Trailing 12-month library revenue $987 million.
  • Michael has grossed $1.013 billion worldwide and is the highest-grossing biopic ever.
  • Shares rose 2.4 percent to $13.26 in late trading, against a 52-week range from under $6 to near $17.
  • CEO Jon Feltheimer: "As we continue to execute our franchise strategy across a deep portfolio of branded intellectual properties, generate increased visibility and stability from our film and television library, and benefit from continued improvement in our operating environment, we are positioned to deliver strong growth in fiscal 2027 and beyond."
  • Brittany Snow recently joined Paul Feig's The Housemaid's Secret opposite Sydney Sweeney, Kirsten Dunst and Paul Anthony Kelly.
  • Feltheimer separately endorsed the Paramount-WBD merger, saying "uncertainty is the worst."

Microdrama Revenue Outside China Hits $3.6 Billion and ReelShort Turns Its First Profit
Unit EconomicsReelShort went from $97 million of revenue in 2023 to a projected $1.05 billion this year, and Media Partners Asia expects the U.S. market alone to reach $3.7 billion by 2031.
CEO Summary
Media Partners Asia projects that ReelShort will generate $1.05 billion of revenue in 2026, up 34 percent, and post its first meaningful profit at scale, at roughly $40 million net. The firm sizes microdrama revenue outside China at $3.6 billion this year, up from $2.7 billion in 2025, reaching $9.5 billion by 2031 at a 21 percent compound annual growth rate. The margin story is marketing: user acquisition falls from just over half of revenue in 2025 to under 45 percent by 2028, with each percentage point worth about $10.5 million of EBITDA.
Key Takeaways
  • Unit Economics: In a subscription-first video business, the franchise is a marketing asset before it is a content asset, because sequels acquire the next cohort without paid media.
  • Distribution: Carrier bundling beats paid social on acquisition cost, which makes telco partnerships the cheapest route to scale in emerging markets.
  • Monetization: Moving billing off app stores and adding advertising converts the same revenue into materially more earnings, since neither line carries a platform commission.
Why It's Happening
MPA attributes the falling acquisition cost to five things: hit franchises and their sequels drawing audiences without paid support and supplying the advertising creative; telco and local partnerships adding subscribers cheaply; billing shifting to ReelShort's own web store; better creative testing; and a maturing paid-social auction after years of new entrants bidding prices up.

The revenue mix explains the rest. Consumer payments and subscriptions are 85 to 90 percent of revenue across the forecast, with subscriptions already 60 to 70 percent of viewer spend. Advertising reaches about 15 percent of revenue by 2028, and because it carries no app-store commission MPA estimates 65 to 70 cents of every ad dollar reaches earnings. Together with direct web billing, those two shifts account for close to half the projected margin expansion.

The upside case is geographic. Latin America and Asia Pacific are roughly three in five of an estimated 70 million global monthly users but generate under a fifth of revenue, while North America delivers 59 percent on a much smaller base.
The Facts
  • ReelShort revenue: $97 million (2023), $400 million (2024), $785 million (2025), a projected $1.05 billion (2026). After an estimated $12 million net loss last year, MPA projects $63 million EBITDA and about $40 million net profit in 2026, rising to $306 million EBITDA at an 18 percent margin and $225 million net profit by 2028 on $1.7 billion of revenue.
  • Outside-China microdrama: $2.7 billion (2025), $3.6 billion (2026), $9.5 billion (2031), a 21 percent CAGR. U.S. from $1.5 billion to $3.7 billion; Asia Pacific ex-China tripling to $2.4 billion.
  • User acquisition and marketing: just over 50 percent of revenue in 2025 to under 45 percent by 2028; each point worth roughly $10.5 million of EBITDA.
  • Market share: ReelShort 29 percent, DramaBox 21 percent, DramaWave 13 percent, NetShort 10 percent, GoodShort 6 percent, remainder across roughly 300 smaller apps.
  • Asia contributes 12 percent of ReelShort revenue in 2026, rising to about $200 million and 14 percent in 2027. A Thailand AIS partnership has run since April; Indonesia and Philippines telco deals are expected by end of 2026; Japan and Korea production and distribution deals, including a Showbox co-production, launch in Q4.
  • MPA CEO Vivek Couto: "Microdrama has begun to be an earnings story rather than a growth story. ... What decides the next phase is distribution and unit economics, not necessarily content volume."
  • Lead analyst Myat Pan Phyu: "User acquisition is the swing factor. It falls from 55% of revenue in 2025 to 44% by 2028 on our model."
  • ReelShort was founded in 2022 by Crazy Maple Studio, has surpassed 286 million downloads and employs more than 1,600 staff plus freelance creators and production partners.

Apple passed on David E. Kelley's Bonfire of the Vanities after reading the pilot
Buyer BehaviorKelley already has two series at Apple, both renewed for second seasons, and the script still did not clear. A source on the pass: "Apple doesn't make that much, and the bar keeps getting higher."
CEO Summary
Apple TV has passed on a series adaptation of Tom Wolfe's "The Bonfire of the Vanities" from David E. Kelley and director Matt Reeves, in development since April, after executives read Kelley's pilot script. It would have been Kelley's third series at the streamer alongside "Margo's Got Money Troubles" and "Presumed Innocent," both renewed. The pass came inside a wider development-roster review that cut numerous scripts after head of development Matt Cherniss' U.S. team absorbed originals previously overseen by departed head of international Morgan Wandell. Kelley and Warner Bros. Television are shopping the project.
Key Takeaways
  • Buyer Behavior: At a buyer that commissions few originals, an incumbent relationship buys consideration and nothing more, so a second and third series with the same shop are not a floor.
  • Org Structure: When a buyer merges two development pipelines into one team, the pass rate rises before any creative judgment is applied, and existing projects get re-reviewed against a shorter slate.
  • IP Valuation: Prestige source material with a documented record of failed adaptations is priced on its reputation rather than its results, which is a recurring way rights get overvalued.
Why It's Happening
Apple TV runs a deliberately curated slate, and its capacity just contracted structurally. Morgan Wandell, one of the first hires under Zack Van Amburg and Jamie Erlicht in 2017, left in May to start his own production company. His international originals moved under Cherniss' U.S. team, and the combined roster was reviewed with numerous scripts cut in the same pass. "Bonfire" was one of several, not a singular judgment.

The material also carries a record. Warners' 1990 film, with Tom Hanks, Bruce Willis and Melanie Griffith, cost $47 million and grossed under $16 million domestically. Chuck Lorre and Warners set up a limited series at Amazon in 2016 that never moved past development. This is the third attempt to stall.
The Facts

Paramount pushed its WBD debt exchange deadline for the seventh time since June
Deal TimingSeven extensions since June 12, now to Aug. 21. As of Aug. 6, 65.43% of the tender notes and 76.04% of the exchange notes were tendered, and holders can still withdraw at any time.
CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance extended the expiration dates on its cash tender offers and note exchange offers for Warner Bros. Discovery debt to Aug. 21, 2026, the seventh such extension since June 12. The offers cover notes issued by Discovery Global Holdings and Discovery Communications, and Paramount says it expects to keep extending until settlement can occur on or promptly after the acquisition closes. As of Aug. 6, roughly 65.43% of tender offer notes and 76.04% of exchange offer notes had been validly tendered, figures Paramount says are not representative of final results.
Key Takeaways
  • Deal Timing: An acquirer running acquisition-conditioned debt offers publishes a higher-frequency read on its own closing timeline than any earnings call provides, because the offers must be rolled every time the close slips.
  • Creditor Leverage: When tenders carry open withdrawal rights against an uncertain close, the debt holders keep optionality the acquirer has already surrendered, and that asymmetry widens with every extension.
  • Transaction Cost: Regulatory and litigation delay in a leveraged acquisition converts into recurring rollover administration, which is a cost the buyer absorbs and the target does not.

The tender and exchange offers cannot settle before the acquisition does, so the expiration date is effectively a proxy for the expected closing date. Paramount states the linkage outright: it anticipates extending until settlement would fall on or promptly following the closing date. Settlement is currently anticipated in the third quarter of 2026.

The delay is not coming from every direction. The UK Competition and Markets Authority approved the acquisition on Aug. 6, one day before this extension, and Paramount reported Q2 results on Aug. 4. PSKY traded at $9.19 on the day, up 1.43%.

Disney's trading card revenue has quadrupled since 2023
Franchise ValueDisney licensing will move about $63 billion in product this year, the most of any company License Global tracks, and the fastest-growing piece of it is cards. Consumer Products moves into the Entertainment division later this year.
CEO Summary
Disney executives told The Hollywood Reporter that the company's trading card revenue has quadrupled since 2023, inside a category some analysts size at $50 billion annually. Disney runs the business through licensees: Topps for Topps Chrome Disney, Topps Chrome Marvel and Star Wars Masterworks, Ravensburger for Disney Lorcana, and Hasbro for Marvel and Spider-Man editions of Magic: The Gathering. Later this year Disney Consumer Products leaves the Experiences division and joins Entertainment, and DCP already engages the studios early so new characters can be built into card products.
Key Takeaways
  • Franchise Value: The fastest-growing category in the largest licensing business in the world requires no new release, because a deep character library monetizes against collecting behavior rather than a release calendar.
  • Org Design: Moving a consumer-products group next to the content creators converts merchandising from a downstream extraction into a design input at the character-development stage.
  • Talent Economics: When signatures and screen-used wardrobe are sold as inserts, an individual's autograph and a production's physical materials become recurring revenue lines, which makes reservation of those rights a live deal term.
Why It's Happening
Cards solve a problem that toys and apparel cannot. Divya Dalal, VP of global hardlines at Disney Consumer Products, points to the price ladder: a doll's cost is fixed by materials and complexity, while a card program can run from a five-card pack to a thousand-dollar collectible off the same art. That lets one property serve every income level in every market, continuously.

The demographic range is the second reason. Dalal: "the same card could be appealing to a seven year old, a 37 year old, or a 67 year old, and that's really rare." Toys sort by age; nostalgia does not.

The flywheel is already being run across divisions: Lorcana starter packs in hotel gift shops, a Lorcana passport activation at the Epcot festival, and cards with cut pieces of screen-used costume inserted into packs.
The Facts
  • Disney trading card revenue has quadrupled since 2023. Analysts size the overall market at roughly $50 billion annually.
  • Disney products will generate about $63 billion in sales this year per License Global, the most of any company tracked; Authentic Brands Group is second at $36 billion.
  • Partners: Topps (Topps Chrome Disney, Topps Chrome Marvel, Star Wars Masterworks), Ravensburger (Disney Lorcana), Hasbro (Marvel and Spider-Man Magic: The Gathering).
  • Disney Consumer Products moves from Experiences into Entertainment later this year.
  • David Leiner, president of Trading Cards for Topps: "they're not just entertainment brands, they're multi-generational storytelling engines."
  • Ryan Reynolds bought a Hugh Jackman-signed Wolverine card at Fanatics Fest last month for $800 plus a doodled Dogpool card, down from a $1,000 ask.

Chinese AI Models Are Still Generating 'The Office' Clips While Three Studios Sue
Territorial RightsMiniMax withheld Hailuo 3 from the U.S. over the pending Disney, Universal and Warner Bros. suit, and a U.S. venture investor generated a Dwight-and-Jim clip through an aggregator on MiniMax's own servers.
CEO Summary
MiniMax released Hailuo 3 this week without direct availability in the U.S. or European Union, citing "ongoing copyright-related legal proceedings specifically concerning generative video AI." Andreessen Horowitz partner Justine Moore then generated a recognizable clip of Dwight and Jim from The Office using a simple H3 prompt through Krea, an aggregator, with the prompt routing back through MiniMax's servers. Separately, the startup VN.ai produced bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear through ByteDance's Seedream 5.0 via a third-party API.
Key Takeaways
  • Territorial Rights: Withholding a model from a market is not an infringement control when aggregators and third-party APIs reach the same servers.
  • Enforcement: Litigation is producing compliance on the parts a company can be publicly attributed for, not on what its models output.
  • Audit: Independent red-team research is becoming the evidentiary layer for IP claims, which makes testability something rights agreements will need to specify.
Why It's Happening
The two Chinese model families behaved differently and the difference is instructive. ByteDance's Seedance 2.5 has not been used to reproduce Hollywood IP at the scale Seedance 2.0 was, which followed cease-and-desist letters from Netflix, Disney and others over the viral Tom Cruise versus Brad Pitt deepfake. So guardrails work when a company builds them.

But ByteDance's image model, Seedream 5.0, still produced recognizable characters under mild red teaming. VN.ai found that prompts for high-profile characters were often denied, and that asking for exact pixel sizes defeated the denial. It reached the model through a third-party API where safeguards may be weaker than on ByteDance's own service. Compliance is being applied per model and per access path, not per company.

MiniMax, meanwhile, quietly scrubbed the promotional Deadpool, Wolverine and Joker videos the studios cited in their complaint, while denying the allegations.
The Facts
  • MiniMax released Hailuo 3 (H3) this week; it is not directly available in the U.S. or EU but has gone viral outside China through third-party access.
  • Justine Moore, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, generated a clip of Dwight and Jim from The Office with a simple H3 text prompt in Krea. The prompt routed through MiniMax's servers.
  • Disney, Universal and Warner Bros. allege in their suit that Hailuo "pirates and plunders copyrighted works on a massive scale," citing MiniMax's own YouTube promotion using Deadpool, Wolverine and The Joker videos. Those videos have been removed. MiniMax denies the allegations and did not respond to a request for comment.
  • At launch, a MiniMax representative said the full model would not be available in the U.S. because of "ongoing copyright-related legal proceedings specifically concerning generative video AI."
  • ByteDance released Seedance 2.5 the same week without comparable IP reproduction. Seedance 2.0 had produced the viral Tom Cruise versus Brad Pitt deepfake, drawing cease-and-desist letters from Netflix, Disney and others.
  • VN.ai generated bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear through Seedream 5.0 via a third-party API, per research reports seen by Deadline. Character prompts were often denied; specifying exact pixel sizes produced a recognizable Buzz Lightyear.
  • ByteDance statement: "ByteDance launches models with safeguards designed to prevent unauthorized use of intellectual property, and continually works to expand and strengthen these in collaboration with rightsholders and creative communities."
  • U.S. studios and the Motion Picture Association were approached for comment.

Versant Raised Guidance in Its Second Quarter as a Standalone Cable Company
Cable EconomicsAdvertising revenue fell just under 1 percent, against a 13 percent drop in the same quarter a year earlier, and the company raised full-year guidance to as much as $6.45 billion.
CEO Summary
Versant, the cable-focused NBCUniversal spinoff running CNBC, MS NOW, USA and Golf Channel, reported June-quarter revenue of $1.64 billion, down 3.8 percent. Linear distribution fell 6.3 percent to $954 million while platforms revenue excluding the divested SportsEngine rose 9.3 percent to $225 million, which the CFO called the fastest-growing part of the group. Net income fell 30 percent to $211 million on separation costs, and adjusted EBITDA fell 9 percent to $624 million, but the company raised full-year 2026 guidance to $6.2 billion to $6.45 billion of revenue and $1.9 billion to $2.05 billion of adjusted EBITDA.
Key Takeaways
  • Cable Economics: Distribution revenue and advertising revenue are decoupling at legacy networks, and only the first is still falling at pace.
  • Sports Rights: Rights are now being underwritten for dual-window use, with the same package serving a pay-TV tier and a free ad-supported one.
  • Buyer Landscape: A spun-off legacy asset with permission to reinvest becomes an active buyer again, which restores a counterparty most sellers had written off.
Why It's Happening
The ad number is the one that changed. A 0.6 percent decline against a 13 percent decline the prior year is the difference between a business in freefall and one finding a floor, and it is happening while linear distribution keeps eroding with the subscriber base. Versant is spending the difference on distribution rather than defending the old one: direct-to-consumer extensions for CNBC and MS NOW, and a rebuilt Fandango aimed at Tubi, Pluto and Roku Channel.

Mark Lazarus described Fandango as a single-brand path from buying a film to watching free at home, with Rotten Tomatoes as the discovery layer. The Bundesliga acquisition follows the same double-use logic: "600 or 700 hours of live sports" bought to serve pay-TV customers premium matches on USA and to create a free AVOD marketplace at the same time.
The Facts
  • Q2 revenue $1.64 billion, down 3.8 percent from $1.7 billion.
  • Linear distribution down 6.3 percent to $954 million. Advertising $423 million, down just under 1 percent, against a 13 percent decline in the year-earlier quarter. Content licensing unchanged at $43 million.
  • Platforms revenue up 0.8 percent to $212 million; excluding SportsEngine, up 9.3 percent to $225 million. CFO and COO Anand Kini called platforms the "fastest growing part" of the group, citing Fandango and GolfNow.
  • Net income attributable to Versant down 30 percent to $211 million on lower revenue and one-time separation costs including higher tax expenses after the SportsEngine divestiture. Adjusted EBITDA down 9 percent to $624 million.
  • Full-year 2026 guidance raised: revenue $6.2 billion to $6.45 billion, adjusted EBITDA $1.9 billion to $2.05 billion.
  • Lazarus: "AVOD is one of the fastest growing areas in media, and we enjoy clear advantages from the well known Fandango brand: broad, connected TV distribution, rich first-party data and unique and exclusive content."
  • On Bundesliga: "a significant number of hours — 600 or 700 hours of live sports — and be able to both serve our pay TV customers with premium matches on USA and create a new marketplace for ourselves in free AVOD."
  • MS NOW posted a seventh consecutive month of year-over-year audience growth and was the No. 1 news organization on YouTube in June. CNBC delivered its highest-rated quarter in more than five years.

Movies and Music Added 9,900 Jobs in July While the U.S. Economy Lost 23,000
Production CapacityBroadcasting and content providers shed 1,500 jobs in the same month, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics revised 103,000 jobs out of its May and June estimates.
CEO Summary
The U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July against analyst estimates of a gain as large as 100,000, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics revised prior months down by a combined 103,000. Employment in movies and music rose by 9,900 to 332,700, reversing some earlier declines, while broadcasting and content providers fell by 1,500 to 335,800. Unemployment edged down to 4.1 percent, a figure the report attributes partly to people leaving the labor force.
Key Takeaways
  • Production Capacity: Employment in production is now moving independently of the broader labor market, which makes below-the-line availability a sector question rather than a macro one.
  • Distribution: Headcount is following where content money is actually spent, not where it is reported, with production adding and legacy distribution shedding in the same month.
  • Labor Leverage: Recovering headcount in an environment of below-inflation wage growth is a weak bargaining position, because volume returning is not the same as pricing power returning.
Why It's Happening
Wage growth is the constraint. Average hourly earnings moved two cents to $37.62 and are up 3.2 percent over the past year, which Mark Zandi of Moody's Analytics called "below the rate of inflation, a clear tell that the job market is operating below full-employment despite the low unemployment rate." He also noted hours worked are "low and are slumping lower."

Employers are citing tariffs and the war in Iran as reasons for caution. Heather Long of Navy Federal called the report "bleak" and wrote that "the labor market is stalling again." A single month of production gains inside that backdrop is a real signal about sector demand and a weak one about compensation.
The Facts
  • U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July. Analysts had estimated a gain of as much as 100,000.
  • Movies and music employment rose 9,900 to 332,700. Broadcasting and content providers fell 1,500 to 335,800.
  • Unemployment fell slightly to 4.1 percent, affected by labor-force exits.
  • Declines in local government education and retail trade. Health care added 22,000 positions, at a slower pace than previous months.
  • May and June estimates revised down by a combined 103,000.
  • Average hourly earnings changed by two cents to $37.62, up 3.2 percent year over year.
  • Heather Long, chief economist, Navy Federal: "The Fed's job just got a lot harder. The labor market is stalling again. Many industries shedding jobs or flat."
  • Mark Zandi, chief economist, Moody's Analytics: "There's no sugar coating the overarching message in the July jobs report – the economy is struggling." Job growth is "at a virtual standstill, and concentrated in a few sectors."

Roku gave a 24/7 FAST channel to an AI startup that produced none of it itself
DistributionFairground launched in 2025, did not make the programming itself, and is developing AI-generated Robin Hood and Dracula adaptations. Roku carried it alongside three catalog channels the same week.
CEO Summary
Roku added four channels this week: catalog feeds for "Mad TV," "Whose Line Is It Anyway?" and Black sitcoms, plus Fairground AI Creator TV, a 24/7 stream of entirely AI-generated content from Colin Petrie-Norris' startup Fairground. The programming comes from creators partnered with Fairground rather than from Fairground itself, and has no consistent theme or genre. Fairground launched in 2025 and is reportedly developing AI-generated adaptations of Robin Hood and Dracula.
Key Takeaways
  • Distribution: Channel position, not programming, was always the scarce resource in free ad-supported streaming, and it is now cheap enough to grant to content with no production cost basis.
  • Competitive Set: Producers of conventional programming are now competing for the same shelf space against suppliers who committed no capital at any point in the chain.
  • Rights Economics: The first commercial AI content businesses are forming around public domain material, which is where they will stay until AI licensing terms make owned IP affordable to them.
Why It's Happening
A platform carrying a channel that costs nothing to license can monetize even weak engagement, because the advertising inventory is incremental and the content acquisition cost is effectively zero. That math does not require the programming to be good, only to exist continuously.

The supply chain shows where the value is being captured. Fairground did not produce the content; partnered creators did, Fairground aggregated it, and Roku carried it. The aggregation layer between creator and platform is the new position, and it is where the economics of the category will be set.

Fairground's own development slate points the same direction: Robin Hood and Dracula are both public domain.
The Facts
  • Four new Roku channels this week: "Mad TV," "Whose Line Is It Anyway?," a Black sitcoms feed, and Fairground AI Creator TV.

LightShed Says Paramount Must Sell Off Part of Warner Before March or Lose the Deal and $7 Billion
Deal TimingTrial runs March 2 to 19, 2027, briefs are due April 5, and the merger agreement dies June 4 with a $7 billion break fee. Paramount had asked for a November trial.
CEO Summary
LightShed Partners argued this morning that Paramount Skydance must settle the state antitrust suits before trial or lose Warner Bros. Discovery outright, because the calendar no longer allows an appeal. Trial is set for March 2 to 19, 2027, post-trial briefs are due April 5, and the merger agreement expires June 4, 2027, at which point Paramount owes a $7 billion break fee that the Ellison family would fund by buying equity at $16 per share. Paramount stock traded at $9.12 Thursday morning. LightShed's proposed remedies include selling one of the two studio lots along with franchise IP such as Harry Potter, DC and Dune, or shedding the Turner networks including TBS, TNT and CNN.
Key Takeaways
  • Deal Timing: A merger with a fixed outside date and a long litigation tail is decided by the calendar, not the merits, because a buyer who cannot appeal within the window has already lost whatever the court eventually says.
  • Break Fees: A break fee large enough to fund the seller's standalone plan stops being compensation and becomes the seller's preferred outcome, which removes the buyer's ability to wait.
  • Franchise Assets: Top-tier franchise IP is the currency of last resort in a contested deal, which means the assets a buyer swore it would never sell are the first ones priced when closing is at risk.
Why It's Happening
The judge gave Paramount a March trial rather than the November date it requested, and there is no fixed deadline for a ruling once post-trial briefs land on April 5. Any decision against Paramount arriving between April and June leaves no appellate runway before the agreement lapses. Paramount's former lead trial counsel had publicly described appealing to the Ninth Circuit or the Supreme Court, which assumes a seller willing to wait; LightShed's view is that a seller collecting $7 billion and regaining the freedom to split itself has no reason to.

The remedy menu is constrained on both sides. Behavioral fixes such as a CNN editorial oversight board do not reduce the market share concentration the complaints are built on. Structural fixes do, but the linear networks would sell at a fraction of what Paramount is paying: Disney's 50% of A&E Networks went to Hearst at under 3.5x EV/EBITDA, and those networks carried neither sports nor news.
The Facts
  • Trial: March 2 to 19, 2027, before Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin. Post-trial briefs due April 5, 2027. Paramount had proposed November 2026.
  • Merger agreement expiration: June 4, 2027. Break fee: $7 billion.
  • Break fee funding per LightShed: Ellison family contributes $7 billion cash to Paramount for equity at $16 per share. PSKY traded at $9.12 on Thursday morning.
  • Plaintiffs: 12 state attorneys general plus the Writers Guild of America. California AG Rob Bonta has signaled he wants the deal blocked rather than settled.
  • Studio remedy floated: sell one of the two lots, its theatrical distribution infrastructure, franchise IP including Harry Potter, DC Comics and Dune, plus a share of the library.
  • Networks remedy floated: shed the Turner networks (TBS, TNT, CNN), leaving Paramount acquiring only Discovery Global Networks out of roughly 50 cable networks.
  • Comparable cited: Disney sold its 50% of A&E Networks to Hearst at under 3.5x EV/EBITDA.
  • If the deal terminates, LightShed expects WBD to split into Warner Bros. studio/HBO and Discovery Global Networks, and names Netflix and a post-split NBCUniversal as possible buyers.

The FCC Repealed the Broadcast Ownership Cap on a 2-1 Vote and Its Own Democrat Called It Unlawful
RegulationAnna Gomez cited three Republicans, including the former House Majority Leader who negotiated the 39 percent cap, saying only Congress can change it. Sinclair's CEO says he will transact as soon as the order hits the Federal Register.
CEO Summary
The FCC voted 2-1 along party lines Thursday to eliminate the 39% national cap on the share of U.S. television households a single station owner may reach. Chairman Brendan Carr argued broadcasters are constrained by anachronistic rules while Google, Netflix, Meta and Amazon reach the world unimpeded. Commissioner Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat, called the move "unlawful on its face" because Congress set the cap in 2012, citing agreement from former FCC Commissioner Mike O'Rielly, former House Majority Leader Tom DeLay and Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz. Two station-group deals sit behind the change: Nexstar-Tegna, which would reach 80% of U.S. households and is already enjoined by eight state attorneys general, and a revived Sinclair-Scripps.
Key Takeaways
  • Regulation: A deregulatory order that the regulator's own dissent and three of the governing party's own authorities call unlawful is a timing window, not a settled rule, and the firms it benefits will race to close transactions inside it rather than wait for the courts.
  • Antitrust Venue: State attorneys general have become the operative antitrust check on media consolidation, so federal permission to do a deal is no longer the same thing as the ability to do it.
  • Buyer Concentration: When a distribution tier consolidates to a handful of owners covering most of a market, sellers into that tier lose price discovery before they lose buyers, because standardized terms arrive ahead of the final merger.
Why It's Happening
The cap traces to radio ownership rules from the 1940s and was fixed at 39% of national household reach by Congress in 2012. Carr's argument is one of competitive parity: station groups cannot reach scale while platforms face no equivalent limit, and he draws an explicit parallel to local newspapers, whose collapse he attributes partly to FCC cross-ownership restrictions maintained in the name of localism.

The legal exposure is unusually well telegraphed. Gomez named three Republicans on the record against the commission's authority, including the legislator who negotiated the 39% compromise and says Congress wrote it into statute specifically to keep the FCC from touching it. Sinclair CEO Chris Ripley told analysts he "fully expects people to challenge this order," then said the company will be able to transact "shortly after the vote happens as soon as it gets into the federal registry." That sequence, expect a challenge and move anyway, is the strategy.
The Facts
  • Vote was 2-1: Carr and Republican commissioner Olivia Trusty for repeal; Gomez against.
  • The cap removed is 39% of reach among U.S. TV households, set by Congress in 2012. Its origins are in 1940s radio ownership regulation.
  • Gomez: "The FCC's decision to eliminate the 39% national audience reach cap is unlawful on its face. Congress set this cap in federal law, and only Congress can change it."
  • Gomez cited O'Rielly ("unequivocal that the FCC lacks authority"), DeLay (Congress wrote the cap to keep the FCC from changing it) and Cruz (skeptical a change can be made absent an act of Congress).
  • Carr: "Repealing the national cap will provide essential relief for local broadcasters by restoring a healthy counterbalance to the growing leverage of national programmers."

Warner Bros. Discovery Studio Earnings Fell 89 Percent and Supergirl Is the Worst DC Release Since Catwoman
Sports RightsOne year without the NBA took 22 percent of WBD's advertising revenue, $1.7 billion for the quarter, while streaming EBITDA rose 75 percent to $512 million.
CEO Summary
Warner Bros. Discovery reported Q2 revenue down 11% to $8.7 billion against $9.2 billion expected, with diluted EPS of 6 cents beating an expected 10-cent loss. The studio division fell hardest: revenue down 39% to $2.3 billion and adjusted EBITDA down 89% to $96 million, with Supergirl grossing $126 million worldwide, the lowest for any DC release since Catwoman in 2004. Streaming went the other way, revenue up 10% to $3.1 billion and EBITDA up 75% to $512 million, while total advertising fell 22% to $1.7 billion on the absence of the NBA.
Key Takeaways
  • Sports Rights: Losing a marquee league does not dent a network's advertising business, it resets it, which means live sports rights are priced against the whole ad line rather than the programming block they fill.
  • Studio Economics: A film division's earnings are a slate outcome, not a business trend, so a company whose subscription line compounds and whose theatrical line swings will allocate capital toward the one that compounds.
  • Franchise Value: A franchise underperforms long before the studio admits it has, because publicly conceding a strategy shift devalues everything still in development under that strategy.
Why It's Happening
The year-ago studio quarter carried A Minecraft Movie, Sinners and Final Destination Bloodlines. This one carried Supergirl. That is the entire 39% revenue decline and most of the 89% EBITDA decline, which is why studio comparisons are close to meaningless as a read on management and very meaningful as a read on volatility.

The advertising line is structural rather than cyclical. WBD carried the NBA for nearly 40 years and did not extend; NBCUniversal took the primary-partner position. Global Linear Networks revenue fell 17% to $3.99 billion, though adjusted EBITDA fell only 4% to $1.4 billion, which says the cost base came down alongside the rights.

Streaming absorbed the difference. HBO Max expanded into key international territories during the quarter and was paced by Euphoria, House of the Dragon, Hacks and The Pitt.
The Facts
  • Total revenue: $8.7 billion, down 11%. Analyst consensus: $9.2 billion. Diluted EPS: 6 cents, versus an expected loss of 10 cents.
  • Studio: revenue $2.3 billion, down 39%. Adjusted EBITDA $96 million, down 89%.
  • Supergirl: $126 million worldwide, lowest DC release since Catwoman (2004).
  • Streaming: revenue $3.1 billion, up 10%. EBITDA $512 million, up 75%.
  • Total advertising: $1.7 billion, down 22%.
  • Global Linear Networks: revenue $3.99 billion, down 17%. Adjusted EBITDA $1.4 billion, down 4%.
  • TheWrap reported quarterly profit down 91%.
  • Context: the $110 billion Paramount merger is in legal limbo, with 12 state attorneys general and the WGA suing to block and trial set for March 2027.
  • David Zaslav said Thursday the Superman sequel looks "amazing," that there is no DC strategy shift after Supergirl, and that staff are "working extremely hard" through the merger uncertainty.

Fox Refuses to Reopen Its NFL Contract and Tells the League Nothing Changes Until 2030
Rights PricingThe NFL wrote an opt-out into all its 11-year pacts so it could reprice mid-term. Lachlan Murdoch told investors Fox "will not be making any amendments" before 2030.
CEO Summary
Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch told investors Thursday that Fox will not amend its current NFL rights deal, which runs through the 2029 season, despite the league seeking to invoke an opt-out clause written into the 11-year contracts it signed with all of its media partners to reset terms to market. The NFL has been holding the same conversation with Amazon, Disney, NBCUniversal and CBS. Murdoch said the relationship remains "incredibly positive" and that Fox sees "a clear path forward" after 2029.
Key Takeaways
  • Rights Pricing: A mid-term repricing clause is worth only what the counterparty will engage with, so a seller that wants a guaranteed reset needs an automatic mechanism, not an option to reopen talks.
  • Leverage: Buyer leverage in premium live rights returns when the buyers' underlying businesses shrink faster than the property appreciates, because paying more today against declining revenue is a worse trade than absorbing relationship risk.
  • Ownership: A league that takes an equity position in one of its distributors changes its own negotiating posture with the others, since it now sits on both sides of the same market.
Why It's Happening
The league wrote the opt-out precisely because live sports is the last category reliably delivering the audiences advertisers and distributors want, and the value of those deals keeps compounding. The distributors' problem is the other side of the ledger: streaming has eroded the traditional television business, and advertising and distribution revenue are both in general decline. Paying a higher fee now, against revenue that is falling now, is a worse trade for Fox than holding a below-market rate for three more years and repricing in 2029.

The comparison doing the most work is NBC's. It is believed to be paying more for its current NBA rights than for Sunday Night Football, which means the benchmark for the next NFL negotiation was set by a different league's auction rather than by the NFL's own value.
The Facts
  • Fox's NFL deal runs through the end of the 2029 season. Murdoch: "We don't see any changes" until 2030; the company "will not be making any amendments."
  • The opt-out clause sits in the 11-year pacts the NFL struck with all of its media partners, allowing terms to be updated to market levels.
  • The league is also in discussions with Amazon, Disney, NBCUniversal and CBS.
  • NBC is believed to be paying more for its current NBA rights than for Sunday Night Football.
  • The NFL has held what are believed to be serious talks with Paramount Skydance about the CBS Sunday-afternoon package; the Redstone-to-Ellison change of control gave the league the right to reopen.
  • The NFL cannot exercise an opt-out on Disney's Monday Night Football deal until after 2030. A recent transaction made the NFL a minority owner of ESPN in exchange for control of NFL Network and other league media assets.
  • Disney announced Wednesday it had sold out all commercial inventory for its 2027 Super Bowl LXI broadcast, months earlier than networks typically disclose.
  • Murdoch praised a recent transaction giving Fox rights to NFL games via its Mexican properties.
  • The NFL, CBS Sports, NBC Sports and Prime Video sports did not comment.

YouTube Is Taking Peacock's Library as Brand-Safety Insurance Against Its Own AI Slop
Brand SafetyA new YouTube account was served 500 Shorts and 21 percent were pure AI slop. Peacock's NFL games, Bravo originals and Law & Order now sit inside YouTube Premium at no extra charge.
CEO Summary
NBCUniversal has placed all ad-supported Peacock Premium content, including NFL games, Bravo originals and Law & Order, inside YouTube Premium at no additional charge for now, with terms undisclosed. Peacock has roughly 48 million subscribers against an estimated 125 million for YouTube Premium worldwide, but Antenna measured Peacock churn at 7% in June, three points above the weighted average. Wolfe Research's Peter Supino called the deal a possible step toward NBCUniversal exiting retail streaming, while Puck argues YouTube's motive is advertiser confidence ahead of a generative-AI content surge.
Key Takeaways
  • Brand Safety: Premium library content has acquired a second buyer motive beyond audience, which means a platform facing an AI content surge will pay for professionally produced programming as inventory insurance rather than as a hit.
  • Distribution: A streamer with high churn and no owned hits will trade the customer relationship for placement inside an app people already open, because discovery is worth more to it than direct ownership.
  • Ad Pricing: Perceived AI generation carries a measurable cost, so platforms carrying generative content will spend on human-made programming defensively, not creatively.
Why It's Happening
The measured harm is specific. A Kapwing study created a fresh YouTube account and found 21% of the first 500 Shorts served were pure AI slop, with another 33% falling into the "brainrot" category. A Raptive study found trust drops roughly 50% when content is perceived as AI generated, and that perception erodes an ad's premium impact by 17%. YouTube lived through the 2017 "adpocalypse," when an investigation into ads beside extremist content drove hundreds of advertisers away, and it now carries NFL Sunday Ticket and will air the Oscars starting in 2029. It has permanently removed 16 channels with a combined 35 million subscribers and 4.7 billion lifetime views.

On the Peacock side the math is churn and cost. Peacock carries its share of a $2.5 billion annual NBA deal, has no sizable hit outside Love Island, and turned profitable only last quarter. Comcast's co-CEOs have described the streaming strategy as a return to the company's wholesale roots, which makes moving the audience into someone else's app a strategy rather than a retreat.
The Facts
  • Deal: all ad-supported Peacock Premium content, including NFL games, Bravo originals and Law & Order, placed on YouTube Premium at no extra charge for now. Financial terms undisclosed.
  • Scale: Peacock about 48 million subscribers. YouTube Premium estimated at 125 million worldwide including YouTube Music, with 10 to 20 million in the U.S.
  • Churn: Antenna estimates Peacock at 7% in June, about three points above the weighted average.
  • Cost base: Peacock carries part of NBCU's $2.5 billion annual NBA deal. It converted to profitability last quarter.
  • Ad-free subscribers still pay for Peacock Premium Plus.
  • Wolfe Research's Peter Supino: the deal "could be a step towards NBCUniversal exiting the retail streaming business in order to shed costs," with a risk that some customers cancel more lucrative YouTube TV subscriptions.
  • Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler: YouTube's subscription business "is growing faster than ads, particularly driven by YouTube Music and Premium."
  • YouTube AI policy: VP of trust and safety Matt Halprin last month named three non-monetizable categories, generic or repetitive content, "unsatisfying" content, and AI personas discussing sensitive topics.
  • Research: Kapwing, 21% of first 500 Shorts pure AI slop plus 33% "brainrot." Raptive, trust down about 50% on perceived AI generation, ad premium impact down 17%.

CEO Summary
The UK cleared Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. on both competition and public interest grounds. The Competition and Markets Authority found no competition issues requiring intervention after examining theatrical film distribution, linear children's TV channels and subscription VOD supply, and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy declined to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice in exchange for legally binding behavioral commitments. Paramount immediately cited the ruling against the US state attorneys general, whose case goes to trial in March 2027. The European Commission approved the deal on July 22.
Key Takeaways
  • Regulation: Two regulators reviewing one transaction reach opposite conclusions when they define the market differently, so an international clearance is a talking point in a domestic case rather than evidence in it.
  • Remedies: Content-supply obligations are becoming the price of clearance for cross-border media deals, which protects local production spend while leaving market structure entirely intact.
  • Opportunity: A behavioral remedy converts a merger approval into committed programming spend, which makes regulatory review a live funding event for producers in the protected categories.
Why It's Happening
The CMA's question was whether the combined company would dominate British theatrical distribution, children's linear channels or subscription VOD. It concluded no. The California complaint is built on domestic market share under a narrower market definition, which is why Paramount's spokesperson called those definitions "misguided and gerrymandered" within hours of the UK decision.

The commitments are worth reading as a set, because every one of them is behavioral: editorial separation of linear from on-demand, ring-fenced commissioning obligations at Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network, editorial independence for Channel 5 News from CBS News and CNN International, archive access for licensees on standard commercial terms, and increased Channel 5 funding for news, children's programming and drama. Behavioral is precisely the remedy category the California plaintiffs have signaled they will not accept.
The Facts

  • Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy declined to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice.
  • Commitments: no consolidation of UK linear channels with on-demand services, distinct editorial identity retained; Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network to remain editorially distinct and keep commissioning and acquiring original UK children's content; Channel 5 News editorially independent and separate from CBS News and CNN International; CNN International to remain available in the UK; licensees keep access to CNN, CBS News and Channel 5 news archives on standard commercial terms; Channel 5 to continue as a Public Service Broadcaster with a UK-focused commissioning strategy and more funding for news, original children's programming and drama.
  • Paramount statement: "These conclusions further demonstrate the misguided and gerrymandered market definitions relied upon by the U.S. state AGs in their antitrust complaint in California."
  • European Commission approved July 22, 2026.
  • US trial: March 2027, brought by California AG Rob Bonta with 11 other state AGs and the WGA.

AI startup Higgsfield has made "Cully Hill Boys," a 110-minute film it says is the first AI-generated production featuring legally licensed celebrity likenesses: streamer N3on, UFC fighters Israel Adesanya and Quinton "Rampage" Jackson, and basketball influencer Matt Kiatipis. Key Takeaways
  • Likeness Economics: When a two-minute voice sample can carry a 110-minute film, the price of a likeness detaches from the cost of a performance and attaches to the value of the audience, which is a different and lower-friction fee structure than any appearance deal.
  • Rights Structure: An AI-adaptation right can be severed and sold separately from a general adaptation right, and that separability is worth more to a rights holder over time than whatever the first such license pays.

That framing lowers the stakes for every participant, which is exactly why the licenses were obtainable and probably cheap.

The script's provenance matters as much as its price. LinkedIn Brand Deals Went From $100 to $500,000 a Year and the Rule Is Keep Your Day Job

CEO Summary
LinkedIn, with 1.3 billion registered users, has become a paying creator platform: the number of creators on it nearly doubled between 2021 and 2025, and rates have moved from roughly $100 offers a few years ago to about $10,000 per month for a single brand deal, putting top creators near $500,000 a year across three or four brands. Eighty-three percent of 2026 sign-ups so far are Gen Z and time spent on content is up 10% year over year. The platform also introduced a "Seems like AI slop" flag last week and is retiring the AI post-enhancement tool it launched in 2023.
Key Takeaways
  • Audience Verification: A verifiable audience prices on the value of each viewer rather than on the count, which is why a 100,000-follower professional audience can command rates a million anonymous followers cannot.
  • Talent Positioning: A platform built on job titles is where a career transition gets announced rather than promoted, which makes it the natural venue for an athlete near retirement or a performer between chapters.

Why It's Happening
LinkedIn users register under real names and job titles. That makes the audience checkable in a way no other platform's is, and checkability is the product: a brand can read a video's comment section and confirm it reached senior people at the companies it is targeting. That offsets a far smaller total audience and is what moved rates from $100 offers to five-figure monthly deals.

The AI crackdown follows from the same asset. A platform that shipped an AI writing assistant in 2023 is now building a button for users to report AI slop, because generative content erodes exactly the authenticity that lets it charge a premium. The deal structure has moved with the money: not discrete sponsored posts but deep native integrations, one of which produced more than 100 pieces of content for a single advertiser.

Nielsen Is Buying DoubleVerify for $2.15 Billion to Fix the Thing Advertisers Stopped Trusting It On
Measurement ConsolidationNielsen is paying $2.15 billion, a 30% premium, for DoubleVerify in an all-cash deal closing by Q1 2027, taking both the measurement and verification layers of the ad market private under one owner.
CEO Summary
Nielsen agreed to acquire ad-verification firm DoubleVerify for approximately $2.15 billion in an all-cash transaction, a 30% premium to DoubleVerify's 60-day trading average. The deal, approved by both boards, is expected to close by Q1 2027 and takes DoubleVerify private under Nielsen, which has itself been privately held since 2022. Providence Equity Partners, holding roughly 11.8% of DoubleVerify's shares, has agreed to vote in favor and will exit its stake at closing.
Key Takeaways
  • Measurement Consolidation: When the company that counts audiences also owns the company that verifies where and how ads ran, both halves of the ad transaction sit behind one owner, removing the independent check advertisers built verification vendors to provide.
  • Deal Structure: Any contract carrying an advertising-based bonus, threshold, or revenue-share provision now needs to specify its measurement source and what happens if the methodology changes, since a single vendor controlling both audience and verification data can move a threshold without any underlying performance change.
  • Disclosure: Nielsen has been private since 2022, and DoubleVerify goes private at close, removing the last independent public disclosure from the measurement layer that underpins ad-supported streaming economics.
Why It's Happening
No industry consensus exists on a single system for counting audiences across streaming, video-on-demand, and linear television, and rivals have been gaining ground; iSpot revealed an expanded pact with Fox last week giving advertisers real-time data on business outcomes. Both companies frame the acquisition around building what their CEOs called "a single currency" that scores media on both audience delivery and environment quality, the same standard-setting position Nielsen has held in linear for decades and has been losing in digital.
The Facts

Two Separate Studios Would Put 34 Films in Theaters Next Year. The Merged One Promises 30.
Release MathWBD and Paramount's own Q2 guidance adds to 34-plus theatrical releases in 2027 if they stay separate; Paramount has publicly committed to only 30 films a year if its merger with WBD closes.
CEO Summary
LightShed Partners calculated from both companies' own Q2 2026 earnings-call guidance that Warner Bros. Discovery, ramping to 19 films in 2027 from 14 this year, and Paramount, on track for 15-plus films in 2027, would together release 34-plus theatrical films next year if they remain separate. Paramount has publicly committed to only 30 films annually if its acquisition of WBD closes. The note also cites Nexstar CEO Perry Sook's and Paramount CLO Makan Delrahim's public comments this week, and reiterates that the merger agreement expires June 4, 2027 with a $7 billion break fee owed, ahead of a March 2 trial.
Key Takeaways
  • Release Math: the first quantified case that this merger reduces theatrical film supply rather than increasing it, since the two studios' own separate guidance already exceeds the combined company's public commitment.
  • Exhibitor Positioning: a theater chain's public endorsement of a distributor merger is a relationship bet on who will control future output, not a supply forecast, when the arithmetic shows the merger itself means fewer films sold into that chain.
  • Deal Timeline: a hard termination date paired with a large break fee converts a merger fight into a calendar problem, and the side that needs the clock to stop is the side that eventually settles.
Why It's Happening
WBD CFO Gunnar Wiedenfels told analysts the studio is "making 14 films this year, ramping that to 19 next year," while Paramount's Q2 release states it is "on track to release 15+ in 2027." Trial begins March 2, with post-trial briefs not due until April 5, leaving no realistic path to a decision before the June 4, 2027 termination date. Nexstar CEO Perry Sook argued a combined Paramount/WBD would gain leverage over broadcast affiliates, a comment LightShed says effectively makes the state attorneys general's antitrust argument for them. Paramount CLO Makan Delrahim spent his public capital arguing for federal preemption of state merger review, a policy question no court in this case can resolve.
The Facts
  • WBD is making 14 films this year, ramping to 19 in 2027, per CFO Gunnar Wiedenfels; Paramount's Q2 2026 release states it is on track for 15+ films in 2027, up from 8 in 2025. Combined: 34+ films if the companies stay separate.
  • Paramount has publicly committed to 30 films annually if the merger closes.
  • Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna publicly backed the merger, saying a long court fight "doesn't put more films in theaters."
  • Nexstar CEO Perry Sook told his own Q2 call that a combined Paramount/WBD "looks to have increased scale and resources to further pressure broadcast affiliates to pay more for less content."
  • Paramount CLO Makan Delrahim argued on LinkedIn for a federal preemption model over state-by-state merger review; JPMorgan is helping finance the WBD/Paramount transaction.
  • Trial begins March 2, 2027; post-trial briefs are not due until April 5. The merger agreement expires June 4, 2027, at which point Paramount owes WBD a $7 billion break fee.
