Netflix Spends 5 Percent of Its Content Budget on 1 Percent of Its Viewing Because Live Cannot Be Faked
Content ValueNetflix spent about $1 billion, 5% of its 2026 content budget, on live programming that draws just 1% of viewing hours; co-CEO Greg Peters says live drove 6 of the platform's 10 biggest sign-up days in five years.
CEO Summary
Netflix devoted roughly $1 billion, about five percent of its 2026 content budget, to live programming that generates only about one percent of total viewing hours, The Ankler reports. Co-CEO Greg Peters said on the July earnings call that live events drove six of the ten biggest new-subscriber sign-up days in the past five years. Producers behind recent Netflix live events, including Plimsoll's Skyscraper Live and Done+Dusted, describe a broader industry shift toward live formats as the one content category that cannot be synthetically generated.
Key Takeaways
  • Content Value: paying a five-times budget premium for one percent of viewing hours signals Netflix is buying subscriber acquisition and cultural moments rather than watch time, and the same logic will extend to any content that is provably unfakeable as AI-generated media becomes cheap and abundant.
  • Deal Structure: live formats carry a different rights structure than series, since sponsorship inventory, short-form clip distribution, and annual-return calendar ownership are revenue lines a standard per-episode deal does not capture, so producers building original live formats should be negotiating format ownership and return-year options rather than per-episode fees.
  • Supply Chain: production groups able to execute complex global live formats, spanning multi-time-zone scheduling, stunt insurance, and directed multilingual commentary, are scarce, which is why Banijay has been building a dedicated live-production business since 2023 and is now expanding it into North America.
Why It's Happening
Producers attribute the revival to authenticity anxiety in an AI-saturated market. Done+Dusted's Melanie Fletcher: "We don't know what's real anymore… Yet we know that if it's live in the moment and there's a big crowd, there's a sense of community." Live delivers measurable mass attention in one moment plus sponsor value and a clipping-distribution engine, and producers are now looking to fashion, luxury, and calendar-anchored moments like holidays as the next frontier.
The Facts
  • Live accounts for roughly one percent of Netflix's viewing hours; Netflix devoted approximately $1 billion, about five percent of its 2026 content budget, to it.
  • Co-CEO Greg Peters said live events drove six of the ten biggest days for new-subscriber sign-ups in the past five years; he did not identify the events.
  • Plimsoll's Skyscraper Live (January 2026), in which Alex Honnold climbed Taipei 101 without ropes, drew 6.2 million views in one weekend and has since climbed to 13 million.
  • Balich Wonder Studio, producer of the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics and this summer's FIFA World Cup ceremonies, has sat inside Banijay since 2023 and now anchors the group's Banijay Live division, extending into North America.
  • Whisper TV, which produced Netflix's Tyson Fury-Arslanbek Makhmudov boxing match in April, hired native speakers to dub each international feed rather than using AI translation tools.

Roku Posted Its Best Quarter Ever and Refused to Hold a Call About It Because Fox Is Buying It
Distribution LeverageRoku's Q2 profit rose 1,464% to $164.2 million on $1.35 billion in revenue, but the company held no earnings call and gave no updated guidance because Fox's pending $22 billion acquisition, closing H1 2027, already fixes its stock price.
CEO Summary
Roku reported Q2 2026 profit of $164.2 million, or $1.08 per share, up 1,464% year over year, on revenue up 22% to $1.35 billion, beating Wall Street's 56-cent consensus. Platform revenue, 90% of the total, grew 25% with ad revenue up 39%. The company held no analyst call and gave no updated financial outlook because of its pending $22 billion acquisition by Fox Corp., expected to close in the first half of 2027.
Key Takeaways
  • Distribution Leverage: platform revenue growing 25% with ad revenue up 39%, dwarfing a hardware business reduced to a rounding error, confirms Roku's actual value is the operating-system layer sitting in front of 100 million households, which is exactly what Fox is paying $22 billion to control.
  • Reporting Discipline: a pending acquisition suspends a seller's practical reporting obligations, since Roku declined to hold a call or refresh guidance despite beating consensus nearly twofold on earnings, and any counterparty with an earnout or revenue-share tied to a company mid-acquisition should expect the same silence.
  • Aggregation Margin: value in streaming keeps migrating from content production to the discovery and placement layer, and a company that owns both programming and the operating system deciding what surfaces on 100 million home screens holds leverage no single content company has.
Why It's Happening
Fox already owns sports rights and an ad-sales operation; Roku supplies the operating system in front of 100 million households and a home screen more than half of U.S. broadband homes now use. The lack of an earnings call is itself the signal: a company that just beat consensus by nearly double on earnings per share would normally hold one, and Roku's stock moved only 0.2% because its price is now set by the merger agreement rather than by results.
The Facts
  • Roku reported Q2 profit of $164.2 million, or $1.08 per share, up 1,464% year over year; Wall Street expected 56 cents. Total revenue grew 22% to $1.35 billion against a $1.3 billion consensus.
  • Platform revenue grew 25% to $1.22 billion; platform profit climbed 30% to $646.8 million, driven by a 39% increase in ad revenue and a 16% increase in subscription revenue.
  • Fox is acquiring Roku in a $22 billion deal slated to close in the first half of 2027; Roku did not hold an analyst call or provide updated guidance because of the pending deal.
  • Total streaming hours grew 7% to 37.9 billion, driven by NBA playoffs and World Cup viewership; Roku reaches over 100 million streaming households worldwide.
  • Roku completed the U.S. rollout of its new home screen, now used by more than half of broadband households, and launched Fox One and Peacock as premium add-ons.
  • Roku shares climbed roughly 0.2% in after-hours trading.

Gareth Edwards Directed an $869 Million Jurassic Film and Universal Is Replacing Him Anyway
Franchise LeverageGareth Edwards, whose Jurassic World: Rebirth grossed $869 million, will not direct the sequel over creative differences; David Koepp's script and stars Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and Jonathan Bailey are already locked, and a new director search is underway.
CEO Summary
Gareth Edwards will not return to direct the next Jurassic World film after creative differences with Universal, TheWrap reports, despite his 2025 film Jurassic World: Rebirth grossing $869 million globally. David Koepp has already written the follow-up script, and stars Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and Jonathan Bailey are expected to return; a new director search is underway. A Universal-side insider described the franchise as having rotated through five different core casts and directing teams across seven films, with producers Steven Spielberg and Frank Marshall as the constant.
Key Takeaways
  • Franchise Leverage: delivering a near-billion-dollar global gross on a legacy franchise did not convert into creative authority over the sequel, since when the IP predates the filmmaker and the studio has already recast the director's chair five times, box office performance alone does not buy control.
  • Package Sequencing: the assembly order, script finished and cast attached before a director is sought, signals materially less creative control for the incoming filmmaker than a project built around the director as first hire, and deal terms on a legacy-IP assignment should reflect which structure is in play.
  • Studio Doctrine: Universal has now stated its Jurassic operating model explicitly, producer-anchored and director-rotating, which sets the baseline expectation for any filmmaker considering a Universal legacy-franchise assignment.
Why It's Happening
The franchise has been led by five different core groups of actors and directors across seven films, with Spielberg and Marshall as the constant. Rebirth itself arrived three years after Jurassic World Dominion, which had been marketed as the last entry, and Koepp's script was fast-tracked into production and released roughly a year after it was first announced, showing the studio has consistently prioritized the IP and its architects over any single filmmaker's continuity on the property.
The Facts
  • Gareth Edwards will not return to direct the next installment in the Jurassic World franchise, citing creative differences, TheWrap reported.
  • Edwards directed 2025's Jurassic World: Rebirth, which grossed $869 million globally.
  • Universal statement: "We had an incredible experience working with Gareth on 'Jurassic World Rebirth.'"
  • A script for the follow-up has already been written by David Koepp. Stars Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and Jonathan Bailey are expected to return, and a director search is underway.
  • An insider told TheWrap the franchise "has always evolved with different filmmakers and cast," with continuity resting on Spielberg and Marshall.
  • Edwards also directed Rogue One and The Creator.

Disney streaming profit doubles to $712 million and consumer products moves under the studio
Portfolio StructureDisney+ and Hulu together made $712 million, up from $329 million, and a consumer products arm that moved $63 billion of licensed retail goods last year is being relocated under the studio.
CEO Summary
Disney reported fiscal Q3 2026 revenue of $25.2 billion, up 7%, and segment operating income of $5.6 billion, up 21%, in Josh D'Amaro's first full quarter as CEO. Disney+ and Hulu's combined operating income more than doubled to $712 million from $329 million, Experiences profit rose 20% to over $3 billion, and Sports profit fell 17% to $853 million on higher rights costs. Separately, Disney is moving the majority of Disney Consumer Products out of Experiences and into Disney Entertainment's Studios group beginning October 2026.
Key Takeaways
  • Portfolio Structure: When a licensing arm outgrows the division that houses it, the org chart follows the IP rather than the venue that sells it.
  • Streaming Economics: Streaming margin at scale is now made on price and retention, not advertising, and the ad line can grow at a fifth the rate of subscriptions even as impressions rise.
  • Sports Rights: Sports buys reach, not margin. Rights and production costs can cut profit at the strongest sports brand in a market during a quarter its viewership grows.
Why It's Happening
The consumer products business did $63 billion in licensed retail sales in 2025, roughly three times its nearest competitor, and it is the second division to move from Experiences into Disney Entertainment this year after Games and Digital Entertainment in March. Both moves put monetization teams alongside the people who greenlight the IP. On the streaming line, subscription fees rose 15% while advertising rose 3% with impressions higher and rates lower, which is the signature of an oversupplied ad market rather than a demand problem. The 17% drop in sports profit traces to contractual rate increases, new rights costs, the timing of NBA rights-cost recognition, four-game sweeps in early playoff rounds, and a carriage dispute.
The Facts
  • Fiscal Q3 2026, quarter ended June, reported August 5. Revenue $25.2 billion, up 7%, slightly below the roughly $25.4 billion expected. Segment operating income $5.6 billion, up 21%. Adjusted EPS $2.06 against $1.85 expected, up from $1.61. Net profit $2.6 billion. Shares rose over 2%.
  • Entertainment profit $1.7 billion, up 64%, on revenue of $11.3 billion, credited to "Toy Story 5" (released June 19, past $1 billion global) and "The Devil Wears Prada 2."
  • Disney+ and Hulu combined operating income $712 million, up from $329 million, on revenue of $5.5 billion, up 11%. Subscription fees up 15%: 9 points subscribers, 3 points rates, 1 point FX. Advertising up 3%. Churn declined worldwide. Disney no longer discloses quarterly subscriber counts.
  • Experiences profit over $3 billion, up 20%, on almost $10 billion revenue. Global guests up 4%, domestic attendance up 3%, per-capita ticket revenue up 5%.
  • Sports profit $853 million, down 17%, on $4.5 billion revenue.
  • Approximately $100 million tariff refund recorded, reversing earlier fiscal-year tariff payments.
  • Disney Consumer Products moves the majority of its businesses to Disney Entertainment, within Studios, beginning October 2026. DCP-licensed products did $63 billion in 2025 retail sales; next largest licensors were Authentic Brands Group at $36 billion, People Inc. at $27 billion, NBCUniversal at $20 billion and Hasbro at $17.5 billion. Lisa Baldzicki remains DCP president.
  • Disney closed the sale of its 50% stake in A+E Global Media to a Hearst affiliate for $1.2 billion in cash, with $1 billion earmarked for share buybacks.
  • Disney plans to triple its Disney+ local original series over three years.

D'Amaro rules out trading direct-to-consumer for licensing and says Disney is weighing free channels
Platform StrategyAsked whether licensing content out beats running Disney+, D'Amaro said exiting direct-to-consumer would leave Disney "strategically and financially" worse off, and named first-party data, not margin, as the reason.
CEO Summary
On Disney's August 5 earnings call, an analyst asked CEO Josh D'Amaro whether direct-to-consumer subscription is a better business for shareholders than licensing content to networks. D'Amaro said exiting direct-to-consumer for licensing "would likely lead to both inferior strategic and financial positions," citing a global user base and first-party data as assets that matter more as AI cycles arrive. He separately confirmed Disney is considering launching free ad-supported channels as a funnel into Disney+ and Hulu.
Key Takeaways
  • Platform Strategy: The reason a major keeps an expensive owned platform is no longer content margin. It is the first-party data set and the ability to talk to the customer directly.
  • Distribution: Free tiers are becoming acquisition funnels rather than products. A platform that says its ad inventory is already well sold is adding free channels to buy reach, not to fill demand.
  • Franchise Value: A subscription service being rebuilt to carry games, merchandise and experiences widens the surface on which downstream participation gets negotiated.
Why It's Happening
D'Amaro's argument is that licensing revenue is lumpy and subject to whoever happens to be buying that year, while an owned relationship compounds. He tied that specifically to what streaming data adds to the data Disney already collects from theme parks and cruise ships, and to the coming technology cycle. On free channels, his stated logic was inventory: unlike many ad-supported competitors, Disney says it is "fairly well sold," so more inventory would accelerate ad revenue rather than cannibalize it, and a free offering reaches a price-sensitive segment that can be upsold. He also said Comcast's split of NBCUniversal and Sky from its cable systems and Fox's $22 billion purchase of Roku do not change Disney's path, calling a more consolidated industry a better investment backdrop.
The Facts
  • D'Amaro: "The shift to a purely licensing model could sacrifice all of that strategic value. Content licensing by nature is a lumpy business ... exiting direct-to-consumer for licensing exclusively would likely lead to both inferior strategic and financial positions for our company and our shareholders."
  • D'Amaro: "A critical first-party data set ... will enable personalization and continued product innovation. And it establishes a foundation that we can build revenue streams on top of over time. This is only possible through a direct-to-consumer relationship inside a wholly controlled and branded environment ... We're just playing a different game."
  • On free channels: "Unlike a lot of our AVOD competitors, we're fairly well sold, meaning more inventory would actually help us accelerate our ad revenue growth ... nothing specific to announce today, but definitely something that we're considering."
  • Disney+ enhancements arriving next spring will include "games, merchandise, and other experiences," with elements of the "comprehensive membership ecosystem" introduced beginning Spring 2027.
  • Disney's content investment is more than $24 billion.
  • On sector M&A, D'Amaro said Comcast's NBCUniversal and Sky separation and Fox's $22 billion Roku acquisition do not change Disney's strategic path.

Paramount says it is "absolutely open" to settling, and the ticking fee is only payable if the deal closes
Deal StructureParamount's $650 million-a-quarter ticking fee to Warner shareholders is "only payable when and if we close," CFO Dennis Cinelli said, alongside a $190 million bridge fee and a $7 billion breakup fee.
CEO Summary
On Paramount's Q2 2026 earnings call, held hours after a judge set a March 2027 antitrust trial date, CEO David Ellison said the company is "absolutely open to finding a solution out of court but believe we will win at trial." CFO Dennis Cinelli itemized the cost of delay: a ticking fee to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders of roughly $650 million per quarter after September 30, which he said is "only payable when and if we close," plus a bridge commitment fee of about $190 million. Paramount would owe a $7 billion breakup fee if the deal collapses.
Key Takeaways
  • Deal Structure: A ticking fee payable only on closing is not a penalty for waiting. It compensates the seller's shareholders for time while leaving the buyer free to walk without paying it, which makes delay far cheaper for the buyer than the headline number suggests.
  • Negotiation: A buyer who says it is open to settling while insisting it will win is naming a price for a concession, not conceding. The two statements are one position.
  • Risk: In a contested acquisition, the number that predicts how hard a buyer fights is the breakup fee, not the trial calendar. It is the floor under abandoning the deal.
Why It's Happening
Paramount promised the ticking fee as a sweetener during the contest for Warner Bros. Discovery, and it is triggered if the deal has not closed by September 30. Because it is contingent on completion, the cost is deferred into the transaction rather than borne during the fight, which means the running cost of litigating is closer to the $190 million bridge commitment fee than to the $650 million quarterly figure that has been widely quoted. Twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America brought the suit last month, and the judge showed initial support for the complaint. Paramount asked analysts to limit merger questions and steered the call toward streaming, production and technology after the opening exchanges. PSKY traded at $8.37 on August 5.
The Facts
  • Ellison: "We are absolutely open to finding a solution out of court but believe we will win at trial."
  • Ellison on financing: "All that has been placed, there's nothing at risk. We're confident we'll close the transaction, and we're working towards that as fast as we possibly can."
  • Cinelli: the ticking fee is estimated at about $650 million per quarter the deal remains pending after September 30, and is "only payable when and if we close."
  • Cinelli: the bridge commitment fee adds up to about $190 million.
  • Paramount would owe a $7 billion breakup fee if the deal unravels. It was not mentioned on the call.
  • Cinelli: "We feel good about where we stand in terms of liquidity and managing through" the merger situation.
  • Trial is set for March 2027. Twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America are the plaintiffs. The deal is valued at $110 billion.
  • Call moderator Kevin Creighton, EVP of corporate finance and investor relations, shifted the call away from merger questions after the opening exchanges.

In its fiscal Q3 disclosure, Disney acknowledged that "Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu" and the live-action "Moana" underperformed at the box office, and in the same passage named what they returned elsewhere: a new Mandalorian-themed Millennium Falcon: Smuggler's Run attraction at Disneyland and Walt Disney World, retail sales, and expected Disney+ performance for "Moana," whose franchise now spans three films, an EPCOT themed area and a global merchandise business. Key Takeaways
  • Advertising: Live-event inventory and general streaming inventory are now two different markets. One clears out six months early at eight figures a spot; the other is being repriced downward by its own supply.
  • Pricing: Streaming advertising softness is a supply problem, not a demand problem. Impressions rising while rates fall is what an oversupplied market looks like, and the platforms are still adding inventory.
  • Marketing: A promotional commitment measured in impressions is worth less each year that inventory grows. The scarce good in a marketing guarantee is now the live-event slot, not the volume.

Regal's CEO backs the Paramount-WBD merger and names the commitments he got

Regal Global Entertainment CEO Eduardo Acuna publicly backed Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery for the first time, citing specific commitments from Paramount CEO David Ellison: at least 30 theatrical films annually, a protected 45-day TVOD and 90-day SVOD window for a minimum of three years, and $30 billion in annual content investment, with an offer to execute a consent decree with state attorneys general. Key Takeaways
  • Regulatory Leverage: A merger under antitrust review generates its most concrete concessions at the moment of maximum scrutiny, and commitments extracted here become the reference floor buyers point to for years, not just through closing.
  • Trade Fracture: A trade association's official opposition no longer reliably represents its largest members; when the two biggest players in a sector break from their own association's position, the association's leverage in the underlying dispute weakens further.
  • Output Commitments: A numeric output or windowing commitment made to win over an industry stakeholder typically carries a defined term, three years here, so the guarantee's expiration date is the number worth tracking, not the merger's closing date.

Cinema United, the trade group representing exhibitors broadly, remains opposed and says it has not heard from Paramount since submitting a list of concerns on July 1 — the split between the top two circuits and their own association is now itself part of the public case for approval.

The merger agreement itself now limits what Warner Bros. Discovery can greenlight
Deal TimingContent deals between $30 million and $400 million now need Paramount's approval, ordinary-course deals are capped at two years past close, and the South Park fight that cost $1.5 billion is the proof case.
CEO Summary
A pending 12-state lawsuit holds up David Ellison's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery until a March 2027 trial, and the signed merger agreement already gives Paramount approval rights over WBD content deals between roughly $30 million and $400 million, caps ordinary-course deals at two years past close, and sets separate limits on "key property" IP and HBO Max bundle deals. A WBD source says Paramount has not withheld consent on anything brought to it yet, but the South Park renegotiation, which stalled for more than a year before a $1.5 billion resolution, is the industry's proof case for how a disagreement plays out.
Key Takeaways
  • Deal Timing: A signed acquisition agreement transfers a share of greenlight authority to the buyer months or years before it transfers ownership, and the constraint starts on signing, not closing.
  • Retention Risk: The company being acquired keeps operating, but every deal that crosses a dollar threshold or runs past a fixed term now has a second decision-maker in the room, which slows exactly the deals a target needs to retain talent during the hold.
  • Negotiating Leverage: A creative weighing a deal at a company mid-acquisition should treat term length as a live negotiating variable — a deal structured to close inside the buyer's consent window is materially easier to get done than the identical deal at a longer term.
Why It's Happening
The thresholds exist to protect the buyer's economics during a hold that could run past two years, but they create the same conditions that made the South Park negotiation public and expensive: when a value or term disagreement arises, the target's narrower options during the hold favor the talent side's leverage, not the studio's. WBD's retention risk is already visible — Quinta Brunson moved her overall deal to Disney's 20th Television, and a legal dispute over a marketing executive's departure to Prime Video shows competitors treating the hold as an active poaching window.
The Facts
  • The lawsuit from 12 states halts the close of the $111 billion acquisition until a winner-take-all trial set for March 2027.
  • Sales or acquisitions of content may require Paramount approval when they hit thresholds "between $30 million and $400 million, depending on the deal, the length and other factors."
  • Ordinary-course deals are restricted to lasting only two years past deal close; anything longer requires giving Paramount first rights to negotiate.
  • Separate limits apply to deals involving undefined "key property" IP (THR notes franchises like Harry Potter, Game of Thrones and DC likely qualify) and to HBO Max bundle agreements, both capped at two years post-closing.
  • The South Park negotiation is the proven failure case: Skydance, Paramount and Park County could not agree on value and length, the season premiere was delayed, and the parties eventually reached a $1.5 billion agreement.
  • Layoff exposure on close: about 2,495 jobs in L.A. County and about 6,000 globally, per a June estimate.
  • Quinta Brunson moved her overall deal from Warner Bros. to Disney's 20th Television; WBD has continued signing others, including John Wells, Ryan Condal, Chris Ferguson and a new one-year deal for John Oliver.
  • On the film slate, no deals yet exist for a Barbie sequel with Margot Robbie, Ryan Gosling and Greta Gerwig; the studio has until December to close talent deals or rights revert to Mattel.
  • The European Commission approved the merger in late July on condition Paramount exits UIP, its international theatrical distribution joint venture with Universal, within 13 months of close.

Streaming chief Cindy Holland and head of originals Jane Wiseman have kept a selective, talent-driven strategy unchanged through the merger freeze, favoring first-look deals over volume.
Key Takeaways
  • Buying Pace: A platform with an established subscriber base buys selectively even during a corporate crisis, while a platform building from nothing has to buy in volume to prove it exists — buying pace signals a platform's starting position, not its ambition.

Why It's Happening
Holland's team built its early slate around female-driven programming to counterbalance Taylor Sheridan's male-led hits (Tulsa King, Landman, Mayor of Kingstown), but Sheridan's confirmed 2029 departure to NBCUniversal creates a dated hole in the platform's most reliable franchise programming, and executives are again considering male-driven titles to prepare for it.

The FCC votes Thursday to scrap the 39% station ownership cap
Deregulation SignalThe FCC votes Thursday to scrap the cap barring one owner from reaching more than 39% of U.S. households, and Sinclair's CEO says the change "de-risks" the large-scale M&A that is "a major objective" for the company.
CEO Summary
The Republican-controlled FCC votes Thursday on eliminating the rule capping a single owner's national TV station reach at 39% of U.S. households. Sinclair CEO Chris Ripley said on the company's Q2 earnings call that removing the cap "de-risks" large-scale M&A and will make counterparties "more likely to want to transact," as Sinclair pursues more deals after a rebuffed hostile bid for E.W. Scripps, and as Nexstar's blocked $6.2 billion Tegna acquisition remains on appeal.
Key Takeaways
  • Deregulation Signal: Removing a regulatory ceiling moves the seller before it moves the buyer; a buyer's public statement that a rule change "de-risks" a deal is itself the signal that counterparties were staying away because of the rule, not the price.
  • Litigation Interplay: A live regulatory action becomes evidence in a company's own pending litigation — Nexstar is arguing the same cap removal is relevant to its blocked Tegna appeal in real time.
  • Reversal Risk: A rule change contested on authority grounds, not merits, carries reversal risk a rule change settled on the merits does not; any deal signed under the new rule is exposed if a reviewing court finds only Congress can eliminate the cap.
Why It's Happening
Sinclair's Q2 results were mixed, revenue up 7% to $840 million and beating consensus, losses widening to $1.06 per share and missing estimates, which sharpens the incentive to add scale through M&A rather than organic growth. Nexstar, the No. 1 station owner, has its own $6.2 billion Tegna deal tied up in a Ninth Circuit appeal that could be strengthened by the same rule change.
The Facts
  • The FCC is set to vote Thursday on eliminating the rule barring a single owner from controlling stations reaching more than 39% of U.S. households; Chairman Brendan Carr has long opposed the cap.
  • Sinclair Q2: revenue $840 million, up 7% year over year, beating consensus; net losses doubled to $1.06 per share, missing estimates.
  • Nexstar's $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna was blocked by a federal judge earlier this year and is now on appeal in the Ninth Circuit; Nexstar reports earnings Thursday, around the time of the FCC vote.
  • Sinclair has made a hostile offer for E.W. Scripps, which Scripps rebuffed; Ripley and other executives intend to pursue other deals.
  • Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat on the FCC, maintains that only Congress can change or eliminate the cap since Congress enacted it in the 1990s. Legal challenges are widely expected.

27% fewer writers earned anything in 2025 than at the 2022 peak
Market Concentration5,072 WGA West members reported earnings in 2025, down 27% from the 2022 peak, while total earnings fell only 1.3% to $1.7 billion, and streaming residuals declined for the first time ever.
CEO Summary
WGA West's annual financial report shows 5,072 members reported earnings in 2025, down 27% from nearly 7,000 at the 2022 peak and down 10.2% year over year, while total up-front earnings fell only 1.3% to $1.7 billion. Feature film earnings rose 7.2% to $521 million even as television jobs fell more than 33% since 2022, and streaming residuals declined for the first time on record, from $346 million to just over $330 million.
Key Takeaways
  • Market Concentration: A contraction that cuts headcount while protecting rates for established talent is a concentration event, not a pay cut — buyers keep paying proven writers and eliminate the tier below them, closing the market on entry rather than on price.
  • Feature Resilience: Feature writing is now the more resilient lane for a working writer: film jobs are down about 14% since 2022 against television's 33%-plus decline, and feature earnings are up 7.2% to a five-year high.
  • Residual Structure: The first-ever nominal decline in streaming residuals removes the assumption that streaming residuals would keep growing to offset other formats; high-budget SVOD residuals are the one category still expanding, up more than 300% over five years, but only on expensive titles.
Why It's Happening
Deadline notes the writers still getting hired skew toward more experienced, well-connected names who command higher fees, which mechanically holds total earnings up even as employment falls — meaning another year of flat earnings paired with continued job losses would signal the crunch has started reaching even seasoned writers.
The Facts
  • About 5,072 writers reported earnings in 2025, down from nearly 7,000 in 2022, per the WGAW annual financial report.
  • From 2024 to 2025, employment fell 10.2% while total up-front earnings fell only 1.3%, to $1.7 billion; total earnings remain about 25% below the 2022 peak.
  • Television jobs are down more than 33% since 2022; feature film jobs down about 14%, to 2,007 members recording earnings last year.
  • Feature film writers reported about $521 million in earnings for 2025, up 7.2% year over year, more than any of the last five years.
  • Residuals fell 4.9% year over year to $535.5 million; streaming residuals fell from $346 million to just over $330 million, the first-ever nominal decline.
  • High-budget SVOD residuals (programs 96+ minutes, budgets $30 million-plus) have grown more than 300% over five years to $77.83 million in 2025.
  • The WGAW says these preliminary numbers reflect information as of March 2026 and are likely to rise toward, though remain below, 2024 levels.

Sources cite creative misalignment and Kelley's dissatisfaction with how the project was handled; Warner Bros. Television and David E. Kelley Productions will shop it elsewhere. Kelley remains in business with Apple on two other series, both renewed for second seasons.
Key Takeaways
  • Buyer Discipline: A low-volume prestige buyer will walk from a package built around a top showrunner and a franchise director after a public pickup, and the pass reads as a verdict on the specific project, not the relationship, since the same buyer renewed that showrunner's other two shows in the same window.
  • Alignment Risk: "Not creatively aligned" is the recurring failure mode at a buyer with a small slate and strong in-house taste; the risk is highest for a project sold on names rather than a script both sides have already agreed on.
  • Asset Retention: The studio behind a dropped project, not the platform that passed, keeps the asset and can remarket it, which is why a studio-set project survives a buyer's change of heart better than one packaged directly with a single streamer.
Why It's Happening
A development sale at a curated buyer functions closer to an option than a firm home: the same slate discipline that makes the buyer selective and desirable to sell into is what makes any individual pickup reversible months into development.
The Facts
  • The series adaptation of Tom Wolfe's 1987 novel, from showrunner David E. Kelley and director Matt Reeves, is no longer moving forward at Apple TV, where it had been set up for development.
  • Warner Bros. Television, the studio behind it, along with David E. Kelley Productions, will shop it to other buyers shortly.
  • Deadline reported in April that the project had been sold to Apple TV; after months of development, the streamer opted not to proceed.
  • Kelley remains in business with Apple TV on two other series, both renewed for second seasons: "Margo's Got Money Troubles," which recently received eight Emmy nominations, and "Presumed Innocent," a four-time Emmy nominee last year.
  • This is Kelley's second adaptation of a Wolfe novel, after the 2024 Netflix limited series "A Man in Full."

The Paramount-WBD antitrust trial starts March 2, 2027, and the $7 million a day clock starts October 1
Litigation TimingParamount wanted November, the attorneys general wanted April. The merger agreement expires June 4, and a spring trial forces Paramount to refile with a Justice Department that already cleared it.
CEO Summary
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín set the trial over Paramount Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery for March 2 to March 19, 2027, closer to the April date sought by twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America than the November start Paramount requested. Paramount owes Warner shareholders a ticking fee of 25 cents per share per quarter, roughly $7 million a day, for every day the deal does not close after September 30, which the trades put above $1 billion by the time trial opens. The merger agreement expires June 4, 2027, and carries a $7 billion regulatory termination fee.
Key Takeaways
  • Litigation Timing: In a contested merger the calendar is the remedy. A challenger who may not win on the merits can still impose most of the cost by winning the scheduling fight, which makes the trial date the first real negotiation in any blocked transaction.
  • Deal Sweeteners: A ticking fee offered to beat a rival bidder converts into the challenger's leverage the moment the deal is contested, because the buyer starts paying for months of delay it never priced.
  • Regulatory Clearance: Antitrust clearances expire. A buyer that races to collect approvals early and is then delayed past a waiting-period deadline has to buy the same approvals twice, at cost and at risk.
Why It's Happening
The ticking fee was Paramount's own instrument. It offered 25 cents per Warner share per quarter to win the assets away from Netflix, as a signal of confidence to the seller's shareholders. Priced against a clean regulatory path it was cheap. Priced against a litigated one it runs to more than $1 billion before a witness is sworn, and the party collecting it has no reason to hurry.

The February 19 waiting-period expiry is the second cost. Sixty-five jurisdictions have cleared or declined to challenge the transaction, and a March trial means the earliest of those clearances start going stale before the case is heard. Paramount told the court that redoing the work "serves nobody's interests." The court set the date anyway.
The Facts
  • Trial set for March 2 to March 19, 2027, before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland. Court hours 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.; dark March 8 and March 15.

  • Ticking fee: 25 cents per WBD share per quarter for every day past September 30 the deal has not closed, roughly $7 million per day, more than $1 billion by trial.
  • Merger agreement expires June 4, 2027. Regulatory termination fee: $7 billion.
  • A Justice Department waiting period expires February 19, 2027; Paramount told the court a later trial forces refiling in the United States and other cleared jurisdictions.
  • California Attorney General Rob Bonta leads 11 other state AGs. Suit filed July 13, followed by a temporary restraining order.
  • Initial case management conference August 19; joint statement due August 13. No timeline given for a post-trial ruling.

  • Paramount told the court it plans to raise output to 30 films per year and that the later date prolongs uncertainty for the creative community.

Netflix moved "La Bola Negra," the Cannes best-director winner from Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, up from November 6 to October 16 in theaters while pushing its streaming debut two days earlier to December 2, creating a 47-day exclusive theatrical window. Key Takeaways
  • Windowing: A platform that spent a decade arguing the theatrical window was obsolete is now extending it voluntarily, which means the window survives as a negotiable term rather than a legacy obligation.
  • Talent Economics: Theatrical exclusivity has become part of what a streamer pays with, so a filmmaker with leverage should negotiate the window in days the way they negotiate budget in dollars.
  • Acquisitions: A festival acquisition can now command better distribution terms than a platform's own development slate, which raises the value of arriving at a market with a finished film and competing bidders.

The window is cheapest to spend where it buys the most. Every title on Netflix's extended-window list is an awards play or a name-director commitment: Los Javis out of Cannes, David Fincher directing Quentin Tarantino's script, Greta Gerwig on Narnia. Exhibitors and awards voters both treat a real run as the price of being taken seriously, and neither can be bought with a two-week token.

The second reason is the talent market. Directors of that tier were not going to sign for a streaming-first release, and a competitor offering a studio release has an argument the money alone does not answer. Netflix has decided it is easier to move the window than to lose the filmmaker.

  • Theatrical Recovery: A year that produces five billion-dollar films after six years of never exceeding three is not a franchise story, it is evidence that theatrical demand recovered and the intervening shortfall was a supply and execution problem.

The Monday number is the one that separates a $1 billion film from a $2 billion one. Opening weekend measures marketing; the following Monday measures whether anyone told a friend. The surrounding year matters too. Summer grosses from May through early August stand at $3.579 billion domestic, and "Dune 3" and "Avengers: Doomsday" are still ahead. The market is tracking toward its first $10 billion domestic year since 2019, which reframes a summer that was being written up as a run of underperforming tentpoles.

Private equity is sitting on about $1 trillion and buying the parts of entertainment AI cannot copy
Capital DeploymentApollo argued in a December white paper that sports hedges AI because the seats are finite and the games run live. KKR has $53 billion to deploy, Blackstone $43 billion.
CEO Summary
Roughly $1 trillion in uncommitted U.S. private equity capital is looking for somewhere to go, and reporting across lawyers, financial advisers and dealmakers found one thesis recurring: sports, live events and other scarce real-world experiences are being underwritten specifically because generative AI cannot replicate them. Private equity already holds positions across the representation and management business and in production, from a $25 billion Endeavor take-private to the $8 billion Banijay-All3Media merger. Firms target 18 to 20 percent annual returns on five-to-seven-year holds, and continuation vehicles that let original investors stay past a fund's expiry are now routine in media.
Key Takeaways
  • Capital Deployment: Committed capital has to be spent whether or not a good deal exists, which means the timing of the next investment wave is set by fund clocks rather than by industry fundamentals, and an operator who understands that timing negotiates from a better position than one who reads it as market enthusiasm.
  • Valuation: Scarcity that a generative model cannot manufacture is becoming the premium attribute in entertainment assets, so a business whose value rests on finite seats, live moments or physical presence now prices above one whose value rests on reproducible content.
  • Ownership: A rollup is assembled in order to be taken apart, so anyone joining or selling into a private-equity-backed platform should treat continuity of the operating relationship as a term to negotiate rather than a property of the deal.
Why It's Happening
The mechanism is a clock, not a mood. A fund that raised money must deploy it, and a fund at year five must either exit or roll its investors into a continuation vehicle. Capital sitting undeployed since last year's hesitancy has to move, and dealmakers describe a production recovery as the catalyst rather than the cause.

What that money wants has narrowed. The mandate distinction is the one that determines what happens after the wire clears: a growth investor is buying scale and diversification, a value investor is buying margin, and the second is where the cost-cutting reputation comes from. Sitting underneath both is the AI hedge, argued explicitly in an investor white paper rather than inferred by observers, which is why sports and live assets are drawing bids from firms with no prior entertainment position at all.
The Facts
  • Midyear estimates put uncommitted U.S. private equity capital near $1 trillion. One corporate dealmaker: "Money has to be invested, whether that money is a useful investment or not."
  • Typical targets: 18 to 20 percent annual returns, five-to-seven-year exits. Continuation vehicles, single-purpose funds letting original investors stay in, are increasingly common in media and entertainment as an alternative to expiry-driven fire sales.
  • Apollo Global Management: $67 billion in private equity; holds HarbourView, Legendary Entertainment and Wrexham AFC; launched Apollo Sports Capital in September; a December 2025 white paper argued sports hedges AI disruption because seats are finite and games are watched live. Took a minority Legendary stake for $760 million in 2022.
  • Silver Lake: $114 billion. Completed a $25 billion Endeavor take-private last year and is part of the $55 billion EA leveraged buyout with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Affinity Partners, cleared by EU regulators July 23.
  • KKR: $255 billion, about $53 billion available. Holdings span Mediawan, Simon & Schuster, Epic Games, ByteDance and Superstruct. Acquired Arctos this year; the only firm approved by all five major U.S. leagues to hold multiple team stakes.
  • Blackstone: $174 billion in private equity, $43 billion available as of June 30. Its $1 billion Candle Media bet has struggled since acquisitions of Hello Sunshine, Moonbug and ATTN.
  • RedBird Capital: $14 billion, dry powder about $965 million. Put $1.8 billion into Skydance's $8 billion Paramount purchase and committed $250 million toward the Paramount-WBD deal. RedBird IMI merged All3Media with Banijay for about $720 million in cash, creating the world's largest independent producer.
  • Providence Equity Partners is buying the remaining stake in The Team; at a reported $3.4 billion valuation the balance costs about $1.36 billion against just under $2 billion of dry powder.
  • EQT: $335 billion total; lost the auction for The Team and told Bloomberg it plans to invest $250 billion in the U.S. over five years. Shamrock Capital raised more than $800 million after selling its Excel stake.
  • Named new entrants circling the sector: Permira ($91 billion), Warburg Pincus ($105 billion, which hired a former major-label chief AI officer last year), Bluestone Equity Partners ($440 million).
  • One dealmaker on the consensus: "Everyone has dry powder for sports."

The WBD merger agreement forces Warner to sue over a departing executive, and California law punishes it for trying
Executive MobilityBarlow's restriction runs to October 2027. Amazon's answer is that Warner is asking a court to bind her while reserving the right to change her owner, her reporting line and her job, with no promise of employment from the buyer.
CEO Summary
Warner Bros. Discovery has sued Amazon over its hiring of HBO Max marketing executive Pia Barlow before her fixed-term contract expired, calling Amazon a "digital bull in a china shop." The Paramount merger agreement bars WBD from failing to enforce employees' restrictive covenants, and a failure to enforce could hand Paramount an argument against paying the $7 billion regulatory termination fee if the deal is blocked, so WBD is pushed toward aggressive enforcement. California's 2024 amendments to Business and Professions Code §16600 cut the other way, requiring courts to read the noncompete prohibition broadly and giving an employee subjected to attempted enforcement of a void restraint their own claim for an injunction, damages and attorney fees.
Key Takeaways
  • Executive Mobility: Deal covenants have become a retention device the employer cannot switch off, so a company inside a frozen transaction will enforce restrictions harder than the underlying relationship warrants and its people should expect that before they take a call.
  • Contract Drafting: A term commitment that the employer can terminate early without paying out the balance reads as a one-way restraint rather than a bargain, which makes termination asymmetry the first thing to test in any fixed-term deal and the first thing to fix at drafting.
  • Leverage: A jurisdiction that gives a restricted employee an affirmative claim with attorney fees converts the cost of enforcement into a two-way risk, so the restricted party in that jurisdiction is negotiating from a real position rather than a nuisance one.
Why It's Happening
The covenant was drafted to protect a buyer's purchase, and in a closing that happened on schedule it would never have mattered. Frozen for eight months, it means the seller is contractually pushed to sue over departures at exactly the moment its people have the most reason to leave and the least assurance about what they would be staying for. Not enforcing risks handing the buyer an argument against a $7 billion fee.

The precedents give both sides something. A decade ago two studios beat a streamer on essentially these facts. Last year a major failed to stop a senior sports executive from moving to a platform, on the argument that a contract terminable at the employer's option was not really a mutual exchange of security for commitment. The judge stopped short of a merits ruling and the parties settled before any appellate precedent existed, so the question of whether a bona fide fixed term survives the strengthened statute is still open.

The litigation choices are the tell. The complaint does not name the departing executive, does not attach the agreement, does not disclose its termination provisions and does not seek emergency relief. It targets the hiring company's conduct instead. That is a case built to avoid the argument that beat the last one.
The Facts
  • WBD sued Amazon over the hiring of HBO Max marketing executive Pia Barlow before her fixed-term contract expired; her restriction would run to October 2027.
  • The Paramount-WBD merger agreement prohibits WBD from waiving or failing to "enforce the restrictive covenant obligations" of current or former employees. Non-enforcement could support a Paramount argument against the $7 billion regulatory termination fee.
  • California's 2024 amendments to §16600 require courts to invalidate noncompetes "no matter how narrowly tailored" and remove the assumption that an unenforceable restraint carries no downside. Whether the statute voids a bona fide fixed-term contract is unsettled.
  • The same legislation lets an employee or former employee facing attempted enforcement of a void restraint sue for an injunction, actual damages and attorney fees.
  • Precedent: 20th Century Fox and Viacom defeated Netflix on executive poaching a decade ago. Last year Disney failed to block former ESPN executive Justin Connolly from joining YouTube; Judge James Chalfant refused emergency relief, found no probability of success, faulted Disney's showing of urgency, and held the balance of harms favored Connolly. Disney appealed; the parties settled before an appellate ruling.
  • Connolly's argument: because Disney could terminate him without necessarily paying the remainder, the deal looked less like security exchanged for a term commitment and more like a one-way noncompete.
  • WBD is represented by Proskauer partner Anthony Oncidi, who represented Viacom in the earlier case. He has not named Barlow as a defendant, attached the agreement, disclosed its termination provisions, or moved for emergency relief, and has emphasized Amazon's conduct, including its promise to absorb the legal consequences of her departure, its selection of counsel for her, and its alleged pursuit of other WBD executives.
  • WBD frames its interest as workforce stability and business planning; Amazon's position is that WBD is preparing to change owners, reporting structures and job definitions.

On the business itself, operating income up 61 percent against 14 percent revenue growth, with the stock down, is a market pricing the next lever rather than the last quarter.

Key Takeaways
  • Valuation: Scheduled, licensed, annually recurring demand is now the collateral that supports record leverage, which reprices sports and franchise licences as financing assets rather than as revenue lines.
  • Slate Strategy: Debt service at this scale rewards sequels and annualized releases and punishes experiments, so a publisher in this position becomes a harder buyer for original IP and a more willing partner on anything franchise-shaped.
  • Ownership: Sovereign capital taking a control position rather than a passive stake introduces a counterparty with a different time horizon, different governance and different sensitivity to public pressure than a strategic acquirer, and those differences belong in the counterparty read before terms are discussed.
Why It's Happening
The size of the debt explains the choice of target. Twenty billion dollars of leverage has to be serviced out of predictable cash, and an annualized sports title with an exclusive licence is close to the most predictable cash in entertainment. That is the same thesis private equity has been articulating out loud all summer: scarce, scheduled, live-adjacent demand is worth a premium precisely because a generative model cannot manufacture it.

The direction of travel is not unique to this company. Ubisoft and Xbox have made the same shift toward bankable releases without a buyout forcing it, which suggests the narrowing is a response to the economics of the category rather than to the capital structure alone.
The Facts

  • The PIF will reportedly own 93.4 percent of the company.

  • EU regulators cleared the transaction on July 23.
  • Affinity Partners is Jared Kushner's firm. Silver Lake also completed a $25 billion take-private of Endeavor last year.
  • EA's recent focus has been Battlefield, EA Sports FC, Madden NFL and The Sims.
  • CEO Andrew Wilson to staff: "As we begin this next chapter, I'm more optimistic than ever about what we'll create together."
  • Comparable transactions: Microsoft's $68.7 billion Activision Blizzard acquisition and its $7.5 billion purchase of ZeniMax Media.

Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison published a guest essay in the New York Times on Tuesday, his first public response to the antitrust suits filed by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America to block the $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Key Takeaways
  • Regulatory Risk: A news asset carried inside an entertainment transaction imports political scrutiny that the entertainment logic of the deal cannot answer, and it will drive the review out of proportion to its share of the value.
  • Merger Advocacy: When a challenge attacks the buyer's fitness rather than the market math, the buyer's own reputation becomes a deal asset, and staying quiet cedes the record to whoever is willing to speak.

Why It's Happening
The plaintiffs sued on concentration. Ellison is answering on stewardship, because he believes the political anxiety about who controls CNN is what actually animates the case, and Trump has repeatedly cited CNN when discussing the deal. That reframing wins a narrative fight and does nothing for the market-definition fight a judge will rule on. The timing carries the rest of the message: the essay ran hours before an earnings call and days before a trial-date ruling that decides whether this closes in 2026 or 2027.

A leaked Microsoft memo asks publishers to let the next Xbox run five generations of games
Back CatalogMicrosoft's memo pitches publishers with the line "You keep rights, pricing, and brand control," and the console it is pitching may ship without a disc drive at all.
CEO Summary
A leaked Microsoft memo obtained by The Verge shows the next Xbox, codenamed Project Helix, is built to run games from all five Xbox generations plus PC titles, which would give it the largest library of any home console. The catch is that none of it is automatic: the memo is addressed to publishers and is a sales pitch, because each form of backwards compatibility requires the rights holder to opt in. One slide reads "You keep rights, pricing, and brand control." Microsoft has not decided whether Helix will include a disc drive.
Key Takeaways
  • Back Catalog: A platform cannot turn its own history into a product by itself, because every generation of the library has to be re-cleared with each rights holder one at a time.
  • Rights Retention: When a distributor leads its pitch with control rather than economics, it is telling you the scarce input is the owner's consent, and consent is what should be priced.
  • Consumer Ownership: Physical media is being converted into a licensing question, since a disc only follows its buyer to new hardware if the publisher agrees to let it.
Why It's Happening
The engineering is evidently solved. What is not solved is permission, which is why the internal document is a pitch deck rather than a spec, and why it dangles profit at publishers instead of announcing a feature. The pitch line itself is diagnostic: you offer rights, pricing and brand control when the other side's objection is loss of control rather than loss of money. The timing sits against a business under pressure, with Xbox revenue down 10 percent in the most recent quarter, hardware prices rising by up to 200 euros, and a CEO memo on priorities issued July 30 after a major reset and layoffs.
The Facts

  • Digitized Xbox One and Xbox Series discs can follow their owner to "any Xbox device," which includes Helix.
  • Microsoft has not decided whether Helix will have a disc drive.
  • Xbox revenue fell 10 percent in Microsoft's most recent quarter while its cloud and AI business grew. Xbox prices are rising by up to 200 euros or 170 pounds. The Xbox CEO issued a priorities memo on July 30 following a major reset.

A judge threw out Terrence Howard's 'Empire' pay suit because his loan-out company would have been paid, not him
Deal StructureFox contracted with Howard's loan-out, Universal Bridges, which paid him a fixed salary. The judge held that a higher fee would have raised the entity's revenue only, making damages too speculative for trial.
CEO Summary
Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Cherol Nellon dismissed Terrence Howard's 2023 suit against CAA on July 31, ending a case that had targeted packaging fees and alleged that conflicted advice cost him market-rate pay across six seasons of Fox's "Empire." The ruling turned on structure rather than conduct: Fox contracted with Howard's loan-out company, which paid him a fixed salary, so the court found that a successfully negotiated increase would have raised the loan-out's revenue without necessarily reaching him, making the alleged damages too speculative for trial. The court also found the agency did push Fox to renegotiate in 2018 and that Fox "rejected all attempts at renegotiation."
Key Takeaways
  • Deal Structure: A loan-out that pays its owner a fixed salary can sever the causal link between a negotiated fee and the artist's own loss, so a structure adopted for tax and liability reasons can quietly defeat that artist's later claim against anyone who advised them.
  • Fiduciary Risk: The most prominent packaging-conflict challenge in years was resolved without any ruling on whether the conflict existed, which leaves the disclosure question open for the next plaintiff whose compensation runs to them directly.
  • Documentation: Contemporaneous evidence that a buyer was asked and refused is what converts a performance claim into a dismissed one, which makes the record of asks and refusals a defensive asset for anyone negotiating on another party's behalf.
Why It's Happening
The court never reached the interesting question. The complaint was built on conflicted representation across a show's actor, its co-creators and its production company, and on the commission structure that rewards bundling them. Summary judgment resolved it two steps earlier, on whether the plaintiff could show he personally lost money.

The answer was that he could not, because the money would have landed somewhere else first. A loan-out that pays a fixed employee salary rather than passing through what it collects turns any counterfactual fee increase into revenue for the entity, and a court asked to award damages to the individual is left estimating what the entity might then have chosen to pay him. The second ground reinforced the first: the buyer was asked, the buyer refused, and evidence that the ask should have been framed differently does not establish that a different framing would have worked.
The Facts
  • Judge Cherol Nellon, Los Angeles Superior Court, dismissed the suit on summary judgment in a ruling issued July 31, 2026.
  • Howard sued in 2023, alleging conflicted advice led him to accept below-market pay across six seasons as Lucious Lyon on "Empire," and targeting packaging fees, the commission paid for bundling writers, directors and actors into one project.
  • He alleged his agents did not disclose developments undermining his leverage, or that the agency also represented co-creators Lee Daniels and Danny Strong and production company Imagine Entertainment.
  • Fox contracted with his loan-out, Universal Bridges, which paid him a fixed salary as an employee. Judge Nellon: "The immediate economic result of an increase in compensation would have been an increase in revenue to Universal Bridges only."
  • The court found alleged damages too speculative for trial, and separately found that the agency pushed to renegotiate while Fox held final say and "rejected all attempts at renegotiation."
  • The relationship soured in 2018 when his side sought profit participation, perks and promotional opportunities beyond the episodic fee; Fox declined to reopen the deal. Talks broke down again a year later over a request to raise the episodic fee from $325,000 to $750,000.
  • Claims brought: breach of fiduciary duty, constructive fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation.
  • A CAA spokesperson said the order made clear the uncontested evidence contradicted the foundation of the complaint, and that the agency sought to renegotiate with Fox in 2018 and Fox refused.

Amazon Prime Video has acquired Fox's Baywatch reboot across Italy, Germany, France, Spain, Portugal, Benelux, Switzerland, Austria, Turkey, Canada, Latin America and India, and will also stream the complete original back catalogue.   • IP Dormancy: A format 25 years off the air sold into more than a dozen markets, which means catalog dormancy is a marketing problem rather than a value problem, and rights holders should discount unexploited libraries more slowly than they do.
Why It's Happening
Twelve new episodes are the reason a buyer takes the meeting; 11 seasons of library are what actually fill the shelf, and Prime Video took both in one package. The territory map is the other half. The owner kept domestic in-house, hired an international distributor to run the rest, and sold Europe-plus to one streamer while a different buyer took the UK and Ireland. That is the pre-global-streamer model, chosen deliberately in 2026 by a rights holder who calculated the pieces clear for more than the whole.

  • Post-Merger Integration: A production consolidator is buying label identity and the relationships attached to it, so the integration test is how few labels get merged rather than how much cost gets stripped.
  • Talent Retention: A structure announcement is when a merger starts losing executives, because everyone who did not get the job finds out on the same day everyone else does.
  • Consolidation Limits: The territory where a merger's operations overlap most resolves last and sets the timetable for everything downstream, so the biggest market paces the integration, not headquarters.
Why It's Happening
Banijay bought creative brands, which is what "the stars are the companies within the group" is asserting, so the integration is deliberately shallow. Seven labels stay separate and the consolidation happens above them in the chief creative, operating and financial officer layer. The same-day departure of an EndemolShine Germany co-managing director to a direct competitor is the predictable cost of that design, and Deadline expects further movement as the remaining appointments land.

TKO Lost $30 Million Staging a UFC Event at the White House and Counted $1 Billion in Earned Media
Event EconomicsTKO lost $30 million staging the White House event and counted $1 billion in earned media against it, then raised guidance for the second time this year.
CEO Summary
TKO Group, the owner of UFC and WWE, reported Q2 revenue of $1.5 billion, up 18 percent, and raised full-year guidance for the second time this year. Executives confirmed the company lost about $30 million staging UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn of the White House, an event at which no tickets were sold. President and COO Mark Shapiro told analysts the night generated more than $1 billion in earned media value and added 25 new marketing partners, many on multiyear or multi-event deals.
Key Takeaways
  • Event Economics: A rights holder with enough scale can run a signature event as a partner-acquisition instrument rather than a profit center, and book the loss deliberately.
  • Portfolio Strategy: Diversification across several live properties is what buys the option to lose money on any one of them, which is why a single-property owner cannot copy this play.
  • Sponsorship: The durable output of a spectacle event is the partner roster it resets, not the gate, and multiyear partner commitments are the only part of an earned-media claim that shows up in later revenue.
Why It's Happening
The $1 billion earned-media figure is a company estimate with no standard methodology behind it, and it should be read as a directional claim rather than a measured return. The 25 new marketing partners are the checkable part, and they are the reason the loss was worth taking: partnerships revenue rose substantially at UFC in the quarter, alongside higher media rights from the new Paramount television deal. Meanwhile live events and hospitality revenue declined slightly, in part because no tickets were sold at the White House. The segments tell the story of the trade. TKO gave up gate revenue on one night and bought partnership inventory that recurs.

Shapiro also closed the door on repeating it, saying the company will not hold another event in the backyard of the White House while continuing to look for new venues and experiences. That is the tell that the play was about singularity, and singularity does not scale.
The Facts
  • Q2 revenue $1.5 billion, up 18 percent. Net income $303.9 million. Adjusted EBITDA $649.9 million, up 23 percent. All segments up year over year.
  • Raised 2026 guidance: revenue to $5.775 billion to $5.825 billion, adjusted EBITDA to $2.275 billion to $2.305 billion.

A $340 million default put Kaufman Astoria Studios under a third-party operator
Studio Real EstateDeutsche Bank foreclosed on a $340 million default and Shadowbox now runs a 500,000-square-foot lot it does not own.
CEO Summary
Shadowbox Studios has taken over management of Kaufman Astoria Studios in Queens, effective today. Deutsche Bank filed a foreclosure complaint in April against the 500,000-square-foot campus and then-owner Hackman Capital Partners over a defaulted $340 million loan; the court appointed a receiver, which appointed Shadowbox as operator. The 11-stage lot, built in the 1920s as Paramount's home, has hosted Goodfellas, Sesame Street, Succession and The Devil Wears Prada 2.
Key Takeaways
  • Studio Real Estate: Owning production real estate and operating it have separated into different businesses with different risk profiles, and only one of them was repriced by the production slowdown.
  • Distressed Assets: A working physical asset with a broken capital structure gets handed to an operator, not resold, because utilization is the recoverable value and leverage is not.
  • Counterparty Risk: Control of a soundstage can change hands inside four months through a process no tenant participates in.
Why It's Happening
The failure was financial, not operational. The campus kept booking premium episodic and feature work straight through; the loan came due last fall against a demand curve that had contracted since it was underwritten. A receiver's job is to preserve going-concern value, and the cheapest way to do that on a soundstage campus is to install someone who already runs stages elsewhere. Shadowbox now holds an operating footprint spanning Atlanta, Shinfield in the UK, a complex in development in Queensland, and New York, none of which requires owning the underlying land.
The Facts

A Court Upheld Howard Stern's NDA Covering His Personal Habits and Political Affiliations
Contract EnforceabilityA New York judge upheld an NDA covering Stern's personal habits and political affiliations because the assistant's consent and consideration were documented.
CEO Summary
A New York judge dismissed a lawsuit by Howard Stern's former executive assistant seeking to void her nondisclosure agreement. The agreement covers the personal affairs of anyone involved with Stern's production company, including his family and friends, plus his daily activities, personal habits and political affiliations. Justice Melissa Crane found the 2025 NDA valid, holding that the assistant knowingly consented as a condition of employment.
Key Takeaways
  • Contract Enforceability: Personal-conduct NDAs reaching well beyond business information survive challenge when consent and consideration are documented, so their strength lies in paperwork discipline rather than in drafting breadth.
  • Evidentiary Standard: A single acknowledging email can establish assent against a forgery claim, which means the practical fight over an NDA is about proof of signature, not about whether the scope was reasonable.
  • Employer Position: Courts treat routine remote administration of work devices as unremarkable, so an employee alleging fabricated records starts from a weaker position than the fact of employer access alone suggests.
Why It's Happening
Two mechanics decided this. Asked by a company employee to review the document, the assistant replied by email, "Signed NDA attached." The court treated that as knowing consent. It separately rejected the argument that the company's ability to administer her computer remotely supported the forgery theory, writing that such access "is not an unusual circumstance as many, if not most, employers can administer their employee's work devices."

The court also leaned on compensation as evidence the bargain was real, noting she was paid over $190,000 across nine months and that the agreement recited the company's reliance on her confidentiality promises in deciding to employ her. Notably the court did not narrow the scope of what the NDA covered. Enforceability was decided on ordinary contract grounds and the breadth of the subject matter was left intact.
The Facts
  • Justice Melissa Crane dismissed Leslie Kuhn's suit seeking to void her NDA. The suit also sought $2.5 million.
  • Kuhn was hired by SiriusXM in 2022 as office manager for The Howard Stern Show, then added to the payroll of Stern's production company One Twelve as his executive assistant. She was terminated for cause earlier this year and sued in April.
  • Two agreements were at issue, from 2022 and 2025. They cover the personal affairs of anyone involved with One Twelve, including Stern's family and friends, plus his daily activities, personal habits and political affiliations.
  • The July 29 order found the 2025 NDA valid, citing her "Signed NDA attached" email and payment of over $190,000 across nine months.
  • Stern separately guaranteed he would not enforce the 2022 agreement. The court declined his request for sanctions, finding no evidence of bad faith.
  • Kuhn had alleged a hostile work environment created by an animal rescue organization run by Stern's wife, and said she sought the order to respond to accusations against her and protect her employment prospects.

  • Calendar Congestion: Streamer-studio and independent wide releases are now dense enough on the far-out calendar to push a major off a date more than three years ahead of it.
  • Writer Leverage: When a studio schedules around an author's name on a first-time director's film, the script is the marketing asset, which is a rare and measurable form of writer leverage.
Why It's Happening
The date chosen is as informative as the date left. May 14 is a frame Warner Bros has used twice before, for Final Destination: Bloodlines and Mortal Kombat II, both mid-budget genre plays rather than tentpoles. Picking it over deeper summer positions F.A.S.T. as a pre-summer genre release wanting clean air more than a marquee weekend.

The vacated weekend now belongs to an Amazon MGM comedy and a Neon thriller. That a major moved rather than held against that pairing says something about how the studio reads its own opening: strong enough to want an uncontested frame, not strong enough to absorb competition for the same audience.
The Facts
  • F.A.S.T. moves from April 23, 2027 to May 14, 2027.
  • The vacated weekend holds Amazon MGM's Spaceballs: The New One and Neon's A Place in Hell.
  • May 14 is currently the only major studio wide entry on the date. Warner Bros previously launched Final Destination: Bloodlines and Mortal Kombat II in that frame.
  • Written by Taylor Sheridan. Feature directorial debut of Ben Richardson (1883, 1923).
  • Cast: Brandon Sklenar, Sam Claflin, Juliana Canfield, Trevante Rhodes, LaKeith Stanfield, Jason Clarke.
  • Producers: David Heyman and Jeffrey Clifford of Heyday Films; Taylor Sheridan and Jenny Wood of Bosque Ranch Productions.
  • Premise: a former special forces commando recruited by the DEA to lead a black-ops strike team against CIA-protected drug dealers.

The production structure around the show is itself unusual. Amazon MGM, Sony Pictures Television and PlayStation Productions are co-producing an adaptation of Sony-owned game IP for a competitor's platform, with a showrunner working under a Sony overall deal. Every one of those parties has a say in a lead casting change made under time pressure.

Dick Clark Productions Built a Studio to Sell Branded Content to Advertisers
AdvertisingDick Clark Productions built a studio to make branded content, and it will serve its own parent's new commercial unit as a client.
CEO Summary
Dick Clark Productions launched DCP Studios, a unit built to expand production capability around its awards franchises including the Golden Globes, the American Music Awards, the Academy of Country Music Awards and Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve. It will also serve as the branded production studio for PMX, the newly established commercial unit of parent Penske Media Corporation. Spider-Man: Brand New Day opens to $927M worldwide and drives the biggest weekend in box office history
Demand CapacitySony's own public projection was $425M worldwide and roughly $200M domestic; the film did $927M worldwide and $355M domestic, about double the studio's guidance in each case.
CEO Summary
Sony and Marvel Studios' Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $355M domestic and $927M worldwide, the second-biggest global debut ever behind Avengers: Endgame. The entire North American market hit a record $428.99M for the weekend per Rentrak, the first all-time domestic weekend record since 2019. Sony's own public projection had been $425M worldwide, and Universal's three-week-old The Odyssey held at -43% alongside it rather than being crushed.
Key Takeaways
  • Demand Capacity: A market's ceiling for event films is set by how many are scheduled, not by how many the audience will absorb. A record opening and a three-week-old tentpole coexisted without either one cannibalizing the other.
  • Guidance: A distributor's public projection on a top-tier franchise title is a floor it expects to beat, not its own forecast. Anyone pricing off studio guidance is pricing off a negotiating posture.
  • Franchise Value: Within a genre, franchise value stratifies rather than declines. A small tier keeps performing at peak-era scale while everything else in the same category resets far below it.
Why It's Happening
The guidance gap is the cleanest evidence. Sony projected $425M worldwide and reportedly guided around $200M domestic; the film did $927M and $355M. That is a 2x miss in the same direction a studio always misses on a title it is confident in.

The capacity point is the more useful one. The previous weekend carried zero new wide releases, on the industry's own assumption that nothing should stand near this opening. The Odyssey then held at -43% in its third frame against the biggest debut in history, and the two together produced the record. The scheduling caution was not supported by what the market actually did.

On stratification: this weekend also produced a clean tier map. A handful of superhero properties still return every three or four years at peak-era scale. Everything outside that tier now models to a $250M-$450M global range, with recent results ranging from $125M at the low end to roughly $520M at the high end. The category did not shrink, it sorted.
The Facts
  • $355M domestic opening, second-best all time, roughly $2M behind Avengers: Endgame's $357.1M record. $927M worldwide across 90,000 screens, second-best global debut ever.
  • North American marketplace: record $428.99M weekend for all titles per Rentrak. Variety reported ~$430M and TheWrap $434M; the Rentrak figure is the measurement-of-record number. Prior all-time record was $402M (final weekend of 2019); best post-Covid weekend was $311.3M (July 2023).
  • Weekend was +246% against the same frame a year ago. YTD domestic box office is $6.19B through August 2, +15% year over year.
  • Sony's public global projection was $425M; The Ankler reports domestic guidance around $200M.
  • International: $572M from 66 markets. China $121.0M, UK $49.0M (#3 all time), Mexico $38.3M (#2), India $31.8M (best ever for a Hollywood picture there, sixth-biggest opening in Indian history), South Korea $25.0M, Australia $21.4M, Germany $20.0M, Italy $18.2M, Japan $10.0M. All-time like-for-like opening records also set in France, Brazil, Spain, Peru, Colombia, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Chile, Turkey, Ecuador and Belgium.
  • Production budget $225M (The Ankler). 24.1M US tickets sold per Entelligence against ~20M for Spider-Man: No Way Home — about 20% more admissions for a 27% larger nominal gross.
  • CinemaScore A. Opening-night audience 63% aged 18-34, 60% male; 36% White, 28% Latino, 20% Black, 10% Asian, 6% Native American/other.
  • Universal's The Odyssey took $51M in its third domestic weekend, -43%, for a $911M global cume.
  • MCU lifetime grosses now $33.3B across 38 films.
  • Rentrak's Paul Dergarabedian: "the likelihood of a $4 billion summer and a $10 billion year just went up exponentially."
