Ellison may have built himself an exit from his own $111 billion Warner deal
Deal StructureWalking away costs Ellison $9.8B, a $7B breakup fee plus $2.8B to Netflix. Closing costs $113B, including $80B of fresh debt, against a standalone Paramount Skydance carrying $12B in net debt.
CEO Summary
David Ellison bypassed settlement talks with the state attorneys general and took the Paramount Skydance / Warner Bros. Discovery merger straight to trial, absorbing potentially $1B or more in ticking fees to do it. William Cohan's read is that the move is optionality rather than confidence: with a June 4, 2027 drop-dead date, Ellison now has eleven months in which he can decide the deal is no longer worth doing. The walk-away math is a $9.8B mistake, the $7B breakup fee to WBD plus $2.8B to Netflix, against a $113B one if he closes.
Key Takeaways
  • Deal Structure: In a long-dated, regulator-exposed acquisition, the drop-dead date is the real option. A buyer who pushes resolution far enough out has bought the right to reconsider the whole transaction, whatever the litigation does.
  • Seller Protection: A seller can now convert a buyer's regulatory risk into guaranteed return. Ticking fees plus a record breakup fee mean the selling shareholders get paid for delay and paid for failure, which makes a contested deal a floor rather than a coin flip.
  • Balance Sheet: An escape hatch is only usable by a buyer who can survive standalone. A $12B-net-debt acquirer whose stock keeps hitting new lows may have to close a deal it no longer wants, which is why leverage, not conviction, decides these outcomes.
Why It's Happening
The sell-side sequence is why the economics landed here. WBD declined an opening $19-a-share bid, put itself into Revlon mode, and signed a merger agreement with Netflix. That forced the Ellisons to $31 a share in cash, a 63% jump from their first bid. The agreement that followed carries the largest breakup fee ever recorded and a requirement that Larry Ellison personally backstop both the equity and the debt.

Ticking fees then added 25 cents per quarter between September and June, taking WBD shareholders to a potential $31.75. Cohan's point is that those terms are strategic documents rather than legal ones: they set who is exposed to time and who is paid for it.

The constraint on Ellison walking is scale. Paramount Skydance carries roughly $12B of net debt against an $8B market capitalization, in a field where Netflix is around $300B and Disney around $167B. Even combined, the two companies land near $113B, still below the five largest players. A standalone Paramount is the weaker outcome, which may leave the buyer with no real choice.
The Facts
  • Drop-dead date in the merger agreement: June 4, 2027. Ellison chose trial over settlement, absorbing potentially $1B+ in ticking fees.
  • Walk-away cost: $9.8B ($7B breakup fee to WBD, $2.8B to Netflix). Close cost: $113B, including a fresh $80B of debt and $42.5B of equity at risk.
  • Standalone Paramount Skydance carries $12B of net debt; market capitalization roughly $8B. PSKY closed at $7.96 on July 31 and continues to hit fresh lows.
  • Comparative scale cited: Netflix ~$300B, Disney ~$167B. Combined PSKY+WBD ~$113B.
  • WBD shareholder outcome: $31.75/share ($31 offer plus 25 cents per quarter of ticking fees, September through June). Zaslav personally receives an additional $550M on close.
  • Sale-process sequence: Ellisons' first bid $19/share, declined; Revlon mode; Netflix merger agreement signed; Ellisons raised to $31/share cash, a 63% increase. Largest breakup fee ever, plus a personal Larry Ellison backstop on equity and debt.
  • Cohan's read on a broken deal: Zaslav would take the $7B fee, pay down debt to investment grade, and revert to the June 2025 split-up plan.
  • Paramount reports Q2 on August 4. Trial-date positions are far apart: Paramount seeks November, the state AGs and WGA seek April.

Universal clears $4 billion worldwide first in 2026, carried by an original epic
Slate CompositionMinions & Monsters, Universal's own animated franchise entry, sits tenth on its own top-10 list at $427M global on an $85M budget, short of the half-billion mark prior entries cleared.
CEO Summary
Universal became the first studio to cross $4B worldwide year to date in 2026, ahead of Disney, split $1.53B domestic and $2.48B international. The milestone was reached with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey at a $911M global cume three weekends in, on a $250M budget and a $125M marketing spend. Universal and Focus hold five of the top 10 worldwide grossers of the year, including three of the top five, and none of those three is a live-action franchise sequel.
Key Takeaways
  • Slate Composition: A major can lead the year without a live-action franchise sequel in its top tier. Adaptation, biography, original epic and genre together carried this slate, which removes the premise that only owned sequel IP can anchor a studio year.
  • Budget Ceiling: A $250M original from a brand-name director is now a demonstrated billion-dollar asset class, which resets what non-franchise material can credibly be budgeted at.
  • Franchise Decay: A studio's historically reliable animation franchise can become the weakest performer in its own top 10 while the rest of the slate sets records. Franchise ballast erodes quietly, and it erodes while the headline number is strong.
Why It's Happening
The composition is the story. Only three films have crossed $1B worldwide in 2026 and two are Universal's, a video-game adaptation and a music biopic. The No. 4 title worldwide is a $250M original auteur epic. The No. 9 is a horror title that became a specialty label's highest-grossing film ever at $475M.

Universal led the global weekend box office ten times this year to get here. Meanwhile the animated franchise entry sits tenth on the studio's own top-10 list: profitable on an $85M budget, but at $427M global it will not reach the half-billion mark its predecessors cleared. The slate's strength and that title's softness are both real, and the second is the one worth tracking.
The Facts
  • First studio past $4B worldwide YTD in 2026, ahead of Disney (first past $3B at the end of June). Fifth time in Universal's history, first since 2023.
  • Split: $1.53B domestic / $2.48B international.
  • The Odyssey: $911M global cume at three weekends. Third global weekend $136.2M ($51M domestic, Nolan's best-ever third domestic frame; $85.2M international). Budget $250M, marketing spend $125M.
  • Only three films have crossed $1B worldwide in 2026. Two are Universal's (The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, Michael).
  • Universal led the global weekend box office 10 weekends in 2026.
  • Universal and Focus hold five of the top 10 worldwide grossers of 2026 and three of the top five: Michael (No. 2), The Super Mario Galaxy Movie (No. 3), The Odyssey (No. 4), Obsession (No. 9), Minions & Monsters (No. 10).
  • Obsession is now Focus Features' highest-grossing film ever worldwide at $475M, and also the highest-grossing film for Blumhouse and Atomic Monster.
  • Minions & Monsters stands at $168M domestic / $427M global on an $85M budget, profitable but short of prior franchise entries and short of the half-billion mark.

IMAX posted its second-best weekend ever without the biggest opening in history
Format AllocationShot entirely for ScreenX from set through exhibition, Brand New Day opened domestic ScreenX at $7M, 2.6 times the format's prior record, while IMAX stayed locked to The Odyssey through mid-August.
CEO Summary
Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $355M domestic on zero domestic IMAX screens, because Universal's The Odyssey holds the entire domestic IMAX network into mid-August and the 70mm screens into September. IMAX still posted $68M globally, its second-best weekend in history, with the format supplying 43% of The Odyssey's $51M domestic third weekend. Denied IMAX, Brand New Day drew 24% of its domestic opening from other premium large formats, including a record $31M global start in 4DX and ScreenX, a format it was shot for end to end.
Key Takeaways
  • Format Allocation: A premium-format screen commitment is a material deal term, not a marketing detail. When one format chain can supply 43% of a wide release's domestic weekend, the allocation is worth negotiating for at the same level as a release date.
  • Production Design: Native format capture beats up-conversion by a wide margin, which moves format from a distribution decision made months out to a production decision made at the start.
  • Exhibition Economics: A premium-format network's revenue tracks which title is programmed into it, not which title is biggest in the market. That decouples format performance from box office leadership and makes the window itself the scarce asset.
Why It's Happening
The two facts only make sense together. The largest opening in box office history got no domestic IMAX screens, and IMAX had its second-best weekend ever anyway. A three-week-old title holding the network outperformed, in that network, a debut nearly seven times its weekend size.

The film that lost the allocation did not respond with marketing. It responded with production. Brand New Day was photographed for ScreenX from set through exhibition, and domestic ScreenX opened at $7M, 2.6 times the format's previous record. Where the film did get IMAX, in the three markets The Odyssey has not opened in yet, it took $23M and set a franchise IMAX record in China.

The concentration on the other side is the risk worth naming. A title drawing 43% of its domestic weekend from a single format chain has extraordinary leverage in that relationship and extraordinary exposure if it ever loses the window.
The Facts
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened on zero domestic IMAX screens. The Odyssey holds the domestic network until The End of Oak Street on August 14, and keeps the 70mm IMAX screens into September.
  • IMAX network weekend: $68M globally, second-highest-grossing weekend in its history.
  • IMAX supplied **43% of The Odyssey's $51M domestic third weekend ($22.1M) and 26% of its $85.2M international weekend ($22.6M). IMAX cume on the title is $221M**, the No. 3 IMAX title of all time and the fastest any film has reached $200M in the format. 70mm locations did $5.1M this weekend for a $27.6M cume, about 12% of the IMAX total.
  • Brand New Day drew 24% of its $355M domestic opening from premium large formats (~$85M): roughly 17% of the total in 3-D, $10M+ Dolby Cinema, $7M ScreenX, $5.2M 4DX, plus undisclosed D-BOX records.
  • 4DX and ScreenX combined for a record $31M global opening across 1,111 screens ($17M 4DX, $14.4M ScreenX), against a prior combined record of $15.7M (Jurassic World: Rebirth).
  • Brand New Day was shot entirely for ScreenX, CJ 4DPLEX's first collaboration running from on-set production through exhibition. Domestic ScreenX opened at $7M, 2.6x the previous format record ($2.7M, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie).
  • Where Brand New Day had IMAX (China, Japan, Korea): $23M combined. China $19M, 16% of the territory opening and a franchise IMAX record there; Japan $2.2M, 18% of that market's debut; Korea $2.4M, 9%.

Marvel canceled Wonder Man after contracts were signed and the writers' room was scheduled
Greenlight RiskDisney announced the renewal in March; contracts were signed and a room was staffed to start this month before the reversal. The same week, Mahershala Ali said of Blade, "You had me under contract."
CEO Summary
Wonder Man showrunner and co-creator Andrew Guest said publicly on Saturday that contracts were signed and schedules cleared for the Marvel Television series' second season before Disney and Marvel reversed course and canceled it. Disney had announced the renewal in March; the writers' room was set to start this month and production early next year. Guest's account: "there was a decision made internally between Disney and Marvel that this didn't make sense for them, even though a few months ago it did."
Key Takeaways
  • Greenlight Risk: A publicly announced renewal plus signed contracts is not a commitment. The exposure sits in the window between announcement and production start, which is exactly the window in which everyone downstream behaves as though the project is certain.
  • Talent Cost: The real loss to a creator in a pre-production reversal is the cleared calendar, not the unpaid episodic fee. Holding-period compensation and release rights matter more as buyers re-underwrite slates inside a single quarter.
  • Buyer Behavior: A buyer re-running its economics quarterly will reverse decisions faster than its own public announcements can be corrected. Announcement cadence and decision cadence have come apart.
Why It's Happening
The sequence is what makes this unusual. The renewal was announced in March. Deals closed. A room was staffed with a start date this month. An episode was written and a season outlined. The reversal came after all of it, and Guest specifically ruled out the two explanations the market had assumed: that the show was being folded into a film, and that a director's calendar had forced it.

What is left is an economic re-underwrite. The same project cleared the bar a few months ago and does not clear it now, with no change to the project itself. That is a buyer whose internal hurdle rate moved, not a project that failed.

The pattern is not isolated to one show. In the same news cycle, Mahershala Ali publicly criticized the same studio over an unmade Blade, saying "You had me under contract."
The Facts
  • Guest, on TikTok Saturday: "This is not a marketing stunt. There is no movie in the works, and [Destin Daniel Cretton's] schedule and no one's schedule was an issue."
  • Guest: "Contracts were signed, schedules were cleared." The writers' room was scheduled to start this month; production was set to begin early next year.
  • Guest on the decision: "there was a decision made internally between Disney and Marvel that this didn't make sense for them, even though a few months ago it did. And that's essentially all I really know."
  • Disney announced the Season 2 renewal in March. Variety reported the cancellation in late July, before the second season launched.
  • Star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II won an Emmy for the role. His response: "Word just dropped that Wonder Man won't be coming back for Season 2... That's life, right? Everything will shake out."
  • Season 1 cast also included Ben Kingsley, X Mayo, Demetrius Grosse, Zlatko Burić, Arian Moayed and Olivia Thirlby. Co-creator Destin Daniel Cretton directed the first episode, and directed Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which opened to $355M domestic the same weekend.
  • Same news cycle: Mahershala Ali on the unmade Blade — "You had me under contract. They have billions of dollars. If they wanted to do it, we would've done it."

Discovery's $110B merger sits paused for up to eleven months pending the state attorneys general's antitrust suit, and Oliver was explicit about the reason for the timing: "We have various prospective business daddies circling, no one fully willing to commit just yet."
Key Takeaways
  • Contract Duration: During a live change of control, a short-dated renewal is the stronger position for talent with leverage. Matching contract expiry to deal resolution preserves the ability to renegotiate against a known owner rather than locking terms with one who may not exist in a year.
  • Talent Leverage: Awards standing and a portable audience are the two assets that survive an ownership change, because a new owner has to price them before touching the show. Everything else is subject to the new owner's discretion.
  • Assurance Value: Commitments made by a buyer before a merger are worth little after it. That is now on the record from marquee talent who has lived through several ownership changes at the same company, and it argues for terms that vest on signature rather than on stated intent.
Why It's Happening
Oliver named the mechanism himself: "business grownups will say one thing before a merger happens and their behavior can be very different afterwards... The rhetoric before a merger and the behavior after, that doesn't always match up. But there's nothing you can do, other than to make it clear that you're not going to be amenable to changes."

His formulation of leverage is the most portable line here: "You always want to be exactly as much trouble as you are worth. So the more you are worth to them, the more trouble you can cause." The awards record is what he calls the armor. Thirty-two Emmy wins from 76 nominations since 2014, plus over 2 million viewers streaming the show on YouTube alone, is the number a new owner has to look at before deciding the show is more trouble than it is worth.

A one-year term where three is the norm therefore reads as a scheduling decision, not a confidence signal in either direction. It puts the next negotiation on the other side of the merger's resolution.
The Facts
  • Oliver picked up an option to extend by one year, through the end of 2027. His prior contract was due to expire at year's end. Typical renewals for the show have run three years.
  • The Paramount / WBD $110B merger is paused for up to 11 months pending the federal antitrust suit brought by state AGs.
  • Oliver on ownership: "We have various prospective business daddies circling, no one fully willing to commit just yet."
  • Oliver on the merger: "Nothing's happening, and everything has stayed the same. That's the only way that we can really move forward, total denial."
  • Oliver on leverage: "You always want to be exactly as much trouble as you are worth. So the more you are worth to them, the more trouble you can cause."
  • Last Week Tonight has delivered HBO 76 Emmy nominations and 32 wins since 2014, with three more nominations this year. Oliver: the Emmys "have built us some level of golden armor over the years."
  • Over 2 million viewers stream the weekly deep dives on YouTube alone.
  • On legal exposure: "They think their job is to stop us getting sued. We think their job is to make sure that when we are sued, we win."

A festival backup file left in production exposed 13,535 industry contact records
Vendor ExposureThe cause was a plain-text backup left in the production environment, found via a public IoT search engine. A separate file held roughly 135,000 contacts Fowler says could seed phishing at scale.
CEO Summary
Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler found 666,369 Tribeca Festival records exposed online, spanning 2019 to 2026, after a plain-text backup file was left inside the production environment. One folder held 13,535 contact entries with names, addresses, phone numbers and emails for filmmakers and actors including Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Guillermo del Toro, Robert De Niro, Jennifer Lawrence and Angelina Jolie. The festival disputes the characterization, saying no talent had personal contact information disclosed and the records were largely public-facing business contacts; Fowler says he saw consumer email accounts in the file.
Key Takeaways
  • Vendor Exposure: Talent contact data concentrates in third-party event and festival infrastructure, which sits outside every studio's and representative's security perimeter. The weakest link in a talent data chain is usually the party with no security budget and no contractual obligation to have one.
  • Contract Gap: Festival, market and submission agreements are typically silent on data handling and breach notification, even though those are the entities actually holding the records. That is a solvable drafting gap, not a technology problem.
  • AI Risk Multiplier: A large contact list is a materially more dangerous asset than it was two years ago, because generating credible per-recipient phishing at scale has become cheap. Old exposures acquire new value.
Why It's Happening
The failure was mundane, which is the point. A backup was left in the production environment rather than taken offline, and it was stored in plain text rather than encrypted. Fowler found it with a public IoT search engine, and every data point was reachable by anyone with an internet connection and a browser.

The dispute over contents is worth holding both sides of. The festival's position is that the records were public-facing business contacts, largely representatives and front-office addresses, and that everything was removed promptly. Fowler concedes some entries were assistants, managers or publicists rather than principals, but says consumer email accounts were also present. Both can be partly true, and either version puts the same conclusion in place: the exposure surface is the operational layer around talent, not talent themselves.

Fowler's forward-looking point is the one that changes the risk calculus. He notes that a 135,000-address list can now be turned into credible individualized phishing at essentially no cost, which makes a historic leak an active threat rather than a closed incident.
The Facts
  • 666,369 exposed records, timestamps spanning 2019 to 2026, found via a publicly available IoT search engine.
  • Root cause per Fowler: "a human error of leaving the backup file in the database, and the backup file was in plain text, unencrypted."
  • One folder, "contacts," held 13,535 entries — names, addresses, phone numbers, emails. Cited: Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Guillermo del Toro, Ron Howard, Robert De Niro, Jennifer Lawrence, Angelina Jolie, Morgan Freeman, Rami Malek, Eva Mendes, Michael J. Fox.
  • A separate document held roughly 135,000 contacts, which Fowler assumes are mailing-list and event signups.
  • Festival statement: "None of the talent referenced in recent reporting had personal contact information disclosed. The vast majority of the information consisted of public-facing business contact information, including PR representatives, talent representatives, front office email addresses, information from the Festival website, and other information that was already publicly available. All information was removed promptly upon discovery."
  • Fowler's response: some contacts were managers or assistants, "but I saw a lot of consumer email accounts, like Google or Yahoo."
  • Fowler found no evidence anyone else accessed it, and credited the festival with responding "very fast and professionally."
  • Fowler on the AI multiplier: "you can feed it information and ask it to create a phishing email... and send it to 135,000 people, and somebody's going to open it."
  • Fowler's base rate: organizations that suffer a data incident "statistically don't have another one for three to five years since it becomes a primary focus."
  • Tribeca was co-founded in 2002 by De Niro, Jane Rosenthal and Craig Hatkoff. Its 25th-anniversary edition ran June 3-14, 2026.

CEO Summary
Warner Bros. Warner Bros. has made roughly six offers over three years; the most recent was declined with no counter. Key Takeaways
  • Sequel Options: A buyer that waives sequel options to close a package converts its own hit into the seller's leverage, and pays the difference on the next film.
  • Reversion: A dated reversion clause transfers pricing power to the rights owner as the date approaches, because the owner's fallback is a cheaper version of the project rather than no project.

The one-movie deal was the price of getting the film made at all. "Barbie" had stalled for years until Gerwig's take unlocked it, and the studio traded sequel optionality to secure her. That trade looked cheap against a $1.4 billion return and eight Oscar nominations; the bill arrives now, under a CEO being measured on cost discipline while the company's own sale sits in legal limbo.

The clock compounds it. Scheduling adds friction on top: Robbie is shooting an "Ocean's 11" prequel, Gosling has Marvel's "Ghost Rider" and a "Star Wars: Starfighter" promo tour, and Gerwig has a "Narnia" campaign early next year.

Licensed Shows Now Drive More Than Half of Netflix's New Subscribers

Parrot Analytics estimates that licensed series drove more than 53% of Netflix's global subscriber acquisitions in the first quarter of 2026, while making up only about 40% of the series on the platform. Netflix will spend roughly $20 billion on content this year, up 10%. The top individual acquisition driver was an original, "Bridgerton," at just over 360,000 signups, but the two titles behind it were licensed: the "One Piece" anime at 178,000 and "WWE Monday Night Raw" at 173,000.
Key Takeaways
  • Catalog Economics: Third-party libraries convert subscribers at a higher rate per title than originals, which makes licensed IP an acquisition asset rather than a cost line.
  • Rights Leverage: When a platform can attribute signups to specific titles, a library owner negotiates from measured performance instead of asserted value.
  • Retention: Live rights and deep back catalogs do different jobs, and the retention job is the one that compounds: WWE content is estimated to have prevented roughly 1.25 million quarterly churn events in year one of a ten-year deal.
Why It's Happening
Originals and licensed content are being bought for different reasons and the accounting has caught up. An event original concentrates global attention in a window and spikes acquisition. A completed multi-season library gives a new subscriber somewhere to go after the thing that brought them in, and a weekly live property gives them a reason to come back on a schedule.

The per-title gap is the arithmetic that matters. Forty percent of the catalog producing 53% of series-driven signups means the average licensed title outperforms the average original on acquisition efficiency, even as originals win the top of the chart. Both facts are true, and only one of them shows up in the headline content-spend number.
The Facts
  • Netflix expects roughly $20 billion in content spend this year, a 10% increase.
  • Licensed series have accounted for over half of global subscribers acquired by shows on the platform since Q1 2025, rising above 53% in Q1 2026.

Newsom Presses California's AG to Settle the Paramount-Warner Antitrust Suit
RegulationParamount agreed July 24 not to close the deal until June 2027 or five days after a ruling, whichever comes first, buying a year to lobby, settle or wear the states down.
CEO Summary
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has told people that state employment will suffer if the 12-state antitrust suit blocks Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, and his office has encouraged Attorney General Rob Bonta to resolve the case out of court, according to a Wall Street Journal report Friday. Bonta has independent authority to bring such suits and filed this one on July 13. Paramount agreed on July 24 not to close the acquisition until June 2027 or five days after the court rules, whichever comes first.
Key Takeaways
  • Regulation: State attorneys general with independent enforcement authority are now a distinct merger-risk layer, and one that responds to in-state employment arguments rather than federal policy alone.
  • Deal Timing: A defendant that trades speed for procedural position is betting the political environment improves faster than the delay damages the business, which is a bet on politics, not on law.
  • Buyer Behavior: A company whose own ownership is unresolved for up to a year stops making forward commitments, so counterparties should expect stalled greenlights and renewals rather than hard refusals.
Why It's Happening
The case has moved off legal ground. The states' complaint is about prices, output and content variety; the pressure now being applied is about jobs. Those arguments answer to different constituencies, and the governor's is the one a state official facing re-election politics has to weigh.

Paramount's July 24 concession is what created the window. By agreeing not to close until as late as June 2027, the company secured its procedural footing and simultaneously handed everyone a year in which to lobby, settle or wear each other down. Support has been arriving from outside the parties as well, including a Wall Street Journal op-ed from a major live-events and representation executive arguing the states should drop the case.
The Facts
  • Paramount's takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery is valued at $111 billion.
  • Twelve state attorneys general, led by California, filed suit July 13: California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Washington.
  • Bonta at filing: "There is no debate here: This merger will snuff out competition, drive up prices, diminish content quality, and produce fewer movies and shows each year."
  • U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín paused the merger July 20; the restraining order was extended July 23.
  • July 24 court filing: Paramount will not consummate the acquisition until June 2027 or five days after a ruling, whichever is earlier.
  • Reps for Newsom and Bonta declined the WSJ's requests for comment.
  • Cinema United has supported the suit; actors Benedict Cumberbatch, Alan Cumming and Benedict Wong called on the U.K. to block the merger.
  • Ari Emanuel, WME executive chairman and TKO CEO, published a WSJ op-ed Monday supporting the acquisition: "When government officials manipulate markets to reach political outcomes, antitrust stops protecting competition and starts threatening it."

FIFA Abandons Its $20 Billion Commercial Rights Sale After a Member Revolt
OwnershipEach member country would have gotten $20M upfront plus a doubled $5M annual stipend, and it still collapsed. FIFA's own COO said the administration had been "deceived."
CEO Summary
FIFA president Gianni Infantino has abandoned plans for FIFA Forward Enterprise, a $20 billion company that would have held the commercial rights to FIFA events including the World Cup, with roughly 20% sold to an investor group led by Joshua Kushner's Thrive Eternal. The retreat followed a UEFA threat to boycott all FIFA events, opposition from Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, the resignation of Infantino's senior strategy adviser, and a statement from FIFA's own chief operating officer that the administration had been "deceived." Infantino faces re-election at the FIFA Congress in March.
Key Takeaways
  • Ownership: Rights whose value depends on the continued participation of many parties cannot be financialized over those parties' objection, however the leadership is structured.
  • Valuation: When the asset is collective consent, the member payout is not the price that clears the deal, because what members are being asked to give up is control rather than income.
  • Governance: Internal defections signal a deal is dead earlier and more reliably than external opposition does, since staff have no incentive to posture.
Why It's Happening
The World Cup is not a property FIFA owns in the way a studio owns a film library. Its commercial value is constituted by member federations agreeing to compete in it. UEFA's boycott threat was therefore not a bargaining tactic against the asset, it was a demonstration that the asset does not exist without them.

The money on offer was real. Each member country would have received $20 million up front and seen its annual stipend double to $5 million. It still failed, which is the informative part: the objection was to a single president selling a stake in the members' collective franchise, not to the size of the check. When the COO says publicly that the administration was deceived and describes the plan as "the project of one person," the institution has already voted.
The Facts
  • FIFA Forward Enterprise would have been a $20 billion company controlling commercial rights to FIFA events, principally the World Cup.
  • Roughly 20% would have been sold to an investor group led by Thrive Eternal, run by Joshua Kushner.
  • Each member country would have received an initial $20 million and a doubling of its annual stipend to $5 million.
  • Infantino's Friday statement: the project "has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place."
  • UEFA threatened to boycott all FIFA events including the World Cup; Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation also opposed.
  • Carlos Cordeiro, senior adviser on global strategy and governance, resigned, calling the proposal "a bad deal" that would "mortgage" the sport's future.
  • COO Kevin Lamour said the administration had been "deceived," called it "the project of one person," and said he accepted he might lose his job over the stance.
  • Infantino is up for re-election to a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in March.

Two Tentpoles Leaked in Two Weeks and Both Still Set Records
Consumer BehaviorThe Spider-Man bootleg reached 5.9 million accounts over nine hours before takedown, and The Odyssey leaked the week before to 2.1 million views in two and a half hours. Neither dented openings.
CEO Summary
A bootleg copy of Sony's "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" circulated on X for roughly nine hours, reaching 5.9 million accounts before takedown. One week earlier, Universal's "The Odyssey" leaked on the same platform, reaching 2.1 million views in two and a half hours. Both films posted record numbers anyway: "Brand New Day" took $72 million in previews, the largest preview gross in history, ahead of "Avengers: Endgame" at $60 million.
Key Takeaways
  • Consumer Behavior: For an event film in its opening frame, demand is not primarily driven by access to the file, which means free availability does not substitute for the theatrical experience audiences are actually buying.
  • Risk: Leak exposure is asymmetric by title type, so a film without four-quadrant scale or a format hook carries the risk that a tentpole absorbs.
  • Distribution: Takedown enforcement cannot outrun distribution volume on a major platform, making the release-window structure the practical defense rather than the enforcement apparatus.
Why It's Happening
Two consecutive event films leaked on the same platform inside a week, which points at a systemic pre-release exposure rather than two unlucky breaches. Studios send infringement notices, but as Variety notes, the volume of posting on the biggest new releases outpaces removal.

What the leaks did not do is dent the opening. That is the useful evidence, and it should be read narrowly: these were the two largest films of the summer, one sold on premium format and one on four-quadrant franchise pull. Neither opening depended on scarcity of the file. The cost of a leak, if there is one, lands later and quieter, on the long tail and on international windows, where nobody publishes a comparison.
The Facts
  • The "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" bootleg was posted on X by an account named Fredrick Bryan at 6:05 a.m. PT and taken down around 3:25 p.m. PT.
  • It reached 5.9 million accounts, with over 143,000 likes and 10,000 reshares. Other accounts posted copies; most were removed quickly.
  • Sony had no comment.
  • "The Odyssey" leaked on X the prior week, reaching 2.1 million views within two and a half hours; the posting account was suspended.
  • Universal statement: "We became aware of the unauthorized posting of the film and immediately initiated takedown protocols. We take copyright infringement seriously and will pursue all appropriate remedies to protect our content and intellectual property rights."
  • "Brand New Day" grossed a record $72 million in previews including Tuesday early access, above "Avengers: Endgame" at $60 million in Thursday previews.
  • Variety did not specify the source or fidelity of the leaked file; a reader comment disputed the "high-quality" characterization.

A Stolen Screener Drive Turns Into a $105 Million Claim Against Netflix
Risk AllocationThe producers demanded $165 million before Netflix stopped sharing investigation details; the filed suit seeks at least $105 million, and both sides agree the copy was unencrypted.
CEO Summary
Writer-producer Simon Afram and his company Op-Fortitude sued Netflix in California federal court for at least $105 million after an unencrypted master of their unreleased WWII thriller "Fortitude," directed by Simon West and starring Nicolas Cage, was stolen from Netflix's Los Angeles office during an acquisition screening. Netflix says it does not bear the risk of loss for a film "delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," and that it withheld investigation details after a demand for $165 million. The producers say they paused sales because any buyer must now be told the film was compromised before release.
Key Takeaways
  • Risk Allocation: Who bears the loss when unreleased material is compromised is a term, and when it is left unwritten the party with a single asset absorbs it.
  • Valuation: The claim is that disclosure of a breach damages an asset's sale value even if nothing ever leaks, which would make content security a valuation input rather than an operating cost.
  • Seller Exposure: Independently financed films carry breach risk that studio-owned titles do not, because the exposure scales with how concentrated the seller's portfolio is, not with how carefully the material was handled.
Why It's Happening
Acquisition screenings routinely move finished, unreleased masters into a buyer's building on informal terms. In this instance the buyer specified the delivery format, the seller hand-delivered an unencrypted copy with verbal instructions to delete after screening, and ten days later the drive was gone along with several others taken from office desks. Netflix's head of film acquisitions called it "a first for us."

That informality is the whole dispute. Both sides agree the copy was unencrypted and both agree it was stolen, so the case turns entirely on which party the unwritten risk falls to. The damages theory then compounds it: the loss claimed is not piracy revenue but sale value, on the argument that every future distributor must be told the film was compromised, which the producers say changes acquisition terms, insurance and marketing.
The Facts
  • Suit filed Thursday in California federal court by Simon Afram and Op-Fortitude, seeking at least $105 million.
  • An unencrypted master copy was on one of several drives stolen from Netflix's Sunset Bronson Studios office last month; Netflix's investigation concluded the other drives were empty.
  • Netflix expressed interest after receiving promotional materials in December 2025 and requested a working cut in June.
  • Per the complaint, Netflix asked for the digital cinema package key so it could test the film internally. A producer hand-delivered the drive June 15, said the DCP was unencrypted, and instructed Netflix to delete the files after screening.
  • Netflix disclosed the theft ten days later. Sean Berney, head of film acquisitions, June 25: "This is a first for us. Unfortunately, someone stole a good amount of drives from our office desks this past week."
  • The suit says Netflix would not disclose whether it filed a police report and declined to involve the LAPD after the filmmakers filed their own.
  • Netflix says it stopped sharing investigation details after a law firm for Afram demanded $165 million for the film in what it called a "hostile attempt to extort money."
  • Netflix statement: it "disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," notes it does not own the rights, and says it offered to monitor piracy sites.
  • The producers say they paused sales despite domestic and international interest.

Spider-Man Sets the All-Time Opening-Day Record, and the Market Sets One Too
Theatrical DemandNRG's pre-release tracking had the domestic opening at $195M; exhibitors and Greenlight Analytics were at $260M-$300M. The film is tracking north of $330M.
CEO Summary
Sony and Marvel Studios' Spider-Man: Brand New Day is tracking to an all-time opening day of $167M to $173M including previews, past Avengers: Endgame's $157.4M, with an opening weekend estimated north of $330M at 4,487 theaters. Previews alone hit $72M, beating Endgame's $60M record. The full North American marketplace is heading for $407M to $412M across all films, which would beat the $402M all-films record set during Endgame's opening weekend in April 2019.
Key Takeaways
  • Theatrical Demand: The ceiling on theatrical demand never came down. It was waiting for the right title.
  • Forecasting: Pre-release tracking systematically understates the top end, and the miss is large enough to misprice a deal.
  • Premium Formats: Premium formats have become a revenue layer that can set records without IMAX in the mix.
Why It's Happening
The marketplace number is the one that matters. An all-films weekend of $407M to $412M beats a record set in April 2019, before the pandemic, before the strikes, and before the streaming reset. Every argument that theatrical's top end compressed structurally now has to explain a post-2019 high.

The forecasting gap is wide enough to be a commercial problem rather than a curiosity. NRG carried a $195M domestic opening estimate; exhibitors and Greenlight Analytics were at $260M to $300M; the film is tracking north of $330M. Any bonus threshold, escalator or greenlight case anchored to a pre-release projection on this class of title started from a number roughly 40% below the result.

A December Rights Reversion Is Doing the Negotiating on the Barbie Sequel
Rights StructureGosling is asking $20M and was just announced as Marvel's Ghost Rider. Mattel's own follow-up without this cast, Masters of the Universe, made $113.5M against Barbie's $1.4B.
CEO Summary
The sequel to 2023's Barbie has stalled at Warner Bros. over contracts with Margot Robbie, Ryan Gosling and filmmaker Greta Gerwig. Warner Bros. has until December to close all three deals or the rights revert to Mattel. Gosling is asking $20M, and was announced last week as the star of Marvel's Ghost Rider; Gerwig and writing partner Noah Baumbach have a story for the sequel but will not begin writing until a deal closes.
Key Takeaways
  • Rights Structure: A reversion date transfers negotiating power to the IP owner without the owner having to say anything.
  • Talent Leverage: Withholding work product and booking a competing commitment are the two moves that actually move a stalled negotiation.
  • Franchise Value: The value in a billion-dollar adaptation sits with the specific team, not the underlying property.
Why It's Happening
The arithmetic that settles the third point is on the record. Barbie grossed $1.4B. The same licensor's follow-up, Masters of the Universe, grossed $113.5M globally. Same brand equity, same corporate ambition, different filmmaker and cast. That spread is the quantitative case for a star's asking price, and it is unusually clean because the confounding variables are so few.

The clock is what makes this unusual. A studio negotiating against a deadline it did not set, on a property it does not own, is bidding against the possibility of losing the asset entirely rather than against another bidder. Mattel's CEO has said publicly the company will not let projects sit on the back burner, which tells the studio the reversion is not a bluff.

One detail worth noting for anyone reading the studio's position: the NYT reported the parent-company CEO rejected his own studio's offers as too generous, and the studio disputed the account. When a buyer's internal authority to close is publicly in question, the seller's incentive is to wait.
The Facts
  • Warner Bros. has until December to lock deals with Robbie, Gosling and Gerwig or the rights revert to Mattel.
  • Gosling's asking price: $20M. He was announced at San Diego Comic-Con last week as the star of Marvel Studios' Ghost Rider, directed by Shawn Levy.
  • WB Motion Picture Group co-chairs Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca, on the record: "We have a rights deal with Mattel in place and have made a series of big offers to try and finalize deals to make the next 'Barbie' film. Unfortunately, we have been unable to reach an agreement thus far."
  • Per the NYT, WBD CEO David Zaslav rejected the studio's latest offers to talent as "too generous." A Warner Bros. spokeswoman disputed the account and said talent representatives have not countered since declining a May offer.
  • Gerwig and Baumbach have a story but are withholding it, and will not start writing until a deal closes.
  • Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz, previously: "We expect projects to move and be in active development. We don't want to sit on the back burner."
  • Mattel's Masters of the Universe grossed $113.5M globally and is currently #1 on Prime Video.
  • Barbie (2023) grossed approximately $1.4B worldwide.

California's COMPETE Act Would Put Theatrical Windows And Multi-Picture Deals Under Antitrust Law
Buyer PowerAB 1776 extends the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time in its 119-year history, and adds monopsonization liability that has passed the Assembly and Senate Judiciary Committee.
CEO Summary
California's AB 1776, the COMPETE Act, has passed the Assembly and the Senate Judiciary Committee and now sits with Senate Appropriations. It would extend the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time in the statute's 119-year history, creating state liability for monopolization and, critically, monopsonization. Puck's Eriq Gardner reports the practices exposed run from theatrical windows to multi-film talent contracts to refusing to license content to competitors.
Key Takeaways
  • Buyer Power: Monopsonization liability would make buyer-side conduct actionable in California for the first time, and buyer-side power is what sets the price of talent.
  • Contract Structure: Long-form exclusivity, multi-picture commitments and output arrangements become litigable structures rather than settled ones, so they need to be drafted now against a statute that has not finished moving.
  • Regulation: The merger fight is a single transaction; this is the operating rules, and it will outlast whatever happens to Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.
Why It's Happening
The bill's mechanics matter more than its headline. It prohibits monopolization by "one or more persons," a deliberate break from federal law, which has always required domination by a single competitor. It also states that certain federal antitrust principles are "not required" to prove a claim, and amendments make federal precedent "at most instructive, not conclusive." That combination means California courts would not be bound by the body of federal case law that has made monopsonization claims almost unwinnable.

Gardner's reporting suggests the enforcement provisions may reach private plaintiffs, not just Attorney General Rob Bonta. If that survives, the exposure is not one state enforcer choosing its battles; it is every counterparty with a grievance and a California nexus. Note the symmetry: a statute that reaches "one or more persons" exercising buyer-side power does not only point at studios.
The Facts
  • AB 1776, the Competition and Opportunity in Markets for a Prosperous, Equitable and Transparent Economy (COMPETE) Act, introduced by Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry on 2026-03-23.
  • Status: passed the Assembly, passed the Senate Judiciary Committee, referred to Senate Appropriations.
  • Would create state-law liability for monopolization, attempted monopolization, maintenance of monopoly power, and monopsonization.
  • Extends the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time since its enactment 119 years ago.
  • Puck reports exposed conduct includes theatrical windows, multi-film talent contracts, and refusals to license content to competitors.
  • Bonta is separately leading the multi-state challenge to the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, alongside the WGA.

Newsom Pushes California Toward a Paramount Settlement While Both Sides Fight Over the Calendar
RegulationParamount pays $7M a day past Sept. 30 and owes a $7B break fee if the deal fails, so it filed for a Nov. 4 trial. The states and WGA filed for April 5, 2027.
CEO Summary
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that California Gov. Gavin Newsom has warned that state employment could suffer if the $110B Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger is blocked, and that his office has encouraged Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle out of court. In a separate Friday filing, Paramount asked for a 12-day antitrust trial starting Nov. 4, 2026, while the 12 state attorneys general and the WGA asked for April 5, 2027. Past Sept. 30, the deal costs Paramount a ticking fee of roughly $650M per quarter, or $7M per day.
Key Takeaways
  • Regulation: Antitrust enforcement against a media merger is politically contestable when the enforcing state carries the job losses.
  • Deal Timing: Delay has become the challengers' cheapest and most effective leverage, because only one side is paying for it.
  • Market Structure: The remedy on the table would create buyers rather than remove them.
Why It's Happening
The calendar is now the whole negotiation. Paramount is paying $7M a day to wait and owes a $7B break fee if regulatory failure kills the deal. The states pay nothing to delay. That asymmetry is why Paramount asked for November and the challengers asked for April, and it is why the eventual concession package is likely to be larger than the CNN divestiture the market has been assuming.

Bonta has already described what he wants, and it is not a divestiture list. He has said the states prefer structural remedies over behavioral ones: a suite of cable channels kept separate, a separate streaming service, a separate news channel or TV studio, a separate film studio. That is a disassembly plan. If any meaningful part of it lands, the market ends with more independent buyers than it has today, which is the opposite of what consolidation planning assumes.

Newsom's intervention is the genuinely new variable, and note which argument moved him. Not consumer prices, not output. Jobs. An LA County analysis put roughly 2,500 local and 6,000 global positions at risk, and a deeper Department of Economic Opportunity study on production workers lands Aug. 18. Employment evidence is what is reaching decision-makers in this fight.
The Facts
  • Newsom has warned that blocking the merger could hurt state employment and his office has encouraged Bonta toward an out-of-court settlement (WSJ). Representatives for Newsom, Bonta and Paramount declined to comment.
  • Trial dates: Paramount filed for a 12-day trial starting Nov. 4, 2026. The state AGs and WGA filed for April 5, 2027, running 12-15 days, allowing a merits decision by June 2027.
  • Paramount called the April request "nothing more than a stonewalling tactic." The states and WGA called a compressed schedule "unworkable, unfair and unjustified."
  • Bonta: "This challenge deserves careful and thorough review and today my office and attorneys general across the country asked the court for a trial date next spring."
  • Cost of delay: past Sept. 30, WBD shareholders receive 25 cents per share quarterly, roughly $650M per quarter or $7M per day. A regulatory failure triggers a $7B termination fee. Closing is deferred to five days after the trial outcome or June 1, 2027, whichever is earliest.
  • Remedy preference: Bonta has said the states want structural remedies, explicitly beyond a CNN sale: separate cable channels, a separate streaming service, a separate news channel or TV studio, a separate film studio.
  • Alleged concentration: 27% of wide-release theatrical distribution, 30% of anticipated blockbuster films, 27% of the basic cable bundle.
  • Jobs: LA County Board of Supervisors analysis found roughly 2,500 local and 6,000 global jobs at potential risk. A deeper Department of Economic Opportunity analysis on production workers is due Aug. 18.
  • Cleared: DOJ, WBD shareholders, the European Commission (conditioned on a UIP exit), plus Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, China, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, South Africa, Ukraine, Montenegro, New Zealand, North Macedonia, and FDI authorities in Spain, Germany, Slovenia, Belgium, Czechia, Italy, France and Romania. The UK CMA decides by Aug. 7.

Netflix And Prime Video Take France's Windowing Rules To Court
RegulationARCOM offered Prime Video $103M a year for a window beyond 12 months or $126M a year for a window at 12 months, meaning roughly $23M buys several months of exclusivity.
CEO Summary
Netflix and Prime Video have each filed separate challenges at the Conseil d'État, France's highest administrative court, against the country's streaming windowing and investment rules. Netflix's industry agreement lapsed at the end of 2025, pushing its release window from 15 months back to the default 17 while its obligation to invest 20% of French revenue in local production continues. Prime Video's convention with regulator ARCOM expired days ago and was extended six months while talks continue.
Key Takeaways
  • Regulation: Netflix has shifted its ask from an earlier window to a cap on mandatory investment, which means the precedent it is now chasing is the one that travels to every other European market.
  • Windows: France has effectively published an exchange rate between window length and spend, and that number is usable anywhere windows are negotiated.
  • Incumbent Leverage: Canal+ has bought a contractual veto over window reform, so the pay-TV incumbent, not the regulator, is the binding constraint on what the streamers can win.
Why It's Happening
The Canal+ mechanism is the part most people will miss. Its new $1.1B five-year commitment buys a six-month window, but the agreement is tied to the current balance of the system: if any streamer gets inside 12 months, Canal+'s deal automatically triggers a three-month renegotiation and Canal+ risks dropping to nine months. So every concession the regulator might grant Netflix or Amazon reopens a signed billion-dollar contract. That is why the streamers went to court instead of back to the table.

The ARCOM proposal to Prime Video is the cleanest number here: $103M a year for a window beyond 12 months, or $126M a year for a window at 12 months. Roughly $23M buys several months of exclusivity. Nobody usually shows that math in public.
The Facts
  • Since January 2022, SVOD services must invest 20% of annual French revenue in local production under France's implementation of the EU AVMS Directive.
  • Netflix's industry agreement expired end-2025, not renewed. Window slipped from 15 months to the default 17. Free-to-air broadcasters get films at 22 months, leaving Netflix five months of exclusivity.
  • Netflix invests $287M+ annually in French content, including roughly $68M in theatrically released films.
  • Source close to Netflix: "For us, it's an unsustainable equation: more obligations, a less favorable release window, and the latest Canal+ agreement locks in the current system."
  • Netflix argues U.S. streamers could fund nearly half of all French production by 2030 (estimates cited by Le Monde).
  • ARCOM's proposal to Prime Video: $103M/year for a window beyond 12 months, or $126M/year at 12 months.
  • Prime Video wants Disney's nine-month slot; ARCOM refused, noting Disney directs 14% of French revenue to cinema, above the minimum.
  • Canal+: $1.1B over five years buys a six-month window; any streamer inside 12 months triggers a three-month renegotiation.
  • Netflix skips Cannes annually because Palme d'Or competition requires French theatrical release.
  • Netflix, Prime Video and Disney+ have jointly filed a further challenge to amendments to France's SMAD decree.

The window restoration and the creator point are the same story told from two ends. The Marcus argument worth repeating in a greenlight room: small and mid-sized originals made the quarter "less dependent on the success of individual tentpole films." CEO Summary
Sony Pictures Entertainment posted June-quarter revenue of $1.978B, down 13%, while operating income rose 21% to $156M. The decline came from two places: television production revenue fell 32% to $571M on fewer series deliveries, and the studio released a single film in the period, generating $30M in theatrical revenue versus $132M from four releases a year earlier. Sony group revenue rose 8% to ¥2.837T ($17.8B) and net income rose 32%, and the company raised full-year operating income guidance 8%.

  • Studio Economics: A studio with no streamer grew operating margin through a quarter with one release, which is the strongest evidence yet that the arm's-length model holds up through a thin slate.
  • Commissioning: Television production revenue for a studio-for-hire moves with how many series a buyer orders, not with how any single show performs, so a 32% revenue drop can happen without any show failing, purely on delivery timing.
  • Platform Strategy: The one part of Sony's portfolio behaving like a streamer is a vertical subscription service, not a general-entertainment one, showing a niche vertical can scale into a real platform asset without a full-catalog play.

The top line looks worse than the business is. Sony put one movie in theaters in three months and still expanded studio operating income by a fifth. What the quarter actually prices is volatility: without a subscription base, earnings ride on delivery timing, so the quarters are lumpy by construction. The offset arrives immediately, since Spider-Man: Brand New Day opens into the September quarter off the best previews in company history.

The number to keep is Crunchyroll, past 21 million paid subscribers and still growing. Sony's one genuine platform asset is a vertical, not a general-entertainment service, and it is the only part of the picture behaving like a streamer.

LightShed published nine questions for Disney ahead of its August 5 fiscal Q3 earnings, and correctly predicted a day early that Disney would sell its 50% A&E Networks stake to Hearst at a low single-digit EBITDA multiple. Its lead question: if a low multiple justifies exiting A&E, what multiple would justify the same logic on ESPN and ABC.   • Portfolio Strategy: Selling A&E at a low multiple forces Disney to state a principle, and any principle that justifies it reaches ESPN and ABC too.
  • Guidance Reliability: A management denial that a business will be separated is not a reliable signal, since Comcast said the same about NBCUniversal in January before reversing under stock pressure.
  • Platform Strategy: Disney is now the last closed ecosystem among its peers, closed to third-party streaming ingestion, absent from vertical video, and holding licenses rather than ownership in games.
Why It's Happening
The consistency trap is the whole note. LightShed's framing is not that Disney should sell ESPN, it is that Disney has to explain what synergy case for keeping ESPN and ABC "does not apply equally to A&E." Management's answer on August 5 becomes the quotable position for a year, and the Comcast reversal is the named precedent for not believing it. LightShed's stated reason Comcast moved: its stock was under pressure. Their observation about Disney: the stock "hasn't moved in over a decade."

The other seven questions are variations on openness. Peacock, Netflix and Fox are all making platform pushes, and Peacock will soon sit inside YouTube Premium. Disney+ ingests only Hulu and ESPN. The Facts

Private Equity Has Repriced the Representation Business Into the Mid-Teens
ValuationEBITDA multiples for talent agencies have moved from low double digits into the mid-teens. One investor puts the EBITDA bar for a public listing at $300M.
CEO Summary
EBITDA multiples for talent agencies have risen from the low double digits to the mid-teens, according to a financial source cited by The Ledger, and nearly every major agency is now controlled by an investment firm. Recent marks include Silver Lake's $25B take-private of Endeavor, Artemis buying a CAA minority stake from TPG at a $7B valuation, Goldman Sachs Alternatives taking majority control of Excel Sports Management for about $1B, and Providence Equity Partners buying out Casey Wasserman's stake in The Team at a reported $3.4B valuation. Investors interviewed name sports exposure as the driver.
Key Takeaways
  • Valuation: Representation has been reclassified from a services business with key-man risk into infrastructure with recurring cash flow, and the multiple moved to match.
  • Sports Rights: What investors are buying is athlete and creator monetization, not entertainment commissions.
  • Ownership: The businesses that represent talent now change hands on a financial sponsor's clock, and that clock shapes how they behave.
Why It's Happening
The stated investment thesis has shifted, and the people quoted are explicit about it. The original case was diversification: exposure to the rising value of content and talent without the project-level risk of financing films. The current case is levered exposure to sports rights and influencer monetization without paying team-ownership prices. That is a different asset being bought under the same name.

The exit math is the part worth writing down. One investor puts the threshold for a public listing at $300M of EBITDA, which sorts the field cleanly: firms above it have an IPO route, and firms below it are structurally pointed at sponsor-to-sponsor sales. The practical consequence for anyone doing business with these firms is repeated ownership turnover at the mid-size tier, with the incentives that come with a hold period ending.

One precedent is worth knowing. When a sponsor took a position in a mid-size firm in 2023, it issued equity to key agents and employees, then funded acquisitions to build out sports, digital and brand businesses. That is now a documented template for how these transactions retain the people whose relationships are the asset.
The Facts

A Munich Court Says It Can Hear AI Training Cases No Matter Where the Training Happened
JurisdictionGEMA's general counsel said Munich can hear the claim regardless of where Suno's training took place. It is GEMA's second German win in nine months, after November's ruling against OpenAI.
CEO Summary
A regional court in Munich ruled Friday that AI music service Suno violated copyrights by training on works covered by the German licensing agency GEMA, ordering it to disclose illicit revenue and pay unspecified damages. Suno disputes the ruling and is weighing an appeal. GEMA's general counsel said the decisive point was jurisdictional: the agency can sue in Munich regardless of where the training took place. It is GEMA's second German win in nine months, after a November ruling against OpenAI over song lyrics.
Key Takeaways
  • Jurisdiction: Where a work can be enforced now matters as much as who owns it.
  • AI Licensing: Rights holders no longer need to win the American fair-use argument to make an AI company pay.
  • Collective Licensing: Pooled enforcement is producing results that individual litigation has not.
Why It's Happening
The copyright finding is ordinary. The jurisdictional holding is not. A collecting society can bring a claim in Munich against a company that trained its models elsewhere, which means any AI service operating in a European market is exposed to any European rights body with standing, no matter where the servers sat.

Compare the two routes. The American cases, including the studios' suit against Midjourney over Star Wars and Superman IP, turn on fair use, a genuinely unsettled question that is years from resolution. The European route does not require reaching that question at all. Two German rulings in nine months have produced disclosure orders and damages while the US standard is still being argued.

That asymmetry sets a floor under licensing negotiations. An AI counterparty that can be ordered to open its books in Munich has a reason to license in advance that does not depend on how a US court eventually rules.
The Facts
  • A regional court in Munich ruled Friday that Suno violated copyrights when it used music covered by GEMA. Suno must disclose any "illicit revenue" and pay unspecified damages, and can appeal.
  • GEMA filed the suit in January 2025.
  • Kai Welp, GEMA general counsel: the ruling was "very gratifying to see the assessment of the legal situation in the USA and the fact that we can sue in Munich regardless of where the training takes place."
  • Tobias Holzmüller, GEMA CEO: "AI models based on the theft of intellectual property do not enjoy legal protection. AI providers must acquire licenses and cannot simply help themselves to our members' works for free... If systems are operated in Europe, legal action can be taken before European courts."
  • Suno spokesperson: "From the beginning, we trained our models to create new songs, not reproduce existing ones... We disagree with today's ruling — which rests on a fundamental mischaracterization of how Suno's technology works, how it is used and how U.S. law applies." Suno does not expect the decision to affect its US cases.
  • Wolfram Weimer, Germany's minister of state for culture and media, called it an "important signal for strengthening the rights of creatives in the digital music market."
  • Second German win: a German court ruled for GEMA against OpenAI over song lyrics in November.
  • US comparison: Warner Bros., NBCUniversal and Disney are suing Midjourney over unauthorized use of copyrighted works including Star Wars and Superman IP. Midjourney argues fair use.

Spider-Man's $309M Promo Partner Campaign Is An All-Time Record
MarketingThe $309M partner campaign exceeds the film's $225M net production cost, and it excludes licensing revenue entirely since Disney, not Sony, holds Spider-Man's merchandise rights.
CEO Summary
Sony says the promotional partner campaign for Spider-Man: Brand New Day carries a worldwide media value of $309M, an all-time record for a Hollywood film, beating Sony's own $288M on Spider-Man: Far From Home in 2019. The campaign involves 165 brands, led by Little Caesars in the U.S. and McDonald's internationally, followed by Samsung and BMW. The figure excludes licensing money, because Disney holds Spider-Man's licensing and merchandise rights.
Key Takeaways
  • Marketing: Third-party partner media on this film exceeds its $225M net production cost, which means the largest marketing budget behind a tentpole is now money the studio does not spend.
  • Talent Economics: Sony is publicly counting cast social reach as campaign infrastructure, naming Zendaya's 216M following alongside its brand partners, which puts an owned audience inside the compensation conversation rather than the publicity rider.
  • IP Ownership: A studio can set an all-time marketing record and still not capture the full value it created, because Disney's separate hold on Spider-Man merchandising sits outside Sony's number even at peak campaign performance.
Why It's Happening
Sony EVP Jeffrey Godsick explains the 165-brand structure as a deliberate mosaic: "When you have a collection of partners like this, you're able to speak to different constituencies, instead of igniting one demographic." That is a different model from the single anchor partnership, and it exists because no one brand reaches an 8-to-80 audience.

The excluded line is worth noting. Most studios fold licensing revenue into reported campaign values; Sony cannot, because Disney holds Spider-Man merchandising. So $309M is the floor of the comparison, not the ceiling, and the gap is a standing reminder of what the Marvel arrangement gave away.
The Facts
  • Worldwide promo campaign media value: $309M, an all-time Hollywood record. Prior record: Sony's $288M on Spider-Man: Far From Home (2019).
  • 165 brands in the campaign. Excludes licensing partner money; Disney holds Spider-Man licensing and merchandise rights.
  • In-film product placement: Little Caesars, Samsung, ASUS, BMW, Liquid I.V. First-time Sony partners: Liquid I.V., Samsung, Takis, poppi.
  • Little Caesars (U.S. fast food) and McDonald's (international) lead campaign value, followed by Samsung and BMW. Little Caesars' Webberoni Pizza box is reselling used at $100 on eBay; its Peter Parker apartment recreation drew 20,000 RSVPs.
  • Samsung launched a "Spidey Tracker" tied to Jacob Batalon's Ned Leeds. BMW wove the Neue Klasse iX3 and 5 Series into the story.
  • RelishMix social reach: 2.86 billion across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram, an all-time firm record, ahead of Endgame (2.4B) and Infinity War (2B), and 3.2x superhero-genre norms. Cast: Zendaya 216M, Tom Holland 70M, Jon Bernthal 5.3M.
  • Godsick: Spider-Man is "a true 8- to-80-years-old movie, it's for everybody."
  • Expected global opening cited: ~$470M.

ITV Studios Goes Independent With U.S. Revenue Down 17%
ConsolidationSky is buying ITV's broadcast arm but not ITV Studios, and separately committed £2.1B to Studios content between 2028 and 2032, a supply guarantee on a business it declined to own.
CEO Summary
ITV posted its first results since confirming the £1.6B sale of its Media & Entertainment arm to Sky, with total H1 revenue up 2% to £1.9B and a £100M share buyback announced. ITV Studios, which is not being sold and is going independent, grew UK revenue 17% but saw U.S. revenue fall 17% and international fall 24%, reversing years in which American streamers drove its growth. Its EBITDA fell 9% while the broadcast arm's rose 37% on World Cup advertising.
Key Takeaways
  • Consolidation: An unowned ITV Studios facing a merged Banijay/All3Media sets up the next round of European production consolidation, with ITV Studios as either buyer or target.
  • Commissioning: A production studio's growth thesis built on American streamer orders can reverse within a single half, because commissioning volume, not audience demand, sets that revenue line, and it can unwind as fast as it built.
  • Deal Structure: A buyer can lock in supply certainty on a business it declines to acquire by committing multi-year content spend as part of the consideration, a cheaper claim on future output than ownership.
Why It's Happening
The 17% UK gain against a 17% U.S. loss is the cleanest read in the numbers. The domestic broadcaster relationship held; the streamer relationship did not. For a producer whose growth thesis for several years was inroads with the American platforms, that is a thesis break, not a soft quarter.

The deal structure alongside it is unusual and worth studying: Sky is buying the network and separately committing £2.1B to ITV Studios content between 2028 and 2032, a business it declined to acquire. An output guarantee is being used as part of the consideration for a transaction it is not part of. Regulatory risk remains live, with Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy expected to issue a Public Intervention Notice and completion not expected until mid-2027.

  • ITV Studios by region: UK +17%, U.S. -17%, international -24%.
  • £100M ($140M) share buyback, described by CEO Carolyn McCall as "an early return of part of the previously announced £950 million net cash return expected on completion of the sale." Interim dividend held at 1.7p (£60M).
  • Sky deal value £1.6B; completion expected mid-2027; Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy expected to issue a Public Intervention Notice.
  • Sky has committed £2.1B to ITV Studios content, 2028-2032. Sky-owned Love Productions (Great British Bake Off) will be sold to ITV Studios.
  • Banijay's CEO played down reports of interest in acquiring ITV Studios this week, following the Banijay/All3Media merger.
  • H2 deliveries include Line of Duty S7 (BBC) and another series of The Gentlemen (Netflix).

Fremantle Builds A Global Scripted Hub Under Katie O'Connell Marsh
Buying AuthorityFremantle did not replace Christian Vesper, who left in January. It created a new division and gave O'Connell Marsh the group's entire scripted investment budget instead.
CEO Summary
Fremantle has named Katie O'Connell Marsh CEO of a newly created Fremantle Global Scripted Hub, a drama and film division built around the role. She starts in August, relocating from the U.S. to London, reporting to Group COO Andrea Scrosati with a dotted line to commercial chief Jens Richter. She will oversee Fremantle's annual scripted investment budget across all of the group's scripted labels.
Key Takeaways
  • Buying Authority: Fremantle's scripted spend now routes through one executive in London rather than label by label, so any approach map built on the old structure is obsolete in August.
  • Consolidation: European independent producers are centralizing scripted commissioning authority into single global hubs at the same time U.S. streamer demand for third-party content is contracting, making these hubs a more concentrated buyer set than before.

The structural move matters more than the hire. Fremantle did not replace Christian Vesper, who left in January; it created a division and handed one person the scripted investment budget plus a seat in the commercial forecasting process. That consolidates both the creative call and the money behind it.

Timing is the second point. This lands the same week ITV Studios goes independent and after Banijay absorbed All3Media. The European independent producer tier is centralizing its commissioning authority at exactly the moment U.S. streamer commissioning is contracting, which makes these hubs a more consequential buyer set than they were eighteen months ago.

Snapchat Bars Fully AI-Generated Video From Spotlight as Meta Promises Infinite Content
DistributionSnap still allows AI-edited content on Spotlight, only banning wholly synthetic video, the same morning major music labels proposed rules to keep AI tracks off the charts.
CEO Summary
Snap said Friday it will ban wholly AI-generated videos from Spotlight, the product that surfaces trending and original content from creators and studios. Content enhanced or edited with Snapchat's AI creative tools remains eligible. The announcement came one day after Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg promoted the company's Muse image and video models as producing a "nearly infinite universe of personalized content," and the same morning the major music labels proposed rules to keep AI-generated tracks off the charts.
Key Takeaways
  • Distribution: AI rules are landing on where content gets surfaced, not on how it gets made.
  • Provenance: Human authorship is now a condition of reach on at least one major platform, which makes it an asset worth documenting.
  • Platform Policy: There is no industry standard forming here, which turns cross-platform distribution into a per-platform compliance problem.
Why It's Happening
Look at where Snap drew the line. It did not restrict the tools; creators using its AI editing features keep their eligibility. It restricted fully synthetic output from the surface that determines distribution. That locates the value in provenance rather than technique, and it is a far more enforceable rule than trying to police process.

The same mechanism appeared twice in one morning in two different industries. Snap gated distribution on Spotlight; the major labels proposed gating chart eligibility. Neither prohibits the technology. Both make the reward conditional. That is the template other platforms and ranking systems are likely to copy, because it is the version that can actually be administered.

The divergence with Meta is the risk to plan around. One platform is treating generated content as inventory to be maximized and the other is treating human authorship as the scarce good. A creator strategy that performs on one may be ineligible on the other.
The Facts
  • Snap will ban wholly AI-generated videos in Spotlight, which surfaces trending and original content from creators and studios.
  • Snap statement: "As low-quality, repetitive, AI-generated content becomes increasingly common across the internet, we want Spotlight to remain a place where people can discover authentic creativity from real people, because we believe there's enduring value in rewarding original perspectives, personal storytelling, and the moments that people choose to create and share themselves."
  • AI-assisted content stays eligible. Creators who have "enhanced or edited using Snapchat's AI creative tools" remain eligible; Snap says "for some, AI plays an important part of the creative process, and we believe it can unlock incredible new forms of expression."
  • The target is prompt-driven output, increasingly common as video models such as Google's Nano Banana and Seedance improve.
  • Mark Zuckerberg, Thursday, on Meta's Muse image and video models: they could lead to a "nearly infinite universe of personalized content." He added, "This is going to make our services a lot more useful and engaging for people."
  • Same morning, the major music labels proposed rules to keep AI-generated tracks off the charts.
