Angel Studios Polls Its Audience Before It Buys, and SK Global Sold Into It
GreenlightingAngel's guild members vote on projects before acquisition, and that same feedback data then sets the film's P&A spend. The Brink of War opens Aug. 14 as the first test.
CEO Summary
Angel Studios, the Provo, Utah-based faith-based distributor, acquired SK Global and 2521 Entertainment's The Brink of War, starring Jeff Daniels as Ronald Reagan and Jared Harris as Mikhail Gorbachev, for an Aug. 14 release. SK Global head of film Elizabeth Haggard says the film went through Angel's guild program, in which members vote on the projects the company takes on, and that the resulting data also informs how it sets P&A.
Key Takeaways
  • Greenlighting: A distributor that polls a committed membership has demand evidence before it spends, which is a different mechanism from tracking.
  • Distribution: The targeted mid-budget film has buyers again, just not the ones that used to buy it.
  • Audience: The addressable audience is being defined more broadly than faith, which is what makes the model scalable rather than niche.
Why It's Happening
The gap this fills is structural rather than a matter of taste. Majors have optimized their slates for titles that scale globally. A drama about the 1986 Reykjavík Summit with a defined domestic audience does not fit that optimization regardless of its cast or quality, which is how a film with Jeff Daniels and Jared Harris ends up at a Utah distributor instead of a studio.

What is genuinely novel is the sequence. Membership voting happens before acquisition, and the same signal carries through to the print and advertising decision. That is demand evidence generated by the distributor rather than purchased from a tracking service, and it is available at the point where the money is actually committed.

Read the enthusiasm with care. This is a supplier praising its distributor in an interview two weeks before release, with no performance data yet. The mechanism is the durable part; the verdict is not in. Aug. 14 is the first checkable test of whether a membership vote predicts an opening.
The Facts
  • Angel Studios acquired rights to **SK Global's co-financed production The Brink of War, produced with 2521 Entertainment, starring Jeff Daniels as Ronald Reagan and Jared Harris as Mikhail Gorbachev, set during the 1986 Reykjavík Summit. Release date Aug. 14.
  • Elizabeth Haggard, SK Global EVP and head of film, on the mechanism: Angel runs a guild program that allows members to vote on the projects the company makes**, and "if they're excited about distributing a movie, they look at the data coming out of [guild feedback] to see if their core audience responds." The Brink of War received "a lot of love."
  • Haggard: "It almost has that early tech company feel; their data is really sound and really exciting. You see that carry through the way that they market the movie, the way that they make decisions about P&A."
  • On the market gap: "It may be harder for a major studio to release a film at this level with a targeted audience that can satisfy that audience, but Angel is able to do that."
  • On audience definition: "it's not even just the faith-based audience, but there's an adjacent audience that is folks who want to watch movies that are family-friendly, that are values-friendly."
  • Haggard was promoted earlier this year. Prior: assistant to Donna Langley at Universal, then Ramona Films (produced A24's Zola), then SVP of narrative film at Participant Media.
  • SK Global, formerly Sidney Kimmel Entertainment, has a slate history including Crazy Rich Asians, Anyone But You and Hell or High Water.

Disney Sells Its Half of A+E to Hearst for More Than $1 Billion
Linear StrategyThe deal is Disney's first actual sale of a linear asset, and comes months after CFO Hugh Johnston said in May the company had no plans to spin off or sell linear networks.
CEO Summary
Disney is selling its 50% stake in A+E Global Media, parent of A&E, History, Lifetime and FYI, to co-owner Hearst Communications for north of $1 billion in cash. The deal is being finalized and is expected to be announced at Disney's earnings call next week. It is the first linear asset Disney has actually sold, and it comes after CFO Hugh Johnston reaffirmed in May that the company does not plan to spin off or sell linear TV networks.
Key Takeaways
  • Linear Strategy: A company's public commitment to holding linear assets describes its core networks, not its whole portfolio.
  • Portfolio Strategy: A major with a franchise core will shed profitable non-core assets rather than restructure wholesale.
  • Asset Quality: Profitable media assets with owned IP can still attract strategic buyers despite negative sentiment around linear television.
Why It's Happening
Nothing about A+E's economics forced this. The company is profitable, carries no debt, owns an unusual share of its own programming, and was early to FAST. That combination is why Hearst wanted it and why the price cleared $1 billion: the fastest exit from a cable asset is the co-owner who already knows it, not the public market. Hearst also keeps a seat at the table, holding 18% of ESPN alongside its now-full ownership of A+E.

The structure is the reason it moved quickly. A 50-50 joint venture with a cash-rich partner needs no auction, no separation costs and no new management team: Paul Buccieri stays, now reporting to Hearst CEO Steven R. Schwartz. Wholly owned networks like FX, Freeform and National Geographic have no such shortcut, which is exactly why the questions on next week's call will be about them.

  • Process: the owners retained Wells Fargo a year ago. Starz, Roku and private equity firms kicked tires early; Hearst emerged as the likely buyer months ago. Started under Bob Iger, closing under Josh D'Amaro.
  • Management: A+E President and Chairman Paul Buccieri expected to continue under Hearst CEO Steven R. Schwartz.

  • ESPN ownership: Disney 72%, Hearst 18%.

Apple's Services Miss Is a Box Office Story

CEO Summary
Apple reported fiscal Q3 revenue above $109 billion, up 16%, with Services at a record $30.7 billion but below both guidance and consensus. Asked why, CFO Kevan Parekh named foreign exchange and one film: last year's quarter included the theatrical release of F1: The Movie, and this year's did not. Apple TV viewership hit an all-time high, Apple landed a record 89 Emmy nominations, and Tim Cook signed off on his 90th and final earnings call before John Ternus takes over September 1.

  • Earnings: For the first time, a theatrical release was named by the CFO of the world's largest company as a reason a reported segment missed.
  • Streaming Economics: Apple TV no longer has to be justified as a brand exercise, which changes what a filmmaker is actually selling into.
  • Slate Cadence: A slate that produces one $634 million title and then nothing creates the comp problem Apple just absorbed twice.

$190 million domestic and $634 million worldwide is a strong result for a sports drama and a rounding error against $109 billion in quarterly revenue. It still showed up, because Services is where Apple books it and Services is the segment Wall Street prices most aggressively. The film did not have to be large relative to Apple. It had to be large relative to the growth rate of a $30.7 billion line.

The awards case is now the second proof point and it is unusually specific: 89 Emmy nominations leading all networks in both major drama and comedy categories, Widow's Bay as the year's most-nominated new program with 19, and a Tony completing the set faster than any streamer in history. Six and a half years in, Apple has bought a permanent seat at the prestige table. What it has not bought is a reliable annual theatrical event, and the June quarter is what that gap costs.

All 55 UEFA Members Vote to Boycott the World Cup Over FIFA's Stake Sale
GovernanceUEFA's 55 members voted to sit out FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, unless FIFA drops its plan to sell roughly 20% of a $20 billion entity to private investors.
CEO Summary
All 55 UEFA member associations voted Thursday at an emergency meeting to boycott FIFA competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups, if FIFA proceeds with selling roughly 20% of a new entity called FIFA Forward Enterprise, valued at about $20 billion, to private investors. Joshua Kushner's Thrive Eternal is among the reported potential buyers. Concacaf has also objected. The first test arrives in October, at the Women's World Cup play-offs.
Key Takeaways
  • Governance: UEFA and Concacaf together hold fewer than half of FIFA's 211 member associations, but a World Cup without European national teams is not the product anyone licensed, giving a minority bloc outsized veto power over the whole competition.
  • Securitization Precedent: The line between licensing rights to a competition and selling ownership in the competition itself is becoming the template distinction other event properties, awards shows included, will be tested against as private capital looks to buy in.
  • Leverage: Years of private capital buying into leagues and rights vehicles met no organized resistance until this vote, which resets what a buyer can expect the next time consent, not just price, is on the table.
Why It's Happening
The distinction is precise: licensing the rights to a competition is ordinary business, while selling an ownership interest in the competition itself makes commercial return a permanent obligation on every future decision about formats and calendars, which is what UEFA says it will not accept.

The money on offer is real: annual member payments rising from $2 million to $5 million, plus a one-off $20 million per association. That is transformative for small federations and irrelevant to large ones, which is precisely how the vote split.
The Facts
  • All 55 UEFA member associations voted to boycott FIFA competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups and the Club World Cup, if the plan is approved. Reported by BBC Sport following Thursday's emergency meeting. FIFA announced the plan Tuesday.
  • Vehicle: FIFA Forward Enterprise, valued at about $20 billion. FIFA would sell roughly a 20% stake.
  • Potential investor named: Thrive Eternal, led by Joshua Kushner, per the Financial Times.
  • Use of proceeds: raise annual member payments from $2 million to $5 million, plus a one-off $20 million payment to each association.
  • Approval requires ratification by FIFA's 211 national member associations. UEFA has 55, Concacaf has 41.
  • Concacaf cited a "lack of due process" and said the plan was revealed before any discussion with governance bodies.
  • UEFA statement: "The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product." And: "The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation."
  • UEFA said no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition "for so long as these proposals remain alive," absent binding assurances FIFA will never again open governance or competitions to private ownership.
  • FIFA president Gianni Infantino has framed the plan as "the democratization of [soccer] worldwide."
  • First test: October, Women's World Cup play-offs.

An AI Question Killed a $2.4 Million Book Deal and Its Film Rights
CopyrightHodgman withdrew the book after writing she could no longer authenticate how the manuscript evolved, once the author's assurance that no AI was used could not be substantiated.
CEO Summary
The unpublished debut novel Call Me, I'll Hide the Body sold to Minotaur/Macmillan for a reported $2.4 million across two books, with international rights selling and film and TV interest building. On Thursday the foreign-rights agent withdrew it, writing that she could no longer authenticate how the manuscript evolved from origin to completion after the author had assured her no AI was used. UTA and Europa Content, who were selling the rights, are no longer involved.
Key Takeaways
  • Copyright: The deal died because nobody could underwrite the copyright, not because anyone objected to AI.
  • Authorship: A manuscript with no documented evolution is now unverifiable in either direction, which puts every unpublished debut in the same bucket, including the ones written by hand.
  • Diligence: An AI representation in the paper is no longer sufficient; buyers will want evidence before the option, not a warranty after it.
Why It's Happening
The mechanism is specific. AI-aided text is treated as an amalgamation of other copyrighted works, so publishers and studios may be unable to register copyright or establish a clean chain of title. As Deadline puts it, a rights buyer could end up with no more protection than someone publishing a work in the public domain. That is not a reputational risk that can be papered over with an indemnity from a first-time novelist who cannot fund it.

Festivals have been arguing about AI for two years and settling nothing, because they were arguing taste. Cannes banned AI films from its official lineup this year; Tribeca screened one. This is the first time the market itself has spoken, and it spoke about title. Title is the argument that moves money, and it will move faster through literary acquisitions than any guild rule.
The Facts
  • Sale: Call Me, I'll Hide the Body to Minotaur/Macmillan for a reported $2.4 million covering the novel and a follow-up. Deadline has withheld the author's name.
  • Withdrawal: Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary, selling foreign rights for Europa Content, pulled the submission Thursday. Her email, obtained by Deadline: "we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion. During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with [the author] for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilizing AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book."
  • UTA and Europa Content had been selling the rights; Deadline reports both are no longer involved. Momentum had accelerated after a large U.S. offer was set.
  • Deadline reports it is routine for publishers and reps to ask authors about AI use, and that all parties proceeded in good faith on the author's assurance. Questions arose once rights began selling worldwide.
  • The commercial mechanism: publishers and film companies may be unable to register copyright or establish a clear chain of title with AI elements in the mix, because AI-aided copy is an amalgamation of many other copyrighted works.
  • The book: protagonist Femi Johnson trades "cleaner" origins in Lagos for a chemistry PhD in Houston; his ability to make bodies disappear leads to work for a cartel operator.

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is sold out in IMAX 70mm through late August in Las Vegas, August 19 in New York and Los Angeles, and September 10 in London, on a global footprint of just 41 screens. Spider-Man: Brand New Day opens this weekend without a single IMAX screen in North America because The Odyssey has all of them, and is still tracking past $200 million domestic. Key Takeaways
  • Premium Format: Nolan, Coogler and Villeneuve have turned a shooting choice into screen allocation and pricing power. "Shot for IMAX" belongs in the deal, not just the campaign.
  • Screen Allocation: One filmmaker just locked the entire North American IMAX footprint for six weeks. Studios can no longer assume availability when they date a tentpole.

Some of the premium share gain measures supply, not demand. PLF screens are the largest auditoriums in the building and get the most showtimes for the biggest releases, so a rising percentage partly reflects where theaters put their inventory. The scarcity number is the one that changes behavior. Forty-one IMAX 70mm screens worldwide, 25 in the US, means the format is a bottleneck rather than a feature. Brenden Theatres in Las Vegas needed 48 days of IMAX technical help to revive a booth that had not run 70mm since Interstellar in 2014, and is now turning a three-hour film six times a day at $51.75 a seat. Netflix Sued for $105 Million After a Screener Drive Was Stolen Off a Desk
LiabilityThe producers say Netflix knew for a week that an unencrypted DCP of the $45 million Fortitude was stolen, before disclosing it under the subject line "Stolen PCP."
CEO Summary
Producer Simon Afram and Op-Fortitude Limited sued Netflix in federal court in Los Angeles seeking at least $105 million, claiming an unencrypted digital cinema package of the $45 million World War II thriller Fortitude, starring Nicolas Cage, was stolen from a Netflix desk after being delivered for an acquisition screening. Netflix says it does not bear the risk of loss on a film delivered "without the proper industry-standard safeguards" and alleges the producers demanded $165 million rather than work with the company in good faith.
Key Takeaways
  • Liability: This is not a piracy case, it is a fight over who owns the danger while a finished film sits in a buyer's building.
  • Contract Terms: Custody deadlines, encryption requirements and breach-notification windows are absent from most submission paperwork and should not be.
  • Seller Risk: A $45 million negative with no distribution and one master out of the seller's hands is the profile least able to absorb the loss.
Why It's Happening
Read Netflix's statement closely, because "industry-standard safeguards" is carrying the entire argument. The position is that the standard of care sits with the party delivering the asset, not the party holding it. If that holds up, every independent seller who ever walked a drive into a buyer's office is exposed, and the fix has to happen in the paper before delivery rather than in court after.

The timeline is the plaintiffs' strongest material. The screening was around June 16. The producers say they were told on June 25, with a subject line reading "Stolen PCP," and that Netflix had known for potentially a full week. Netflix's executive reportedly reassured them the drive would be sold for scrap because unlocking a DCP requires a key. This DCP had no key, and the complaint says Netflix knew that.
The Facts
  • Filed Wednesday in U.S. District Court, Los Angeles, by Simon Afram (producer, writer, financier) and Op-Fortitude Limited. Damages sought: at least $105 million.
  • Claims: conversion, breach of bailment contract, breach of implied contract.
  • The unencrypted DCP was delivered to Netflix for screening and possible purchase, with instructions to delete the files after screening.
  • Per the complaint, Netflix screened around June 16, then "failed to provide the promised instructions for picking up the unencrypted DCP for over a week." On June 25 a Netflix executive emailed with the subject line "Stolen PCP": "someone stole a good amount of drives from our office desks this past week."
  • The executive said security teams had "no luck" and piracy teams were "on high alert," and that the drive would likely be "sold for scrap given that they require" a key. The complaint alleges Netflix knew the DCP was unencrypted and openable without a key.
  • The film cost over $45 million to make. The complaint says Netflix refused to disclose whether it filed a police report and, on Tuesday, refused to involve the LAPD in its private investigation.
  • Netflix statement: it "disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," says it does not own the rights to Fortitude, has conducted a thorough investigation and offered piracy-site monitoring, and declined to share details "given their hostile attempts to extort money from Netflix over this situation, including immediately demanding $165 million for the film."
  • A Netflix source says there is no evidence the film has leaked.
  • Fortitude: directed by Simon West, with Nicolas Cage as double agent Dusko Popov, plus Matthew Goode, Ben Kingsley, Ron Perlman and Michael Sheen.

The WGA East Walked Away From a 12-Year Festival Sponsorship Over an AI Sidebar
LaborSpikes learned the WGA East was dropping its 12-year Urbanworld sponsorship through a forwarded email, over the festival's new AI Sidebar built with the New School.
CEO Summary
The Writers Guild of America East ended a 12-year sponsorship of Urbanworld, the BIPOC-focused New York film festival, over the festival's new "AI Sidebar," which will screen AI-generated films and host tech demos in partnership with the New School. Founder Stacy Spikes learned of the decision through a forwarded email; the guild declined to comment and said its decision stands. Cannes banned AI films from its official lineup this year; Tribeca screened one last month.
Key Takeaways
  • Labor: A guild has now defunded a festival for hosting the conversation, which is a different line than refusing to screen an AI work.
  • AI Policy: A film made with AI tools is eligible at one festival, banned at the next, and unbondable at a third, and that is the real cost to filmmakers.
  • Distribution: A film that cannot premiere where a distributor needs it to premiere is worth less regardless of its merits.
Why It's Happening
Spikes is not making an argument for AI. He is making an argument about influence: walk away from the venue and you forfeit the ability to shape what young filmmakers do with the tools they are already using. "There's young kids right now that are playing with this technology," he said, and if the guild is absent from that room it cannot say "here's how we will help you get paid." That is a strategic disagreement inside the labor-side coalition, and it is now public.

The practical effect lands hardest on the people with the least capacity to absorb ambiguity. An established filmmaker can navigate inconsistent festival rules. A first feature cannot, and the tool decisions get made long before anyone reads a submission policy.
The Facts
  • The WGA East dropped out as a sponsor of Urbanworld's 30th edition in October, ending a 12-year partnership.
  • Trigger: the festival's new "AI Sidebar," launched with the New School, screening AI-generated films and shorts plus conversations and tech demos for AI tools.
  • Spikes learned of the decision through a forwarded email and requested a call. "There wasn't a lot of insight into their full thinking process." And: "Given a 10-year relationship, you don't want it to go up in flames like that." The guild said its decision would stand.
  • Spikes acknowledged the guild sponsors do not write "massive checks," but worried the move could affect the pipeline of submitting filmmakers.
  • Spikes: "The danger is for people to start to tell creators what tools they can and cannot use is a very slippery slope." And: "How they make their movies is not something that we, you know, we don't have a dog in that fight."
  • The WGAE declined to comment or make anyone available. It has run an #AINeedsHumans campaign and made AI a pillar of its 148-day 2023 strike.
  • The AI category has not been an issue for other Urbanworld sponsors, whom Spikes declined to name.

NBCUniversal's New CFO Comes From the NFL
Executive MovementHalpin spent nearly a decade at the NFL, most recently as chief strategy and growth officer, before becoming COO and CFO of People Inc., formerly IAC.
CEO Summary
NBCUniversal named Christopher Halpin chief financial officer ahead of its spin-off from Comcast, effective September 8. Halpin was COO and CFO of People Inc., formerly IAC, and before that spent nearly a decade at the NFL, most recently as chief strategy and growth officer. He reports to Mike Cavanagh, who becomes NBCU's CEO after the separation, which Comcast expects to complete by next summer.
Key Takeaways
  • Executive Movement: A spin-co that picks an NFL strategist over a studio finance executive is telling investors what it thinks it sells.
  • Studio Positioning: Positioning a project at NBCU now means arguing downstream value across Peacock and Sky, not prestige.

Why It's Happening
Cavanagh said it plainly: Halpin has built businesses "across sports, media and entertainment, the areas that will drive NBCUniversal's growth in the years ahead." Note the order. This is a company preparing to be underwritten on distribution and live rights, with Universal as a contributor rather than the headline.

Comcast is running the Versant playbook a second time, and the pattern now holds across the majors: separate the growth story from the declining one, then staff the growth entity with capital-markets and sports operators rather than programming executives. A counterparty this deep into a public-debut buildout is optimizing its balance sheet first, which is worth factoring into the timing of any renewal falling inside the next twelve months.
The Facts

  • Comcast has said the split should be completed by next summer, following the approach used with Versant, now separately traded.
  • Cavanagh: "Chris has spent his career helping build and grow leading businesses across sports, media and entertainment, the areas that will drive NBCUniversal's growth in the years ahead."

Jason Cloth, Financier Behind Joker And Longlegs, Charged In A $100 Million Ponzi Scheme
DiligenceThe Ontario Securities Commission alleges Cloth raised more than $500 million from over 500 investors between 2013 and 2022 and diverted at least $70 million.
CEO Summary
Jason Cloth, the film financier behind Joker, Longlegs, Babylon and Judas and the Black Messiah, was arrested Tuesday and charged with seven counts of wire fraud in a federal indictment alleging he and his Creative Wealth Media Finance Corp. fraudulently obtained more than $100 million from investors. Creative Wealth was the principal financier of Bron Studios, which went bankrupt in 2023. A parallel Ontario Securities Commission proceeding alleges Cloth raised more than $500 million from over 500 investors between 2013 and 2022 and diverted at least $70 million; final arguments there are set for August 4.
Key Takeaways
  • Diligence: Joker grossed over a billion dollars. The quality of the slate told investors nothing about the structure underneath it, because the films were the product being sold, not the thing being audited.
  • Financing Risk: Any package leaning on one private financier needs the money verified at source, with escrowed production funds, before talent attaches.
  • Capital Costs: The next round of non-studio equity will price in disclosure and oversight that this decade of film finance never required.
Why It's Happening
The scale is the reason this is a market event rather than a crime story. The Canadian regulator's numbers, $500 million raised and $70 million diverted, represent a meaningful share of a decade's independent film equity moving through a single intermediary with essentially no verification between the capital and the slate.

There is live exposure attached. Filmmakers financed through Creative Wealth or Bron may have deferred fees, unpaid backend, and rights sitting inside a bankruptcy or a federal forfeiture estate. Prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of at least $12.25 million "for the projects," which puts specific titles inside a federal proceeding.
The Facts
  • Cloth, 60, of Beverly Hills, was arrested Tuesday and arraigned in Los Angeles. A 12-page indictment was filed the same day in US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.
  • Seven counts of wire fraud, each punishable by up to 20 years in federal prison.
  • Prosecutors allege Cloth and Creative Wealth obtained more than $100 million from an Illinois investment adviser, that adviser's clients and other investors on false representations, while intending to use funds for other purposes including a Canadian real estate development, and used some investor funds to repay prior investors.
  • Forfeiture sought: at least $12.25 million.
  • Credits over roughly a dozen years include Joker, Longlegs, Babylon, Judas and the Black Messiah, Ghostbusters: Afterlife, The Birth of a Nation, The Addams Family and its 2022 sequel, Americana, Goodrich and the series Kin.
  • Creative Wealth was the main financier of Bron Studios, which filed for bankruptcy and closed in 2023. Both had been prior targets of investor lawsuits.
  • A 2021 Southern District of New York suit by investor Hudson Private alleged misappropriation and non-repayment on 2017–2020 film loans, claiming Bron owed at least $14.3 million plus interest on films including Bombshell, Capone, The Survivor and Greyhound, and that Cloth made "various knowingly false representations."
  • The Ontario Securities Commission alleges that between 2013 and 2022 Cloth and Creative Wealth raised more than $500 million from over 500 investors in Canada and the US, diverted at least $70 million, and collected tens of millions in loan-facilitation fees. Final arguments before the Capital Markets Tribunal: August 4.

DAZN is becoming the exclusive streaming home for MSG Networks and the YES Network, absorbing their linear feeds and on-demand programming as the 2026-27 NHL and NBA seasons begin. Both networks are abandoning the Gotham Sports App, the joint streaming venture they launched only in 2024, which will wind down after the migration. The rights covered include the Yankees, Knicks, Rangers, Nets, Devils, Islanders and Sabres. ESPN executives had publicly courted regional sports network programming since launching their flagship streamer last summer and did not win it.
Key Takeaways
  • Streaming Scale: If the two best-positioned RSNs in America cannot sustain a streaming venture after two years, that is a live warning for any mid-size content owner weighing the same bet.
  • Sports Rights: A Blavatnik-backed challenger beat the incumbent aggregator for the largest sports market in the country. That is a real read on what ESPN is currently offering rights holders.

This is an operating-cost decision dressed as a distribution deal. YES and MSG hold New York's marquee inventory and roughly the best RSN economics in the country, and they still concluded that running a streaming platform is not a business they should be in. Deadline notes the persistent technical complaints about the Gotham app, which is the polite version of the same finding.

DAZN's position is the other half. It has 20 million paying subscribers worldwide but has been a boxing-and-soccer niche in the US. One deal buys it instant relevance in the largest media market in the country, and turns it into a live American buyer.
The Facts

  • Both networks migrate off the Gotham Sports App, launched in 2024, which winds down after the migration.
  • Rights covered: Yankees (YES); Knicks and Rangers (MSG); plus the Brooklyn Nets, New Jersey Devils, New York Islanders and Buffalo Sabres. SNY, whose anchor tenant is the Mets, streams via the MLB app and was never in the Gotham JV.
  • Pay-TV subscribers to YES and MSG get DAZN-streamed programming at no extra charge.
  • DAZN, backed by Len Blavatnik, recently reported 20 million paying subscribers worldwide, with strength in Europe and a US presence focused on boxing and soccer.

  • Jon Litner, CEO, YES Network: the partnership "reflects the YES Network's continued commitment to elevate the streaming experience for our direct-to-consumer subscribers and TV Everywhere users."

Crunchyroll And Starz Bundle On Prime Video At $16.99
Platform StrategyCrunchyroll has grown to 21 million subscribers from 5 million when Sony bought it from AT&T in 2021, and now bundles with Starz's 17.6 million on Prime Video at $16.99.
CEO Summary
Starz and Crunchyroll launched a US bundle through Prime Video at $16.99 a month, 23% below the combined standalone price. It is Crunchyroll's first such US pairing. Crunchyroll, a Sony Pictures Entertainment division, has grown to 21 million subscribers from 5 million when Sony bought it from AT&T in 2021. Starz ended 2025 with 17.6 million subscribers after separating from Lionsgate.
Key Takeaways
  • Platform Strategy: Crunchyroll quadrupled its subscriber base in five years while its parent stayed out of general-entertainment streaming, making a genre-specific DTC service the real streaming asset behind a studio with no flagship platform of its own.
  • Distribution Economics: Amazon collects distribution economics on subscribers it never had to acquire. Anyone taking a Channels deal is trading margin for reach on someone else's terms.

Why It's Happening
The pairing is deliberately non-overlapping. Anime and premium adult drama share almost no audience, so this bundle is not built on taste affinity. It is built on the arithmetic that $16.99 clears a churn threshold neither service clears alone, which is a different and more durable logic than the same-audience bundles that preceded it.

Complementary-genre bundling suggests the unit of competition is shifting from the service to the storefront. That is a structural change in who captures value, and Amazon is on the winning side of it without originating a single hour.
The Facts
  • Bundle price $16.99 a month via Prime Video, 23% below the combined standalone cost. Sign-ups began Wednesday.

  • Terry Li, Chief Product Officer and EVP, Emerging Business, Crunchyroll: the bundle is "a meaningful step in expanding how fans can discover and connect with the series they love."
  • Matt Huntley, Director of US Channels, Prime Video: the launch "reflects Prime Video's commitment to delivering value and convenience for customers."

Central Casting Opens In All 50 States As Production Leaves The Hubs
Production GeographyLos Angeles shoot days fell 12.7 percent year over year while New Mexico drew $91 million and Illinois $47 million in second-quarter production spend.
CEO Summary
Central Casting, the 100-year-old background casting company whose name became an idiom, is open for business in all 50 states as of Thursday, having previously operated only in California, New York, New Jersey, Georgia and Louisiana. It will offer casting, payroll and compliance services nationwide, while keeping its full-service "premium" tier confined to the original five states. The move lands as 39 states plus Washington DC and Puerto Rico compete on film and TV tax incentives, with Illinois and New Mexico drawing $47 million and $91 million in second-quarter production spend.
Key Takeaways
  • Production Geography: When the company synonymous with Hollywood casting decides it has to operate in Oklahoma, decentralization has stopped being a cycle.
  • Production Costs: The friction premium that priced casting, payroll and compliance outside the traditional states is shrinking, which changes what a given budget buys.
  • Infrastructure: Los Angeles shoot days fell 12.7% year over year while New Mexico drew $91 million in a quarter. Infrastructure no longer holds production in place.
Why It's Happening
The tiering is the honest part of the announcement. Nationwide, productions get casting, payroll and compliance. In Texas, Oklahoma and New Mexico they get a "production-driven" service where teams hire extras off a casting-director-supplied lookbook, with the casting director available for support but not running the process. The premium tier, where company casting directors manage every step, stays in the five original states.

Central Casting is not claiming every market is equal. It is conceding it can no longer afford to be absent from the unequal ones, and it is delivering a thinner product where the volume is growing. That thinner product is arriving in the states with the weakest union density, which is worth watching alongside this week's unionization votes at CBS's Cupertino and among Star Wars on-set VFX workers.
The Facts
  • Central Casting is open in all 50 states as of Thursday, July 30, expanding from California, New York, New Jersey, Georgia and Louisiana.
  • Nationwide services: casting, payroll and compliance. The "premium" tier, with company casting directors on every step, remains limited to the original five states.
  • Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and others get the "production-driven" tier: hiring off a casting-director lookbook, with support available but not driving the process. Multi-state productions can run a hybrid.
  • Toni Avalos, VP of casting, Central Casting: "Production is no longer confined to a handful of markets, and our clients are increasingly looking for casting solutions that can move with them."
  • 39 US states plus Washington DC and Puerto Rico now offer film and TV tax incentive programs.
  • California remains the top production-spend site per ProdPro, with New York, New Jersey and Georgia still powerhouses. Illinois drew $47 million and New Mexico $91 million in Q2 2026 production spend.
  • FilmLA reported a 12.7% year-over-year decline in Los Angeles County shoot days for the most recent quarter, with most of the 170 projects awarded expanded California tax credits still to come.

Matt Stoller Puts Paramount's Odds Of Losing WBD At 60 Percent
Antitrust StrategyStoller puts the odds of a block at roughly 60 percent, citing that the merger's financing runs through the Middle East, banks and Oracle, whose stock has collapsed.
CEO Summary
Antitrust writer Matt Stoller puts the probability that the Paramount-WBD merger gets blocked at roughly 60%, through legal or financing risk, noting the financing rests on Middle East capital, banks and Oracle, whose stock has fallen sharply. Paramount moved Beth Wilkinson into the lead litigator role over the weekend. Stoller predicted the state AG challenge in February, including its mechanics.
Key Takeaways
  • Antitrust Strategy: A merging company that never articulates what the combined entity is actually for hands its challengers the exact gap they need to point to at trial.
  • Merger Odds: The market has traded on "the deal closes eventually"; a 60% block call from the analyst who saw the AG suits coming is a materially different starting point.
  • Deal Financing: A backer's own stock decline is an independent failure mode for a merger's financing that no judge has to trigger, and it can go underweighted relative to the litigation risk.
Why It's Happening
The litigator swap is the tell Stoller reads hardest: bringing in Wilkinson mid-stream is what a defendant does when the current posture is not working. The WGA case adds a channel where named showrunners like Mike Schur and Adam McKay testify about market structure, a form of guild leverage in M&A that is distinct from bargaining and appears to be working on the timeline as much as the record.
The Facts
  • Antitrust writer Matt Stoller (BIG newsletter) told Richard Rushfield he puts the probability that the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery merger gets blocked at roughly 60%, "either through legal risk or through financing risk."
  • On financing: "The financing behind this is coming from the Middle East, from the banks and from Oracle — and Oracle stock has really collapsed."
  • Paramount framed its decision to pause the merger pending the antitrust cases as a "significant win." Stoller: "It's a big loss for Paramount to do this, or a tactical loss. It makes them look stupid. It makes them look unprofessional." He adds the company is "kind of in shambles right now."
  • Paramount changed lead litigators over the prior weekend, moving Wilkinson Stekloff's Beth Wilkinson — who defended Microsoft in its 2023 Activision acquisition — into the top role.
  • The suits from 12 state attorneys general and the WGA have halted the merger; Paramount cannot close until the cases resolve or June 2027, whichever comes first.
  • Stoller predicted the state AG challenge in February 2026, including the mechanics: a judge orders the entities operated separately for up to 15 months pending trial.
  • He believes the WGA case adds material risk through testimony: "having writers like Mike Schur and Adam McKay, who are speaking out and saying, 'Look, I'm an important writer. I've seen how this works, and these mergers are a problem' — I think that's a very powerful thing for a judge to hear."
  • Stoller also notes what Paramount is not saying: "The one thing they're not talking about is what they're gonna do with the merged entity... They just seem excited about buying things."
  • He allows the other side: "There is going to be a trial. Paramount could very well win that trial."

'The Odyssey' Passes 'Oppenheimer's Domestic Lifetime In 13 Days

CEO Summary
Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is expected to cross $330 million domestic by end of day Wednesday, its 13th day of release, matching a total Oppenheimer took 595 days to reach. That makes it Nolan's third-highest domestic grosser and already Matt Damon's biggest film in a leading role. Its third weekend is projected to ease at most 50% against Spider-Man: Brand New Day's arrival.
Key Takeaways
  • Box Office Velocity: The director-brand audience that used to arrive over nineteen months now arrives in two weeks, at 2026 prices, in premium seats.
  • Backend Timing: First-dollar and escalator structures written against a long tail leave value on the table when the money lands this fast.

The 595-days-to-13 comparison needs care: Oppenheimer's $330 million was a long-tail number at 2023 prices with a smaller premium-format base, so the ticket-count gap between the two runs is large. CEO Summary
California AG Rob Bonta says there are no settlement talks on Paramount Skydance's $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, and that the only remedy he seeks is a block. Paramount has agreed to hold the deal until the suits resolve or June 2027, paying WBD shareholders roughly $650 million per quarter beginning Oct. 1, with a $7 billion termination fee if the deal dies. Key Takeaways
  • Regulatory Precedent: State AGs blocking a merger the DOJ already cleared is becoming a template dealmakers now have to underwrite, not an edge case.
  • Antitrust Strategy: Courts are narrowing "we need scale to compete with Netflix and Amazon" as a justification for media M&A, calling it ancillary to the core market at issue.
  • Settlement Talks: Market pricing of a deal's odds and a regulator's actual stated position can diverge sharply; take a named official's own words over consensus assumption.
Why It's Happening
The counterintuitive read, sourced to a former federal antitrust attorney, is that Paramount may prefer a full trial and even a fast loss, because it opens the appellate path sooner and caps ticking-fee exposure. That reframes the standstill from capitulation into clock management. The carry cost is real either way: three quarters of ticking fees through June is $1.95 billion, on top of the $2.8 billion breakup fee already paid to Netflix, against $15.5 billion of gross debt. Inside WBD nothing has changed operationally so far, per a senior TV executive and a senior TV lit agent, so the near-term risk for anyone with a deal there is delayed decisions, not collapse.

Paramount's process asset is Delrahim, who prosecuted AT&T-Time Warner for the government and now defends its mirror image.

Dealmakers struggle to name what it would buy: floated targets include Lionsgate, A24, Mediawan, Take-Two and a Sony tie-up, while Sky has already agreed to acquire ITV's media arm for $2.1 billion.
Key Takeaways
  • M&A Targets: Every floated target is duplicative, structurally unlikely to sell, too small to change scale, or, in A24's case, arguably destroyed by being acquired.
  • M&A Posture: Declaring buyer status this insistently is being read by some dealmakers as an advertisement of the opposite.
  • Production Volume: Citing the Taylor Sheridan model as a substitute for acquisition scale makes this a structurally favorable moment for producers who deliver volume.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day Is Tracking to a $465M Global Opening, Sony's Biggest Ever Reported
Distribution StrategySpider-Man: Brand New Day is tracking to a $465 million opening on a $225 million budget, with domestic estimates split between NRG's $195 million and rivals near $250 million.
CEO Summary
Sony/Marvel's Spider-Man: Brand New Day is tracking to a roughly $465 million global debut, which would be Sony's biggest reported opening ever and the third-biggest post-Covid bow. Domestic forecasts range from NRG's $195 million to rival estimates near $250 million, with about $270 million international and $45 million projected in China, where the franchise has not released since 2019. Production cost is $225 million net.
Key Takeaways
  • Distribution Strategy: Sony's biggest-ever opening on a $225 million spend is the case for the one major that distributes without a wholly owned streamer.
  • Format Windows: With The Odyssey holding Imax across most of the world, Sony opens its biggest title of the year into PLFs and 2D, a scheduling input that now shapes release dates.
  • International Box Office: A $45 million projection for a franchise absent there since 2019 proves nothing about the broader market until it lands.

Four Former FCC Chairs of Both Parties Ask the Agency to Drop Its Early Review of Disney's ABC Station Licenses
Regulatory PressureThe FCC ordered ABC's eight station licenses reviewed early, with the first not due until 2028, one day after the President and First Lady criticized a Jimmy Kimmel joke.
CEO Summary
Four former FCC chairs from both parties, including Mark Fowler, Dennis Patrick, Alfred Sikes and Thomas Wheeler, filed with the FCC calling its early review of Disney's eight ABC station licenses "an assault on free speech disguised as regulatory process." The FCC under Brendan Carr ordered renewal applications in May, though the first license was not due to expire until 2028; the filing notes the process began one day after the President and First Lady criticized a Jimmy Kimmel joke about them.

  • Regulatory Pressure: The FCC has denied nothing; pulling renewals forward two years changes broadcaster behavior without ever ruling.

  • Editorial Risk: A tool available against any licensee over editorial content raises the cost of late night, news and satire first, and indemnity language drafted for commercial disputes does not reach it.

Ofcom Finds Netflix Has Passed the BBC as UK Viewers' First Stop
Audience TrendsOfcom finds 26% of UK viewers turn to Netflix first versus 25% for the BBC, a gap that widens to 36% versus 14% among 16-24 year-olds.
CEO Summary
Ofcom's Media Nations report finds 26% of UK viewers now turn to Netflix first, ahead of the BBC at 25%, with the gap at 36% to 14% among 16-24s. Major streamers' UK revenue rose 18% to 5.2 billion pounds, which Ofcom attributes to price increases rather than subscriber growth, and third-party funding of broadcaster content hit a record 748 million pounds.
Key Takeaways
  • Audience Trends: The one-point crossover sits inside the margin and a methodology change; the age gradient is not a close call.
  • Co-Production Terms: Record co-production funding arrives attached to full rights ownership, so the UK co-pro question is what the concession is worth, not whether funding exists.
  • Subscriber Economics: Revenue up 18% on price rather than subscribers is a maturity signal that pushes streamers toward retention and cost discipline, which is where content budgets get squeezed.

  • Broadcast Economics: The tentpole live event moving behind a subscription while over-the-air keeps the rest is now a multi-country pattern.

  • Distribution Terms: Print count is left to the studio after delivery, worth pinning down on any film whose gross leans on premium screens.

The Ankler Argues AI Mockbusters Will Draft Off Studio Marketing Spend, Starting With The Odyssey
AI ContentMusk floated backing a Mel Gibson AI Odyssey with $100 million, arguing Grok could draft off Universal's $250 million production and $125 million marketing campaign.
CEO Summary
The Ankler's Erik Barmack argues AI-generated mockbusters will draft off studio marketing spend, starting with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, after Elon Musk suggested Grok could generate its own version and floated backing a Mel Gibson AI Odyssey with $100 million. The thesis: AI does not need a better film, only the demand signal Universal's $125 million campaign creates. This is a columnist's analytical read, not reporting on a funded project.
Key Takeaways
  • AI Content: The named threat is harvesting a studio's paid demand signal at near-zero cost, a different problem than AI replacing crews.
  • Copyright: Public-domain stories were always free; production cost was the gate, and removing it opens what Barmack calls the largest open-source story library in history.
  • IP Protection: Value shifts to likeness, performance rights, attachments and controlled IP, which makes that language load-bearing in any public-domain adaptation deal.

TriggerElon Musk has argued Grok could soon generate its own version of Homer's Odyssey, cheaper and more "historically accurate," and suggested backing a Mel Gibson AI-generated Odyssey with a $100M investment
The targetChristopher Nolan's The Odyssey: roughly $250M production, $125M marketing campaign, shot on 70mm for IMAX, designed as a theatrical event

Peacock's positionTurned a profit for the first time last quarter. Has struck bundles with Apple TV, Prime Video and Roku over the past year, and hosted Starz as an app within its own platform.

Discovery, headlined "A TV and cinema calamity could be disastrous for what you watch and what you know. Act now to stop that."

Economic case cited180,000 U.K. jobs supported by the industry; £6.8 billion in production spend reported last year; independent film acquisitions at Sundance down roughly half between 2019 and 2025.
Balance-sheet case citedWarner Bros.' estimated $84 billion in debt and roughly $6 billion in synergies promised to investors, which the authors translate as "redundancies, cancelled productions, fewer films commissioned and fewer risks taken." They cite the 2022 WarnerMedia-Discovery merger and the roughly 2,000 layoffs following Skydance's Paramount merger last year.
News-assets case citedChannel 5 and CNN International, plus the combined CNN and CBS news archives of more than 4.25 million videos, images and media spanning nearly half a century. They also cite a report that Paramount's chief executive told Donald Trump he would make "sweeping changes" to CNN if the deal closed.
Where the deal standsThe EU conditionally approved the acquisition on July 22. Twelve U.S. states led by California sued this month in federal court. Over the weekend Paramount agreed not to close until the court rules on whether the deal violates antitrust law.

The challengersNetflix and Prime Video have appealed to France's Council of State to challenge the financing and release-window system, which makes them wait 17 months for newly released films. Their argument is that their investment levels should entitle them to earlier access.

Netflix India Is Building Unscripted Formats It Owns, After 'Lock Upp' Hit 50 Million Hours
Format OwnershipLock Upp, a format Netflix owns, hit 50 million hours viewed since June 27, while Too Hot to Handle and Love Is Blind are licensed from Fremantle and Kinetic Content.
CEO Summary
Netflix India content chief Monika Shergill says the service is developing Netflix-owned global unscripted formats, after Lock Upp, a format Netflix owns, hit 50 million hours viewed since its June 27 launch. Netflix does not own its biggest reality franchises; Too Hot to Handle and Love Is Blind sit with Fremantle and Kinetic Content. Netflix also struck a co-exclusive deal with YouTube for Season 2 of India's Got Latent.
Key Takeaways
  • Format Ownership: Netflix's biggest reality franchises are licensed from others, and format ownership is the money it now wants back.
  • International Expansion: A format revived from a defunct local streamer just proved owned unscripted IP can be built cheaply in non-English markets.
  • Distribution Exclusivity: A co-exclusive season running on Netflix and YouTube at once cuts against the premise that a platform deal requires leaving your own channel.
The Facts
The disclosureNetflix India VP of Content Monika Shergill told Deadline the service is developing Netflix-owned unscripted formats for India: "We are working on a couple of very interesting, big global formats, which are Netflix formats, and they will be coming to India." She declined to name them.
Why ownership mattersNetflix does not own Too Hot to Handle or Love Is Blind. It holds exclusive international production deals on both, but the underlying format rights sit with Fremantle and The North Road Company-owned Kinetic Content respectively.
The performance driverLock Upp, a Balaji Telefilms-produced "captive reality" show on which Netflix is the rights owner, has amassed 50 million hours viewed since its June 27 launch, plus 2.5 billion social interactions within three weeks. It spent two weeks on the Global Top Non-English Series list and is the second-most-watched series by hours in Netflix's most recent What We Watched data.
Scaling in-flightEpisode output was raised from five per week to six on "audience demand and overwhelming success," running through the Aug. 5 finale.
Format travelAsked about a second season or an adaptation outside India, Shergill declined to confirm either but said: "The format is getting a lot of interest internally. I cannot confirm either of those questions, but since it's doing so well, I think it has a long life."
Provenance of the showLock Upp began in 2022 on ALTBalaji, the now-defunct Balaji Telefilms streamer, and on MX Player, recently subsumed into Prime Video India. Netflix revived it with hosts Farah Khan and Riteish Deshmukh.
Creator viewCreator Ekta Kapoor said she rejected two other offers to go with Netflix, citing support beyond financing: "sense of ownership is mutual, and respect is mutual. If I make a show for Netflix, I know that Netflix won't abandon me midway, because it's not doing well."
The YouTube wrinkleNetflix struck a co-exclusive deal for Season 2 of Samay Raina's YouTube show India's Got Latent, which Shergill calls a "great experiment" and a potential precursor to similar agreements, with "both platforms, Raina and his audience all responding positively."

Sean Astin Says He Made $250,000 on a $2.9 Billion Trilogy and Had to Sell His House
Talent LeverageAstin says he earned about $250,000 across a trilogy that grossed $2.9 billion and had to sell his house; Orlando Bloom made $175,000 for the same three films.
CEO Summary
Sean Astin told The Guardian he had to sell his house after earning roughly $250,000 across the Lord of the Rings trilogy, which grossed $2.9 billion worldwide. Orlando Bloom has said he made $175,000 for the same three films. The trilogy was shot back to back, and the franchise is returning with The Hunt for Gollum; Astin is not confirmed for it.
Key Takeaways
  • Talent Leverage: Shooting three films at once erased the renegotiation point where cast normally captures franchise upside.
  • Backend Terms: On any multi-film block, escalators and participation belong in the original deal, because no reset moment ever arrives.
  • Franchise Deals: Studios are again committing to multi-film blocks on unproven IP, which is why a 2001 pay figure still works as a comparable.
The Facts
The quoteSean Astin told The Guardian: "There was a disconnect between the attention that I was getting and how much money we had. It was not a lot of money! In fact, I had to sell my house because I negotiated such a small amount on the trilogy."
The numbersAstin has previously said he earned roughly $75,000 per film, about $250,000 across all three. Orlando Bloom said on The Howard Stern Show in 2019 that he was paid $175,000 for the trilogy.
What the films earnedThe Lord of the Rings grossed $2.9 billion worldwide between 2001 and 2003.
The structural causeAll three films were shot at once. As Elijah Wood put it to Business Insider last year: "Because we weren't making one movie and then renegotiating a contract for the next, it wasn't the sort of lucrative scenario that you could sort of rest easy for the rest of your life."
The studio's rationaleWood said New Line Cinema took a "real gamble" filming all three at once, and to mitigate the financial risk the ensemble was offered "not massive salaries."
What the cast got insteadWood: "The benefit of that was that we were also signing up for something that was going to be a part of our lives forever."
Where Astin is nowSays he is "very comfortable financially now." He is also the current president of SAG-AFTRA, which on Saturday resolved to oppose the Paramount-WBD merger absent enforceable U.S. production guarantees.
Why it is live againThe franchise is returning with The Hunt for Gollum, directed by Andy Serkis, and a new film co-written by Stephen Colbert. Astin is not confirmed for either. Asked whether he would fight for better pay: "Goddamn right."

Paramount Is Paying $7 Million a Day From October 1 to Buy Itself a November Antitrust Trial
Litigation StrategyThe Wrap estimates $1.7 billion in fees if the freeze runs its full course; twelve days earlier, Paramount said it was still confident of closing by September 30.
CEO Summary
The price of Paramount's merger delay is now legible: it will pay WBD shareholders $7 million a day from October 1, roughly $650 million a quarter, under the agreement barring the deal from closing until five days after an antitrust trial verdict or June 1, 2027. Paramount is targeting a November trial; The Ankler models that path at roughly $1 billion in fees, against close to $3 billion had a preliminary injunction pushed trial out a year.
Key Takeaways
  • Litigation Strategy: Paramount read the injunction fight as a likely loss and paid to convert an open-ended risk into a dated one, which is why both sides declared victory on Friday.
  • Deal Conviction: A buyer paying $650 million a quarter to hold a deal open will fight for the asset, and is tighter on every other commitment until trial.
  • Litigation Tactics: Twelve state AGs and the WGA extracted a $7 million daily meter without winning anything on the merits, and the playbook will be reused on the next big media transaction.
  • Merger Timeline: Paramount held a September close twelve days before agreeing to a June 2027 backstop; anyone timing a deal, overall, or slate commitment against its stated dates should use the litigation calendar instead.
Why It's Happening
The fee lands on a balance sheet already carrying the $110 billion price, the $2.8 billion WBD paid Netflix to break the prior deal, and repeatedly extended exchange and tender offers, with PSKY near its 52-week low. Morningstar calls the incremental debt almost inconsequential and caps the ticking-fee exposure around $2 billion. That is true arithmetically and false operationally: a company burning $650 million a quarter to hold a deal open has less room for everything else it does between now and trial.

'The Odyssey' Hits $639.6M Worldwide in Two Weekends With Premium Formats at 57% of the Domestic Gross and Imax at $140M
Premium Format70mm Imax tickets are running $22.46, a 32 percent jump from Oppenheimer's $17.03 three years ago, with 41 screens sold out into September.
CEO Summary
The Odyssey took a $215.3 million second global weekend, down 18%, for $639.6 million worldwide in two frames. Premium large format supplied 57% of the domestic weekend gross, up from 53% in weekend one, and Imax's $140 million cume already runs at roughly 72% of what Oppenheimer's entire multi-year run produced in the format.
Key Takeaways
  • Premium Format: At 57% of domestic gross and rising into weekend two, with Imax already turning the screen over to Spider-Man in Asia and The End of Oak Street domestically on August 14, premium format is the primary economics of this class of film, and both screen-share commitments and format-window length belong in the deal, not left to distribution.
  • Filmmaker Economics: Nolan's second weekend beat Oppenheimer's opening; at this tier the measure is format ownership and hold, both functions of the director's brand, which is the argument for first-dollar-gross on a filmmaker-driven original.
  • Studio Leverage: With three $1 billion titles in reach for 2026 and Odyssey's $375 million all-in cost covered inside two weeks, any negotiation with Universal this half prices against the strongest leverage of any major.
Why It's Happening
Part of the Imax number is price: 70mm tickets at $22.46 against $17.03 for Oppenheimer three years ago, a 32% increase. The rest is capacity discipline, with 41 sold-out 70mm screens into September and a formatted-screen calendar Universal has locked through mid-August. These economics are being set by a scarce distribution asset, not by wide availability, and the share rising rather than decaying into weekend two is the opposite of the normal PLF pattern.

'Toy Story 5' Crosses $1 Billion and Becomes 2026's Highest-Grossing Film, Five Days After Pixar Took the Deepest Cut in Disney's Layoffs
Franchise EconomicsFive days after Pixar cut 116 jobs in Emeryville, Toy Story 5 became the year's top film while Disney's Moana remake, same $250 million budget, sits at $228.2 million.
CEO Summary
Toy Story 5 crossed $1.022 billion worldwide, becoming 2026's highest-grossing film, five days after Pixar absorbed the deepest cut in Disney's studio layoffs with 116 jobs in Emeryville. In the same frame, Disney's live-action Moana sits at $228.2 million worldwide on the same $250 million budget, with The Ankler putting its theatrical-window loss at $150 million or more.
Key Takeaways
  • Franchise Economics: A 31-year-old property in its fifth installment produced the year's biggest film while Pixar's original opened and faded, hardening the internal case against one-off pitches that cannot scale into something bigger.
  • Live-Action Remakes: A loss of $150 million or more on a live-action conversion makes that strategy harder to defend and Disney more selective about which animated titles justify the treatment.
  • Labor Economics: Pixar took the deepest cut days before delivering the year's biggest film, so the durable protections for producers and executives are project-specific terms, not staffing assumptions.
  • International Box Office: $1 billion with only $41.6 million from China says the strongest family franchises scale globally without China carrying the model, worth revisiting in backend assumptions.

Bleecker Street's New Event-Cinema Label Crosswalk Opens 'Hadestown' to $9.7M, the Biggest Live-Capture Debut Since 'Hamilton'
Event CinemaHadestown opened within $400,000 of Hamilton's $10.1 million benchmark, and five of the weekend's domestic top ten releases were independent films.
CEO Summary
Bleecker Street's new event-cinema label Crosswalk opened Hadestown: The Musical to $9.7 million on 1,949 screens, the biggest live-capture debut since Hamilton's $10.1 million, and is extending what was designed as a five-day run. Five of the weekend's domestic top ten were independent releases.
Key Takeaways
  • Event Cinema: A specialty distributor built a branded, repeatable event-cinema pipeline (a K-pop concert film, a tour film, now a Broadway capture) and hit a top-five weekend inside a year; expect the structure to be copied.
  • Capture Rights: Capture cost is a fraction of a feature and the window is short and defined, so the negotiation is capture rights, territory, window, and streaming tail, and this weekend reset what those are worth for stage and touring IP.
  • Run Extension Terms: The surplus from an overperformance shows up in the extension of a limited run, and the distributor holds it unless the deal says otherwise.
Why It's Happening
Audiences are paying for occasions, not availability: the same demand curve driving premium-format pricing on The Odyssey filled 1,949 screens for a filmed stage show. Hamilton, the category benchmark, was a Disney acquisition that ultimately went to streaming; Hadestown got within $400,000 of it on a theatrical release from an indie.

Domestic Box Office Is Tracking to $10B for the First Time Since 2019, and the Winners Are Not Where the Money Was Budgeted

The profit stories span the extremes: Obsession has grossed $426M on a $750,000 budget, Backrooms took a 20-year-old YouTube creator to A24's biggest opening and total ever, and Project Hail Mary did $683M as Amazon MGM's first theatrical hit.
Key Takeaways
  • Theatrical Recovery: A $10B year with 2019-level summer revenue empirically weakens every buyer's dying-window argument, and it should be priced that way.
  • Slate Strategy: Event tentpoles at the top and near-zero-budget genre at the bottom are working simultaneously, breaking the consensus that only established IP can open a movie.

Obsession's second, third, and fourth weekends each beat its debut, a word-of-mouth pattern that barely exists in the modern era, and its $426M on $750,000 makes the micro-budget participation case by itself: the negative recoups in a day, so every point of gross is enormous relative to the fee. The unlock nobody names is supply. Per Alamo's CEO, the calendar finally has both a good pipeline and a diverse balance within the slate.

Sony Takes a Long-Term Lease on the Cinerama Dome and the Old ArcLight, Building an Owned Exhibition Arm
Exhibition StrategyThe complex has sat dark for six years since Covid; Alamo's CEO Michael Kustermann also now holds the title Head of Sony Pictures Experiences.
CEO Summary
Sony Pictures and Alamo Drafthouse signed a long-term lease with Robertson Properties Group: Sony will operate the Cinerama Dome and Alamo reopens the adjacent former 14-screen Hollywood ArcLight, with renovations starting next month and an early-2028 reopening targeted. The deal follows Sony's 2024 Alamo acquisition and its Cosm investment, all under a division called Sony Pictures Experiences.
Key Takeaways
  • Exhibition Strategy: The only major without a streaming service is spending the difference on owned physical distribution: a direct audience relationship and exhibition margin it otherwise hands to AMC and Cinemark.
  • Related-Party Terms: When a Sony film plays a Sony venue, rental terms are set internally, so any participation tied to distributor gross needs an arm's-length-terms provision covering affiliate exhibition.
  • Premium Format: Premium-format capacity is the binding constraint on the format-driven theatrical event, and owned 70MM screens turn format commitments into something a filmmaker can actually negotiate for.
  • Vertical Integration: If a second major follows studios back into theater ownership, the assumption that studios stay out of exhibition stops holding and windowing leverage shifts back toward distributors.
Why It's Happening
The timing is the tell. This was announced in a year running 10% ahead of 2025 with domestic grosses tracking toward $10B, and dated to reopen in early 2028. Sony is underwriting a premium-format bet that the theatrical recovery is structural, not a one-year Odyssey spike.

A Finished 'Dungeons & Dragons' Sequel Script Is Sitting Unmade on Budget Math Alone
Greenlight EconomicsThe original grossed about $205.5 million against a $150 million budget; the same directors are now developing the next Star Trek film for Paramount instead.
CEO Summary
Co-director Jonathan Goldstein says a commissioned Dungeons & Dragons sequel script is written and delivered but may never be filmed "for a number of financial reasons." The 2023 original scored 91% with critics and 92% with audiences but grossed about $205.5M worldwide against an estimated $150M budget, co-financed by Paramount and Hasbro's Entertainment One. Goldstein and John Francis Daley are now developing the next Star Trek film for the same studio.
Key Takeaways
  • Greenlight Economics: A liked cast, a 91% score, and a finished script cannot get a sequel made when the first film lost money.
  • Mid-Budget Films: The $150M IP film is the tier studios can no longer justify. Cheap genre works below it, star-driven events work above it, and the middle is where scripts go to sit.
  • Writer Protections: When a studio's own economics can shelve a delivered script indefinitely, reversion triggers and delivery-vesting bonuses are the only protection commissioned sequel work has.
  • Buyer Relationships: Goldstein and Daley lost the sequel but kept the buyer, and landed on Star Trek, the franchise Paramount actually has to make.
Why It's Happening
The math is unforgiving: $205.5M worldwide against a $150M negative does not recoup after marketing and the exhibitor split, before the co-financing structure divides what is left. A sequel to a film that lost money has to be made materially cheaper, and a fantasy ensemble with a returning name cast is the hardest genre to take cost out of. The timing compounds it. Paramount is barred from closing the Warner Bros. Discovery deal until at least next year and is carrying the financing costs, and discretionary greenlights on unrecouped mid-budget IP are the first thing that posture kills.

Shapiro: Advertising Is Having a Golden Age and a Gilded Age at Once, and AI Attacks It From Three Sides
Participation TermsSeventy-five percent of global ad growth from 2020 to 2025 went to four companies; brands that stop advertising see sales fall about 16 percent after one year and 25 percent after two.
CEO Summary
Doug Shapiro argues advertising is having a golden age and a gilded age at once: U.S. ad spend is approaching its highest-ever share of GDP, while 75% of global ad growth from 2020 to 2025 accrued to Google, Meta, ByteDance, and Amazon. Nearly 60% of new streaming subscribers chose ad-supported tiers in Q1 2026.
Key Takeaways
  • Participation Terms: With most new subscribers arriving on ad tiers, participation and bonus definitions keyed to subscriber metrics are drifting away from what a streaming title actually earns.
  • Ad Concentration: Studios and streamers compete for ad dollars against four platforms that took three quarters of all growth, the structural reason content spend stays disciplined in a strong revenue year.
  • Ad Measurement: A brand deal transacted through a platform that can prove outcomes prices differently from one that cannot, and agentic ad buying pushes value further toward full-stack platforms.
  • Talent Brand: When anyone can make content, a named creator brand with a verified audience becomes more valuable, not less.
Why It's Happening
The historical work is the caution against every advertising-death thesis: the remote, the DVR, ad blockers, and ad-free SVOD were each supposed to kill it, and nearly every ad-free service cited as proof has since launched an ad tier. Of Shapiro's three AI fronts, falling creation costs and agentic buying probably grow the pie; the AI intermediary layer is genuinely unknown. In every scenario the concentration gets worse.

Paramount Agrees Not to Close the Warner Bros. Discovery Deal Until a Trial Verdict, or June 1, 2027
Litigation StrategyThe break-up fee is $7 billion if the deal collapses on regulatory grounds; PSKY fell 3.3 percent to $8.21 the same day, touching a 52-week low of $8.17.
CEO Summary
Paramount, twelve state attorneys general, and the WGA filed a joint stipulation in federal court Friday: the Warner Bros. Discovery deal will not close, and no integration steps will be taken, until five days after a trial verdict or June 1, 2027, whichever comes first. In exchange, the plaintiffs withdrew their preliminary-injunction requests. Paramount still owes WBD $7 million a day for every day past September 30 the deal stays open.
Key Takeaways
  • Litigation Strategy: This reads as a plaintiffs' win, but Paramount just traded an injunction it looked likely to lose for a straight run at trial.
  • Ticking Fees: At roughly $650 million a quarter in ticking fees, Paramount spends the wait as a cost-cutter, not a flush buyer.
  • Labor Litigation: The WGA case going to trial will put studio-side writer compensation and deal-term practice on the discovery record, and that record favors the writers' side of the table.
Why It's Happening
The tell is the financing. Paramount extended its WBD note tender and exchange offers for a fifth time the same day, and said it expects to keep extending until close. The debt architecture of a $110 billion deal is now tethered to a close date that could be eleven months away. That is the cost Paramount agreed to eat for a trial date, and per a Morningstar analyst cited by TheWrap, the standstill effectively caps its ticking-fee exposure around $2 billion while preserving a real chance to close.

CEO Summary
Warner Bros. Discovery sued Amazon in California Superior Court on July 21 over Amazon MGM's hire of an HBO Max EVP of originals marketing who was under a term contract running to October 2027. The complaint alleges intentional interference, cites a second failed attempt on a senior HBO programming executive, and seeks an injunction barring Amazon from hiring any WBD employee under a term agreement before it expires. Amazon announced the hire three days after the suit was filed.
Key Takeaways
  • Talent Retention: California voids non-competes, so the fixed-term contract enforced against the poacher is the studios' only real retention tool, and this case tests whether it holds.
  • Executive Mobility: With the Paramount close pushed out as far as mid-2027, WBD's equity handcuffs loosen and every contracted executive there becomes courtable.
  • Litigation Risk: Damages are a cost of doing business for Amazon; a class-wide hiring ban would reshape how tech buyers staff entertainment divisions from legacy studios.
Why It's Happening
Precedent favors WBD: Netflix lost the Fox poaching fight in 2021, and YouTube recently settled Disney's suit over a former ESPN executive. The seats being fought over are the signal underneath: originals marketing and drama and comedy programming, the functions that decide how a series is positioned and what gets ordered. This is the first known senior Warner Bros. defection of the merger limbo, and the contract is now the only thing holding the roster. The complaint also attacks Amazon's alleged promise to defend and indemnify departing employees, turning a quiet market practice into discoverable evidence of intent.

A Former Studio Distribution Chief Makes the Case for Variable Ticket Pricing, and Warns Exhibitors Not to Let the Ordinary Auditorium Rot
Participation TermsThe interview subject ran domestic distribution at a major studio from 2019 into this year and now advises a theatrical analytics firm he founded in 2010.
CEO Summary
A former president of domestic distribution at a major studio, now a consultant, is publicly arguing that theatrical's flat-ticket convention is obsolete: premium pricing where scarcity supports it, cheaper tickets for low-demand screenings. He also warns exhibitors not to fund premium-format upkeep by letting ordinary auditoriums decay.
Key Takeaways
  • Participation Terms: Variable pricing breaks the link between admissions and gross, so any participation being papered now should define gross against admissions and net rental in a way that survives a pricing change.
  • Premium Pricing: Premium surcharges are already de facto price discrimination; screen counts by format, window length, and how format revenue flows into defined gross are negotiable today.
  • Ticket Pricing: Lower standard-screen pricing improves the theatrical case for drama and modest originals without touching production cost, an argument to have ready when a buyer says a picture cannot open.
Why It's Happening
Treat the proposal as coming from an interested party: the analytics firm he advises sells exactly the data variable pricing would require. It is still the sharpest available articulation of where pricing is heading, from someone who set release strategy at a major through the entire post-Covid rebuild, and it lands the same week a premium-format-driven original is setting hold records.
The Facts
  • The interview subject ran domestic distribution at a major studio from 2019 until earlier this year, after prior runs at two other studios. He is now an independent consultant and a board member and advisor to a theatrical analytics firm he founded in 2010.
  • His warning to studios and exhibitors as the box office heads toward its strongest year since Covid: do not get cocky.
  • On premium formats: "If they want a premium experience, the industry should be able to offer them premium experiences." Premium screens drove the opening-weekend grosses on the summer's dominant release.
  • On the risk: theaters must not prioritize upkeep of premium large-format screens over the quality of ordinary auditoriums. "Going to the movies is an elective, out-of-home choice. And as such, the industry cannot afford to have one of their experiences be bad in order to force customers to go to something better."
  • On variable pricing, his central proposal, analogized to premium versus upper-deck seats at a ballpark: "Supply and demand dictate that if you have limited supply and great demand, you should be able to charge more. If you have less demand on the regular experience, perhaps a lower ticket price might make sense (for those screens), which might spur additional moviegoing and remove price being a barrier from going to the movies."
  • On the flat-price convention: a documentary of the conversation itself would carry the same ticket price as the summer's biggest release, "and that doesn't make an awful lot of sense to me."
