A Documentary Subject Sends Netflix a Cease-and-Desist Over the Trailer, Two Days Before Premiere
Marketing LiabilityNetflix says the featured trade was placed in May 2025, before any Nevada court order; Kalshi counters the screenshot is fabricated, citing 'bet slip' wording its platform does not use.
CEO Summary
Prediction-market app Kalshi threatened Netflix with a defamation suit over the trailer for The Prediction Games, a documentary premiering Sunday, claiming footage implies trades made in violation of a Nevada court order. Netflix says the featured bet dates to May 2025, before the order, and Kalshi's own chief executive participates in the film.
Key Takeaways
  • Marketing Liability: Clearance covers the film, but the trailer is cut later by a different team, and timeline compression that is harmless over two hours becomes an implied fact in ninety seconds.
  • Subject Agreements: The CEO sat for the film and the company still sent the letter, so subject cooperation agreements should say plainly what they cover on promotion and advertising.
  • Litigation Risk: As unscripted moves into finance, betting, and regulated tech, litigious-by-default subjects will use premiere dates as pressure points; plan a public response, not just a legal one.
The Facts
  • Prediction-market app Kalshi threatened Netflix with a defamation suit over the trailer for "The Prediction Games," a documentary premiering Sunday on the streamer.
  • The dispute is over trailer footage showing traders celebrating Kalshi winnings from the recent World Cup final while partying in Las Vegas, after a court order requiring Kalshi to block sports-related markets in Nevada following a Nevada Gaming Commission suit.
  • The letter, obtained by CNN, claims the trailer contains "misleading statements portraying trades being made on Kalshi in violation of a court order." Kalshi says it is complying with the order.
  • Netflix's response: the event was filmed last weekend in Vegas, but the most prominent trade depicted was placed in 2025, long before the order. The featured trader "showed us a screenshot of his bet that was made in May 2025, prior to any Nevada court order," a Netflix spokesperson told CNN.
  • Kalshi further claims the screenshot itself was "fabricated," pointing to terms like "bet slip" that do not appear on its site, which avoids gambling terminology.
  • The company's chief executive participates in the documentary.
  • Kalshi is regulated as a commodity-trading platform rather than as gambling, but multiple states have sued to enforce gaming laws against it.

CEO Summary

The court ordered Paramount, the twelve state AGs and the WGA to confer and file a joint report by July 24, kept the August 3 preliminary-injunction hearing, and noted it cannot extend the TRO again. Key Takeaways
  • Litigation Timeline: The TRO cannot be extended again, so either the parties stipulate to a longer freeze or the court grants or denies an injunction; there is no comfortable third path.

Why It's Happening
The fight has moved from the merger to the calendar, and the calendar is the weapon. Delay is not symmetric: Paramount carries a ticking fee reported around $650 million a quarter, so every week of freeze is money out against a closing that may not happen on the original terms. Brussels clearing the deal does nothing about a US district judge who already found the theatrical-distribution theory serious enough to freeze a $110 billion transaction.

The July 24 joint report is the cheapest tell available. A stipulated longer freeze would mean Paramount concluded it loses a rushed hearing, which shifts the odds toward a 2027 resolution and makes standalone-WBD planning a base case, not a tail.

  • Exhibition Capacity: One screen in a hundred delivering one dollar in five means the constraint in theatrical is not the movie or the marketing, it is the small number of rooms that can show the film as shot.

  • Sale Process: A sale process running alongside record results means the winner gains structural leverage over every large-format release, including competitors'.

Imax has been explicit that building many more 70mm-capable rooms quickly is impractical, so capacity is structurally constrained while demand for it is now proven. That makes premium-format access a rationed, negotiable resource in the same way a release date is, and it points to calendar congestion in premium rooms becoming the real release-date fight, with studios trading format access against each other.

Atari Licenses 10 Classic Game Properties to Universal in a Single Package
IP LicensingUniversal has already bought the first project from the ten-title package, an original screenplay from two writer-producers, one a former Universal executive.
CEO Summary
Atari, partnered with a management-production company, signed a deal giving Universal Pictures the right to develop 10 classic game properties for feature film, including Asteroids, Pong, Centipede and Missile Command. Universal has already bought the first project, an original screenplay by two writers who also produce, one a former Universal executive. The catalyst was the spec, not a studio development push.
Key Takeaways
  • IP Licensing: A studio that will not buy an original large-scale action-adventure will buy the same script with a licensed legacy title on the cover, so knowing which catalogs are available and unencumbered is now part of a package's value.
  • Backend Value: For the writers, the negotiation that matters is passive participation and first-look on subsequent titles from the ten-title package, not fees on film one.
  • IP Packaging: A management-production company at the center of a ten-title studio package occupies territory a studio's own IP-acquisition group would normally hold; whether it keeps that territory says where packaging leverage sits next.
Why It's Happening
The IP is thin by design. Asteroids and Pong have no characters, no world, no narrative; they have title recognition with a trademark attached. Universal is buying ten pre-cleared, recognizable titles it can attach to original screenplays, a cheap way to convert a spec into a "known IP" greenlight. The branding is being reverse-engineered onto the material, not extracted from it. Expect more of these packages: game and toy catalogs offer recognition without creative constraint, which filmmakers prefer to a franchise carrying 40 years of canon, and the good catalogs will go quickly.

  • The catalyst was an original spec, not a studio-initiated development push. One of the writers is a former Universal executive who moved to writing and producing.
  • Stated creative aim is large-scale action-adventure.
  • Atari chairman and CEO Wade Rosen: "For more than five decades, Atari has created games and worlds that have remained part of popular culture long after their original release."

If it does, international economics for Indian tentpoles reprice upward and this becomes a standing category. The answer arrives in November.
The Facts

Nearly two in five drama shoot days are incentive-driven while the total still fell 13%; 443 feature shoot days in a quarter, in the historical center of the film business, is structural relocation, not a cyclical dip. UK Regulators Face a Test Case on Whether Representation Can Be Sold as a Service
Conflict of InterestA 2023 email said the agency 'only represents' actors who 'regularly train and attend our classes'; one employment-law partner called the messages grounds to suspect a Regulation 5 breach.
CEO Summary
A Deadline investigation reports that staff at a prominent British children's talent agency told prospective clients, in messages spanning 2021 to 2025, that the agency prefers to sign talent through paid acting classes run by a commonly owned stage school. UK law bars agencies from making work-finding conditional on the purchase of other services; three lawyers consulted called the messages grounds to suspect a breach. The agency strongly denies wrongdoing and has engaged an external consultant. Enforcement sits with the Fair Work Agency.
Key Takeaways
  • Conflict of Interest: Common ownership of an agency and a paid-services arm plus a stated sourcing preference creates legible conflict even without an explicit quid pro quo, and the arrangement is common across the youth-talent market.
  • Agency Economics: An agency earns on the client's earnings, not on the client; any revenue line that comes from the talent itself invites the regulatory question.
  • Regulatory Risk: The same principle, that access to work cannot be sold, applies to every discovery-adjacent product marketed at entrants, from pitch access to paid showcases.
Why It's Happening
This is a compliance story about the structure of a representation business, not a scandal about one firm. Regulation 5 does not ask whether the classes were good; it asks whether work-finding was conditioned on buying an ancillary service. The practical force is reputational: a specialist in a market built on parental trust now has a documented allegation attached to a named regulation. And social-media-led discovery is outrunning frameworks written for agencies; a large short-form following used to market both representation and lessons is a new channel for an old conflict, and likely the first of several enforcement questions in that lane.
The Facts
  • A Deadline investigation reports emails and messages spanning January 2021 to October 2025 in which staff at a prominent British children's talent agency told prospective clients the agency prefers to take on new talent through paid acting classes run by a commonly owned stage school.
  • Quoted messages include a 2023 email saying the agency "only represents" young actors "who regularly train and attend our classes," and a 2022 message saying actors "need" to attend a course to be considered for a new voice-work division.
  • UK law prohibits entertainment agencies from charging upfront fees; they may only earn commission on client earnings. Regulation 5 of the Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 bars agencies from making work-finding services conditional on the use of other services.
  • Three lawyers and two industry experts consulted by Deadline said the messages were grounds to suspect a Regulation 5 breach. One employment-law partner: "It seems pretty open and shut, and I can't see any exemption within the regulations." A media-law partner: "access to work should not be used as leverage to pressure actors, performers, models or other work seekers into paying for add-ons."
  • A dozen current and former students and parents told Deadline they understood paid lessons were necessary to be considered for representation.
  • The agency's spokesperson "strongly denied" that representation was "ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services," denied "allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct," and said an external consultant has been engaged to review processes.
  • Enforcement sits with the Fair Work Agency, which can inspect agencies and fine those that fail to remediate. It declined to comment on the specific agency but said it would examine relevant complaints.

The sequencing is the strategy: the Venice slot is the marketing asset that justifies going wide against studio product rather than platforming into it. The frame's crowding is also less than it looks; three of the six titles are horror or genre plays and one is a re-release, leaving the adult-drama lane on September 25 contested mainly by one studio title. A prestige film with a festival stamp and a star-produced package is positioned to own that lane outright.

Patreon Cuts 20% of Staff, Citing 'Profound' Changes in the Creator Economy
Creator MonetizationPatreon's podcasters generated $629 million in revenue last year, up 33 percent, even as the company cut 93 employees, its largest layoff since a 2022 cut of 80 people.
CEO Summary
Patreon is laying off 20% of its employees, 93 people, its largest cut since 2022. CEO Jack Conte told staff the core business remains strong but the platform must respond to "profound" market changes, flattening the org chart and redirecting teams toward core creator and fan experiences. The company said in April its podcasters generated $629 million in revenue last year, up 33%.
Key Takeaways
  • Creator Monetization: The center of creator monetization has moved to advertising and commerce on platforms the audience does not pay for, compressing direct subscription into a secondary income surface.
  • Revenue Diversification: A creator business built on direct patronage as its primary engine carries platform-retrenchment risk that only a second monetization surface offsets.
  • Exclusivity Terms: Platform-exclusive subscription deals concentrate risk in the platform's own health, which makes performance floors and degraded-support exits the terms that matter most.
Why It's Happening
The stated reasoning does not fully hold: companies with strong, growing core businesses do not cut a fifth of staff and flatten the org. This reads as a growth-rate problem, a mature subscription product competing against ad-supported video that pays creators without asking audiences for a monthly commitment; the same week produced a video-first podcast network relaunch and an $11 billion YouTube ad quarter. It is not a creator-economy collapse: $629 million growing 33% is a healthy category. What is failing is a particular monetization architecture at a particular cost structure. The unprompted "AI is not the reason" line is its own data point about what the market currently assumes.
The Facts
  • Patreon is laying off 20% of its employees, 93 people, with at least 16 weeks of severance.
  • CEO Jack Conte said in a note to staff that the "core business" remains "strong and consistent," but the platform must respond to "profound" market changes this year affecting how Patreon navigates the creator economy.
  • Conte: "We need to adjust our cost structure to ensure that we remain a stable, dependable rock for our creators as we work toward our long term ambition."
  • Internal changes include flattening the org chart and redirecting teams toward "improving core creator and fan experiences" and "helping creators grow their audiences and businesses."
  • Conte addressed AI directly and said it is not the reason for the cuts: "We are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans."
  • Patreon hosts a wide range of entertainment podcasts, including several fronted by well-known film, comedy and lifestyle figures.
  • In April the company said its podcasters generated $629 million in revenue last year, up 33% year over year.
  • This is the largest cut since 2022, when Patreon let go 80 employees, about 17% of staff, and reduced its creator partnerships team.

A Management Company Rebuilds Its Podcast Network as a Video-First Business

CEO Summary
The Roost Podcast Network is relaunching as Podium, a video-first business, two years after being acquired by talent management and media company Night. The network reaches 50 million monthly video and audio impressions and 66 million social followers, and launches with the signing of an established creator podcast with 160M+ lifetime views, handling its distribution, audience development and brand partnerships.
Key Takeaways

  • Format Strategy: A podcast is now a video format with an audio channel, so production values, clip strategy and YouTube rights belong in the deal from the start.
Why It's Happening
"Distribution, audience development and brand partnership" are the three functions that determine what a creator earns, and Podium performs all three for talent its parent company also manages. Whether that beats commission-based representation depends on terms nobody publishes, but it is unambiguously a different economic model. The convergence cuts both ways: the same infrastructure that makes creators harder to sign also makes them easier to package into traditional film and television.
The Facts

A preliminary injunction that runs eight months does not need to defeat the merger on the merits; at that rate it is an economic weapon, which is why Paramount will trade a longer TRO for a faster ruling.

The New Development Path: Make It for $1,000, Post It to Instagram, Then Take the Meeting
Built-In AudienceTwo writers made a 12-episode comedy for $1,000 total and drew 1.5M views in under three months; one creator with 530,000 followers is turning down Hollywood offers.
CEO Summary
Two writers stuck in TV development made a 12-episode buddy comedy for $1,000, posted it to Instagram, drew roughly 1.5M views in under three months, and now have brands offering to fund a second season. The Ankler counts more than two dozen vertically-shot scripted comedies in the space, plus a fully financed six-episode indie season made with no distributor attached and a brand-funded workplace comedy with 530,000+ followers whose owner is declining Hollywood offers.
Key Takeaways
  • Built-In Audience: A greenlight conversation that used to argue whether an audience exists now argues how large a known audience is, and that is a different negotiation.
  • Creator Leverage: A brand-funded show with a large following treats a studio offer as an option, so acquiring one is buying a working asset with a revenue line, and it should be papered that way.
  • Audience Pricing: Reps are already articulating "de-risk content spend by leaning into built-in audience," which means built-in audience gets priced into standard offers within a year.
Why It's Happening
Three models sit inside one trend and should not be blurred: proof-of-concept made for nothing to sell a half-hour; a fully financed indie season with no distributor, the indie-film model finally working in TV because the production floor fell; and the brand-funded owned show that never needs to sell. The third is the one Hollywood is least prepared for. If the no-distributor season recoups even once publicly, the number of series reaching market without a buyer's approval goes up and gatekeeping leverage goes down.

Instagram over YouTube is a cost fact, not a taste fact: the algorithm rewards a sub-three-minute episode, which is what $1,000 buys, and creators are rewriting scripts to fit the distribution math.
The Facts

The financed modelA production company run by a former head of comedy and drama at a major streamer won a social-first series away from a major studio by fully financing a six-episode first season with no distributor attached. It was made cheaply enough that direct distribution on YouTube and social remains a viable fallback that could still recoup
Benchmark citedThat series' pilot: 260,000+ YouTube views. Comparison from a streaming launch: a well-known comedy original averaged 800,000 viewers for its first five episodes after 11 days (per a third-party analysis)
Why Instagram over YouTubeRecommendation algorithms plus short-form focus — cheaper to produce than the long-form volume YouTube's watch-time economics demand. Only a handful of creators do scripted at scale on YouTube
Format constraintThe writers reconfigured their scripts because the Instagram algorithm favors videos under three minutes
Entry bar"You don't want to start a show with less than 100,000 followers," per one comedy creator

  • Auteur Value: The unit of commercial trust in theatrical is moving from the producer-custodian of a universe to the filmmaker, whose audience travels across studios and genres.

The mechanism is structural, not sentimental: film-fan culture on Letterboxd, Reddit and YouTube gives a filmmaker a direct, portable audience relationship, the thing that made stars bankable in an earlier era. That asymmetry is the argument for retained rights and derivative participation, since a buyer is renting an audience that leaves with the filmmaker, while a franchise seat's value stays with the IP.

The market holds both propositions at once: an auteur event picture leads this week's box office while a superhero tentpole is projected to open larger next weekend. What is new is that the auteur lane is underwritable at event scale, which was not true in 2016.

News Corp Countersues Over the Middleman: Scraping and Reselling Content to AI Companies
Litigation TargetNews Corp seeks statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringement; Brave sued first, in March 2025, seeking a ruling that its use of the articles is fair use.
CEO Summary
News Corp countersued Brave Software in federal court in Oakland, accusing it of scraping Wall Street Journal and New York Post articles and reselling them to AI companies, and seeking an injunction plus statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringement. Brave had sued first, in March 2025, seeking a declaratory judgment that bundling licensable articles is fair use. The suits follow failed licensing negotiations between the two.
Key Takeaways
  • Litigation Target: Unlike suits against model developers, this attacks the aggregator layer that lets AI companies acquire content without ever negotiating with the owner, a defendant far easier to identify and enjoin.
  • Likeness Rights: "An unlicensed channel destroys the incentive to license" is close to the argument a performer could make about likeness and voice data packaged by third-party vendors, and there is now a template complaint on a live docket.
  • Copyright Registration: Statutory damages at $150,000 per work scale catastrophically against a large corpus, but only registered works unlock the number.
Why It's Happening
The economic claim in the filing is the part that generalizes: the harm is not just that copying occurred, but that a cheap unlicensed channel destroys the market for the licensed one. If a model developer can buy a bundle from a third party, it has no reason to sign a direct license. Studio and talent-side content sits in exactly the same posture.

The pattern across the AI-content market is now negotiate, fail, litigate, and let the ruling set the price. Rights holders waiting for a market rate to emerge by consensus should expect it to be set by whoever litigates first.
The Facts
  • News Corp filed a countersuit Tuesday in federal court in Oakland against Brave Software, accusing it of "flagrant theft" for distributing and selling versions of Wall Street Journal and New York Post articles to AI companies.
  • News Corp says Brave's "covert scraping" and resale fall "nowhere near the bounds" of fair use. It seeks an injunction, unspecified monetary damages, and statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringement.
  • The core economic claim, quoted from the filing: "The more content Brave copies and sells, the more revenue it generates, and the less incentive AI companies have to negotiate licenses with the publishers who produced the content. Brave profits while publishers are cut out."
  • Procedural posture is inverted: Brave sued first, in March 2025, seeking a declaratory judgment that bundling licensable copyrighted articles is not infringement. It filed a revised complaint in May 2026 after what News Corp calls failed negotiations for a "fair, market-based agreement."
  • Brave's defense: indexing to make content searchable, and serving users snippets and "high-level summaries," is fair use. Brave has also argued News Corp is threatening to disrupt generative AI advances.
  • News Corp's chief executive said Brave's conduct shows "blatant disregard," adding: "This era of tacky tech trafficking must come to an end if journalism is to have a sustainable future."
  • The New York Post, Dow Jones, and News Corp's British and Australian operations are also defendants in Brave's suit.

Pictures Animation and DC Studios, voted 84-35 to join IATSE, creating a unit of 137 animators, digital puppetry artists and CG modelers. IATSE called it one of its largest recent organizing drives and publicly demanded that Swaybox and Warner Bros. reach an industry-standard agreement.
Key Takeaways
  • Labor Arbitrage: A studio routing a tentpole to a regional non-union shop can no longer assume the cost basis survives the production, so budgets and backend models built on that assumption are less reliable than last week.
  • Union Strategy: IATSE's demand that Warner Bros. come to the table, not just the vendor, directly attacks the standard position that vendor-shop labor is the vendor's problem.

Why It's Happening
Three structural facts collide in one vote: a major put a nine-figure DC picture into a non-union shop in a tax-credit state; the technique escapes existing craft agreements; and the workers organized at a 70% yes margin anyway. The economics of the regional-vendor model only work if the studio's cost basis stays outside the union framework. If organizing follows the work into the vendor, the arbitrage compresses, and any producer signing a production-services agreement in a right-to-work jurisdiction should price the possibility that the shop organizes mid-schedule.

  • Creatives at Swaybox Studios, a New Orleans-based studio producing Dynamic Duo for Warner Bros. Pictures Animation and DC Studios, voted to join IATSE in an election concluding Tuesday. The tally: 84 for, 35 against.

  • IATSE international VP Mike Miller called on Swaybox and Warner Bros. to "come to an industry standard agreement immediately."

California's Next Incentive Fight Is About Post, Not Principal Photography
Tax Credit PolicyThe proposed 35% credit would for the first time pay productions that shoot elsewhere but finish post in California; it faces a Senate Appropriations hearing on August 3.
CEO Summary
AB 2319, California's proposed 35 percent postproduction tax credit, was left out of Gov. Newsom's final budget and must now secure funding through a trailer bill, with a Senate Appropriations hearing set for August 3. SAG-AFTRA's president intervened directly this week, urging members to lobby for it. The bill would, for the first time, pay productions that shoot elsewhere but finish in California, and its coalition already includes Netflix, Apple, the Editors Guild and the California IATSE Council.
Key Takeaways
  • Tax Credit Policy: Paying a Georgia or Hungary shoot 35 percent to finish in LA is defensive industrial policy that competes only for the segment the state can still win.
  • Post Infrastructure: Two location-agnostic buyers lobbying for a California post credit means their post infrastructure is here and sticky, useful whenever either claims finishing costs are immovable.
  • Post-Production Terms: A 35 percent credit is large enough to change where a production finishes, moving post from administrative afterthought to a negotiated point with money attached.
Why It's Happening
Post is where incentive arbitrage bites hardest because it is the easiest work to move: a colorist, mixer or ADR loop group can sit anywhere with bandwidth. The performer constituency in play is voice and ADR labor, the actor-side work most exposed to offshoring and to synthetic substitution; the credit functions as a jobs floor for a category whose leverage is otherwise thin. August 3 is the date, and Senate Appropriations in a cash-strapped year is where bills die quietly. If it stalls, expect post migration to continue and the coalition to reload for 2027.
The Facts
  • Gov. Gavin Newsom's final state budget, unveiled June 29, did not include funding for AB 2319, California's proposed postproduction tax credit. The bill survives and now must secure funding via a trailer bill.
  • AB 2319, carried by Assemblymember Nick Schultz, would offer a 35 percent base tax credit to productions that locate postproduction work in California but shoot elsewhere, or that shoot in California without receiving a production credit. Under current law, post expenses qualify only if principal photography also occurs in-state.
  • SAG-AFTRA's president released a video to THR ahead of a California Post Alliance (CAPA) town hall held Tuesday night on the Sony lot, urging members to lobby their representatives. This is the union's first top-officer intervention; SAG-AFTRA had filed a written letter of support earlier in the month.
  • The union's stated ask: the $750 million production tax credit was a win, but "now we have to incentivize companies to keep postproduction work in California."
  • Existing coalition backing the bill: CAPA (sponsor), the Editors Guild (co-sponsor since June), L.A. Mayor Karen Bass, the California IATSE Council, Netflix and Apple.
  • The bill has passed the state Assembly and enters the Senate Appropriations Committee on August 3, in what THR characterizes as a cash-strapped budget year.

Key Takeaways
  • AI Disclosure: Awards bodies are converging on audit-on-demand aimed at the production, not the vendor, so eligibility now rides on documentation a production may not have kept, and a film that cannot reconstruct who did what with which tool will struggle regardless of what it actually did.
  • Human Authorship: "Human achievement in originating, shaping and realising the final artistic outcome" is a clean, awards-tested articulation of the human-authorship line, drafted by a body with no stake in either side's deal.
  • Awards Strategy: BAFTA keeps the ban on double nominations in a category while AMPAS lifted it, so dual-campaign strategy is no longer symmetrical.
Why It's Happening
The design avoids the definitional swamp: nobody decides in advance whether a de-aged face or generative previs disqualifies a film, and the ninety-nine percent of mundane AI use goes unpoliced. The cost is a case-by-case, opaque standard; nobody knows where the line is until a specific film is asked to explain itself, privately. The casting-chapter vote points the same direction: in a season where "what counts as a performance" is the live question, the people who assemble performances now help judge them.
The Facts
  • BAFTA published eligibility and voting changes for the 2027 film awards, characterized by Variety as small tweaks relative to AMPAS's recent Oscar changes.
  • The AI language. Having added "human achievement" to the rulebook last year, BAFTA has now added: the awards recognize "outstanding human achievement in originating, shaping and realising the final artistic outcome, regardless of the tools used to bring this work to life. Where the use of Generative AI or other digital tools is relevant to the consideration of the work, BAFTA reserves the right to request additional information regarding the nature of such use and the extent of human creative involvement."
  • BAFTA's executive director of awards and content said the addition gives BAFTA the "opportunity to just dig in a bit deeper if there's something we want to check," with the film committee ruling on eligibility. Asked whether a fully AI-generated film or performance could ever be nominated: it "would always be a human that picks up a BAFTA."
  • Outstanding British Film: longlist expands from 15 to 20 after round one; nominations stay at 10 (five by membership vote, five by jury).
  • Performance categories: BAFTA's casting chapter will now vote alongside the acting chapter in longlisting and nominations, to "increase the expertise" across 700+ candidates in four categories.
  • BAFTA is not following the Oscars in permitting multiple nominations for one performer in the same category — previously allowed, banned after a review, and retained as banned to "level the playing field."
  • Bullying and harassment: CIISA-alignment declarations remain mandatory for British categories; BAFTA now requests the information from all submitted productions, with a stated expectation it becomes a requirement in future years.
  • Key dates: entries open July 22; round one voting Dec. 4; longlists Jan. 7; nominations open Jan. 19; final voting Jan. 26; ceremony Feb. 21.

A Broadway Musical Grossing $1M a Week Is Now a Money-Loser — and Only Five New Ones Are Set for Next Year
Cost BaseCats: The Jellicle Ball capitalized at up to $18M against Hadestown's recouped $11.5M and an arriving technical show capitalized up to $31M; only five new musicals are set for next year.
CEO Summary
Cats: The Jellicle Ball, the Tony-winning ballroom-competition revival, announced an August 8 closing after roughly five months on Broadway despite grosses hovering around $1 million a week and high attendance. The problem was average ticket price against elevated operating costs, not demand. Only five new musicals have been announced for next year.
Key Takeaways
  • Cost Base: When a $1M-a-week musical with strong attendance loses money, the cost base has passed what audiences will pay for anything without a star or a pre-sold title, and celebrity-carried plays are increasingly the only productions clearing it, making a screen star's ability to open a play a distinct, priceable asset.
  • Adaptation Pipeline: Five new musicals a year means fewer proven properties entering the stage-to-screen pipeline, which raises the price of the ones that work and rewards whoever already holds one.
  • Capture Rights: The same week this revival closed for want of ticket revenue, a live capture of another Tony-winning musical opened in 1,944 theaters, which argues for capture rights as a separately negotiated asset, not a documentary afterthought.
Why It's Happening
Star-and-IP conditioning now governs two markets at once. Audiences trained that value equals names plus known titles have made original stage work the residual category, the same pattern theatrical exhibition ran a decade earlier. And nobody has proposed a collective fix: the composer's public call for owners, producers and unions to convene has produced individual budget trimming, not structural change, so expect continued contraction and continued migration of the form toward captured and screen distribution.
The Facts
  • Cats: The Jellicle Ball — the critically acclaimed revival restaging the musical as a queer ballroom competition — announced an Aug. 8 closing after roughly five months on Broadway. It won three Tony Awards but missed Best Revival.
  • Grosses were hovering around $1 million a week pre-Tonys, with high attendance. The company was told at a July 13 meeting that the show could not generate enough revenue to cover expenses.
  • THR's reporting locates the problem not in attendance but in average ticket price: the show could fill seats, but not at prices sufficient to cover elevated Broadway operating costs.
  • Capitalization comps in the piece: Cats: The Jellicle Ball up to $18M (described as relatively low for this era); Hadestown $11.5M, recouped, now in year seven; Paddington, a technical show arriving in spring, capitalized up to $31M.
  • Only five new musicals have been announced for next year.
  • Cost drivers cited: post-pandemic supply-chain and materials inflation, utilities, theater rent, and rising rates for actors, musicians, stagehands and creative teams. Musicals are hit hardest — larger casts plus an orchestra — while plays increasingly carry celebrities who can command higher prices.
  • A lead producer on a long-running Tony-winning musical, quoted: "I'm watching a lot of shows not quite find the audience that can sustain them… There have always been more shows that fail than succeed. I think the proportion right now feels distorted."
  • The show's composer wrote publicly on July 14: "Without action, Broadway risks rivaling Hollywood's empty soundstages: increasingly dark theatres where bold new work once lived," calling on theater owners, producers and union leaders to convene.
  • Producer responses so far are individual, not collective: fewer set pieces, less automation, smaller casts, longer marketing runways, discounted previews. One incoming musical's lead producer: "The amount of time that you have for your show to pick up has shortened."
  • On audience conditioning: "We've trained audiences that the shows of value are the ones with stars and recognizable IP, and so now we have to try to dig ourselves out of that behavior pattern because that's not sustainable either."

A Written Marketing Floor and a Guaranteed Window: What It Actually Took to Move a Top-Tier Director Between Studios
Deal StructureUniversal's winning bid included a marketing floor committed in writing at parity with the $100M budget and first-dollar gross; the follow-up film was never taken to auction.
CEO Summary
Variety reconstructs the deal that moved a top-tier director to Universal after his longtime studio put its 2021 slate day-and-date on streaming. Universal won the 2021 auction with a guaranteed lengthy exclusive theatrical window, a marketing floor committed in writing at parity with the $100M budget, and first-dollar gross, a reported ~$100M in fees and back end. The follow-up film was never taken to auction, and the result was a ~$265M global opening with a projected $1B run.
Key Takeaways
  • Deal Structure: He left over a distribution decision and was won with written release and marketing guarantees, not a bigger fee.
  • Window Protection: The old studio's seven-figure make-good in arrears failed, the named precedent for valuing window protection over any make-good that follows a breach.
  • Renewal Leverage: A filmmaker willing to skip the market is giving the studio something worth real money, and it should be traded for window guarantees, a marketing floor, or sequel participation, not gifted as goodwill.
Why It's Happening
The two winning provisions, a written marketing-spend floor tied to budget and a guaranteed exclusive theatrical window, are chronically under-negotiated because attention goes to the gross definition instead. Both are askable and enforceable. First-dollar gross also survived twice at this altitude, including on the "more standard" second deal, a usable comp against any claim that first-dollar participation is extinct. Sourcing caveat: the terms are unnamed-insider reporting with both camps declining comment, so treat the shape as reliable and the precise figures as directional.

The Judge Grounded the Merger Pause in Theatrical Distribution, Not Cable or Streaming
Antitrust StandardThe court found 27% wide-release share compelling evidence of harm, below the conventional 30% presumption threshold, and rejected streaming efficiencies as a defense in footnote 5.
CEO Summary
The court's written TRO order evaluated the Paramount-WBD merger on the market for distribution of wide-release theatrical films, not cable or streaming, and found the combined firm's 27% share "compelling evidence" of substantial market share despite sitting below the 30% presumption threshold. Footnote 5 rejected streaming-market efficiencies as a defense outright. The preliminary-injunction hearing is August 3; trial is unlikely before 2027.
Key Takeaways
  • Antitrust Standard: A court presumed harm at 27% of wide-release distribution, below the conventional bar, so future studio pairings get judged on combined slate volume, not subscribers.
  • Legal Defense: Efficiencies in an ancillary market do not excuse harm in the relevant one, so "we need scale to compete with Netflix" is a press-release argument now, not a legal one.
  • Litigation Timeline: The TRO bar is low; a granted preliminary injunction means a counterparty in litigation limbo into 2027, the scenario any dependent deal should be planned against.
Why It's Happening
The precedent raises the strategic value of every remaining independent wide-release distributor, as buyer and as target, since their count is now what the law protects. The court also weighed Paramount's post-September 30 ticking fees and ruled them subordinate to public harm, which makes the buyer's pressure point readable: the closer to September 30 without a favorable ruling, the more motivated it becomes to settle or restructure. If a settlement path opens, the likeliest concession given the court's chosen market is a binding annual wide-release commitment, a durable win for anyone whose value is theatrical.

Thousands of Crew Flagged for Removal From the Industry Roster, With the Numbers That Explain Why
Production RunawayIATSE hours fell 36% since 2022 and $40M+ starts fell 37% since 2021; staying on the roster took one union day in three years, rejoining now needs 30 days in one.
CEO Summary
A few thousand IATSE members have been flagged for removal from the Industry Experience Roster, the preferred-hire list covering ~47,000 West Coast freelance crew, in the first enforcement round since 2022. Staying on required one day of union work in three years; getting back on requires 30 days in one year. The context: IATSE hours fell 36% from 2022 to 2025, and $40M+ U.S. live-action starts fell 37% from 2021 to 2025.
Key Takeaways
  • Production Runaway: A 36% hours decline and a 37% drop in big-budget U.S. starts are structural relocation, not cyclical noise, and the roster purge converts it into permanent individual consequences.
  • Labor Migration: Flagged crew are still working, on non-union indies, reality, and self-produced projects, a quiet migration that weakens the unit before it bargains in 2027.
  • Labor Negotiation: The eligibility threshold is a contract term the unions themselves agreed to, unchangeable until the AMPTP renegotiation, which makes roster access a known agenda item for anyone dependent on union crew supply.
Why It's Happening
The asymmetry does the damage: crew who fell below a one-day-in-three-years bar during the thinnest production stretch in modern memory now face a bar roughly thirty times higher to return, at the moment work is hardest to find. For a production planning a domestic shoot in 2027, tighter availability of experienced department heads is a reasonable planning assumption. The 37% starts decline is also the evidence base for the federal film incentive push, which now has an organized constituency and a concrete grievance behind it.
The Facts
ItemDetail
The listThe Industry Experience Roster, administered by a nonprofit founded under collective bargaining agreements since 1965. Tracks West Coast freelance crew (grips, makeup artists, plumbers) with role experience. Employers agree in union contracts to hire from it first.
Scale~47,000 currently listed (IATSE, Teamsters Local 399, LiUNA Local 724, UA Plumbers Local 78). A few thousand IATSE members flagged for removal in recent weeks.
ThresholdGenerally one day on a union project in a three-year period, here April 1 2023 to March 31 2026.
RequalificationReapply and requalify from scratch, which for many classifications means 30 days on eligible productions in one year versus the one-day-in-three that maintained status.
First since2022. Removals normally run annually but were paused post-strikes by agreement between employers and unions.
Production dataIATSE members worked ~78.9M hours in 2025, down ~36% from ~122.9M in 2022. Live-action scripted U.S. starts at $40M+ budgets fell 37% between 2021 and 2025 (ProdPro).
Union positionIATSE leadership condemns "this purging of the workforce," blames foreign tax incentives, and ties it to the push for a federal film incentive.
The bindEligibility is set by contract terms the unions themselves agreed to with the AMPTP. Next renegotiation: 2027.
ProcessFlagged members can protest; dispute resolution expected over the next few months. Several Locals filed blanket protests.

Three Chinese Local Titles Crowd the Global Chart as Hollywood's Best Performer There Manages $3.6M
China Market RiskKung Fu Soccer alone has a $214.3M China cume; the best-performing Hollywood title there, Minions & Monsters, made $3.6M in its third weekend on a $40.3M cume.
CEO Summary
Three Chinese local-language titles took the No. 2, No. 6, and No. 8 global box office slots this weekend, led by "Kung Fu Soccer" at a $214.3M cume from China alone. The best-performing Hollywood film in that market, Universal's "Minions & Monsters," did $3.6M in its third weekend for a $40.3M cume. "The Odyssey" opened to $263.7M globally, No. 1 nearly everywhere, and does not open in China until August 14.
Key Takeaways
  • China Market Risk: When local titles beat the entire studio slate by an order of magnitude, the ex-China view is the honest base case for greenlights, backend projections, and bonus thresholds, with China as separately argued upside.
  • Territory Terms: A market that can swing a worldwide total by nine figures and behaves unpredictably for imports belongs explicitly in any worldwide-gross participation, not buried in a global number.
  • Box Office Test: The Odyssey's China opening is the cleanest test available of whether the ceiling is structural or title-dependent, a dated, falsifiable data point worth calendaring.
Why It's Happening
The holiday-season framing in the trade coverage understates the chart: a Universal animated title's $40.3M China cume still makes China its biggest offshore territory, while a local comedy sits at $214.3M in that one market. For anyone thinking about international IP or co-production, the returns keep pointing to films originated inside the market rather than shipped into it.

The Premium-Format Ceiling: Only 41 IMAX 70mm Screens Exist Worldwide, and the Projectors Can't Be Rebuilt
Format AccessNo new IMAX film projector has been built in about 50 years and IMAX no longer holds a complete manufacturing blueprint; a year of scavenging produced a net gain of just eleven screens.
CEO Summary
Only 41 IMAX 70mm locations exist worldwide, 25 in the US, for the current Universal release, and demand has some theaters sold out into the fifth week. No new IMAX film projectors have been built in about 50 years; many parts no longer exist, and IMAX no longer holds a complete manufacturing blueprint. A year of scavenging units and training 60 projectionists from scratch produced a net gain of eleven screens.
Key Takeaways
  • Format Access: With 25 US screens and week-five sellouts, large-format capacity is rationed, so screen count and hold length belong in a format-native filmmaker's distribution agreement, not in assumptions.
  • Theatrical Differentiation: A hardware constraint that cannot be streamed or replicated at home is the most defensible remaining differentiator for theatrical, a real input when weighing a theatrical partner against a streamer.
  • Exhibition Capacity: The projector shortage is one cap; the other is exhibitor capex on 1.43:1 auditoriums, and the existing 12-site AMC deal is the template for how capacity actually expands.

For a movie star whose likeness and signature role are the thing being visited, the experiential comp set, a premium Vegas venue, studio theme parks, now a standalone Strip destination, is public enough to price against rather than waive cheaply.

The Indie Completion-Bond Market Just Went From Two Players to One
Financing ConsolidationA director-led feature that premiered at Tribeca 2026 was financed, bonded, produced and post-supported entirely inside the same combined group, and is now seeking distribution.
CEO Summary
Film Finances International is acquiring Media Guarantors, combining the two largest completion-bond guarantors for independent film under one company inside the STX Entertainment and Film Services International family. The group also finances, physically produces, and posts films, and says it will invest in data-driven risk-assessment tools to speed bond issuance.
Key Takeaways
  • Financing Consolidation: The bond is a hard gate on any film financed outside a studio, and one counterparty now substantially sets the fee, the schedule conditions, and the working definition of "bondable."
  • Bundled Services: A group that finances, produces, posts and bonds will discount the package; pricing the bond standalone and resisting any clause conditioning bond issuance on using the group's other services is far easier now than mid-picture.
  • Credit Scoring: Applied to schedules, budgets, and plausibly filmmaker track record, with no appeal process, an adverse early read could follow an emerging filmmaker across pictures.
Why It's Happening
The same corporate group can now sit on both sides of a picture, as the service provider taking fees and as the risk assessor deciding bondability, which is the firm underwriting the risk and selling the remedy. The honest counterargument from the reporting: bonding is a shrinking niche most films skip, and one healthy vendor may beat two weak ones. Guarantors consolidate when volume shrinks, so this is also a leading indicator that indie financing is thinner than the box-office recovery narrative suggests.

Sony Moves to Take the Cinerama Dome, Extending the Only Studio-Owned Exhibition Arm
Exhibition StrategySony already spent $100M on immersive-dome company Cosm this year and acquired Alamo Drafthouse in 2024; it also holds a $457M majority stake in the Peanuts brand.
CEO Summary
Sony Pictures is in early talks to lease and operate the Cinerama Dome in Hollywood, with Alamo Drafthouse likely involved in running it. The move extends an exhibition build that already includes the 2024 Alamo Drafthouse acquisition and a $100M investment in immersive-dome company Cosm this year. Both sides declined comment and there is no opening date.
Key Takeaways
  • Exhibition Strategy: The only major without a platform is the only major systematically acquiring exhibition, which makes it the structurally cleanest fit for talent prioritizing ownership and backend over a platform buyout.
  • Participation Terms: When a studio distributes into theaters it operates, the exhibition split becomes an internal transfer, so participations on its releases should contemplate affiliated exhibition and arm's-length rental terms. Small today, structural if the footprint grows.
  • Deal Status: This venue has been rumored to reopen for six years, both sides declined comment, and one venue plus a chain is nowhere near distribution control.
Why It's Happening
The timing matters more than the nostalgia: Sony is assembling controlled premium exhibition at exactly the moment premium-format access has become contested and exclusive-able, and a studio that owns screens does not negotiate for them. The venue is also premiere and awards infrastructure in an L.A. market that has lost Landmark Pico, the Bruin, and the Fox since 2022, with a studio, a chain, an immersive startup, and a filmmaker consortium all now buying rooms traditional operators abandoned.

Public and Commercial Broadcasters Pool Streaming Inventory in Germany — Former Rivals Combining Against the Global Platforms
Licensing LeverageProSieben carried ZDF's content without an agreement, lost in court, and is now carrying it anyway under a formal deal starting Q4 2026, free and without ads.
CEO Summary
German public broadcaster ZDF will integrate its on-demand content into commercial rival ProSiebenSat.1's streaming service Joyn from Q4 2026, free and without ads, resolving a dispute the courts decided in ZDF's favor last year. It joins a wave of similar moves: Channel 4 in talks with the BBC, TF1 onto Netflix, France Televisions onto Prime Video, and Disney+ content deals with four European broadcasters.
Key Takeaways
  • Licensing Leverage: European buyers that once bid separately now share shelf space, which means fewer genuinely competitive bids per territory and a direct leverage loss on international licensing.
  • Platform Strategy: ZDF did a domestic pooling deal and a global-platform deal within twelve months; the choice is which aggregator to join, and the answer is more than one.
  • Content Commissioning: Everything announced is carriage of existing inventory; a new tier of European buyer only appears if pooled platforms start commissioning originals with pooled budgets.
Why It's Happening
The regulatory divergence is the structural fact: Germany's State Media Treaty actively encourages the public-commercial combination that got this done, in the same week a US state antitrust action froze the largest domestic media merger. Two regimes moving opposite directions on consolidation changes where projects and companies can transact. The dispute history is the leverage tell: ProSieben took the content without agreement, lost in court, and still ended up carrying it, because the content was valuable but the destination was not.

Judge Grants Temporary Restraining Order To Pause Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery Merger For 14 Days
Litigation PostureThe judge waived the bond requirement and set a preliminary-injunction hearing for August 3; Paramount owes WBD $7M for every day past September 30 the deal stays open.
CEO Summary
A federal judge granted the 12 state AGs a 14-day temporary restraining order barring Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery from closing or integrating their $110B merger, writing that the states' market-share evidence lets the court "presume the proposed merger is likely to violate antitrust laws." A preliminary-injunction hearing is set for August 3 and could extend the freeze indefinitely. Paramount owes WBD a $7M-per-day ticking fee for every day past September 30 the deal stays open.
Key Takeaways
  • Litigation Posture: The judge pre-committed a view on the merits, so August 3 opens with the states ahead, not at zero.
  • Settlement Pressure: At $7M a day after September 30, the state AGs can bleed Paramount without ever winning the case, and a counterparty under a running clock concedes on terms, exclusivity, and pace.
  • Merger Uncertainty: Greenlight authority, slate consolidation, and post-merger structure at either company are legally contested facts, not settled ones.
Why It's Happening
DOJ closed its own investigation in June and saw no antitrust problem; the state track just overrode that with the first legally binding check on the deal. The theory that persuaded the judge is theatrical concentration, wide-release and top-grossing-film distribution, not streaming. Procedurally the schedule is fast: states' motion Thursday, Paramount opposition July 27, reply July 30, hearing August 3. Paramount had already signaled willingness to hold the close 28 days, and the judge waived the usual bond requirement, citing the public interest in antitrust enforcement.
The Facts
  • U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted a 14-day temporary restraining order, issued Monday (7/20), barring Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery from "closing or consummating the Transaction or taking any steps, directly or indirectly, to integrate or consolidate their operations."
  • The TRO responds to the antitrust suit filed by California AG Rob Bonta and 11 other state AGs, arguing the combined firm would hold outsized market share in wide-release theatrical distribution, top-grossing-film distribution, and basic-cable-channel licensing.
  • The judge wrote the states "present compelling evidence" of market-share concentration and that "on this combined firm market share alone, the Court is persuaded that it can presume the proposed merger is likely to violate antitrust laws."
  • States sought the TRO because Paramount had not guaranteed it wouldn't close after July 22 — the date the EU is expected to rule on the deal. At Friday's hearing, Paramount's lead attorney Jeffrey Kessler had already signaled a willingness to hold off closing for 28 days.
  • Judge waived Paramount/WBD's usual bond/security requirement given the "public's vital interest in antitrust enforcement."
  • Preliminary injunction schedule set: states' motion due Thursday, Paramount opposition due July 27, states' reply July 30, hearing August 3 — this could halt the merger indefinitely pending the outcome.
  • Financial stakes: Paramount faces a $7M-per-day "ticking fee" owed to Warner Bros for every day the deal isn't closed after September 30 — a sweetener Paramount added to win the WBD bidding war.
  • Paramount's spokesperson called the states' antitrust theory "without any basis in modern market realities" and vowed to "vigorously defend the transaction." Bonta: "This is a critical first win in our case to ensure this megamerger never sees the light of day." NY AG Letitia James echoed the consumer-harm framing.
  • Context: this had been trending toward a close — DOJ closed its own investigation in June and stated it did not view the deal as anticompetitive; the state-AG action is a separate, parallel track.

A Dozen States Sue to Block the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery Merger; Judge to Rule on TRO by July 22
Antitrust RiskThe states built their case on 27% of wide-release theatrical share and 30% of anticipated blockbuster films; the ruling lands the same day as the EU's own approval deadline.
CEO Summary
Twelve state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, sued to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, a month after the DOJ cleared the deal. A federal judge heard the TRO motion Friday and will rule by July 22, the same day as the EU's provisional approval deadline. The suit alleges the combined company would control roughly 30% of anticipated top-grossing theatrical films.
Key Takeaways
  • Antitrust Risk: State AGs can restart an antitrust fight the federal government already waved through.
  • Market Definition: The states built their case on movie-screen concentration, not streaming, and that market definition is reusable against the next studio merger.
  • Deal Leverage: Until the ruling lands, litigation is leverage to hold current terms with either studio rather than treat post-merger terms as locked.
Why It's Happening
The states' Clayton Act theory carves out wide-release and "anticipated top-grossing" theatrical distribution as their own antitrust markets: a combined Paramount/WBD would hold about 27% of wide-release distribution and about 30% of anticipated blockbusters. Paramount's own counsel says the deal will not close by July 22 regardless of the ruling, and active state litigation persists either way. The CEO's stated commitment to 30+ films a year post-close is a concrete benchmark to hold the buyer to if the deal survives.
The Facts
A coalition of 12 state attorneys general (led by California's Rob Bonta) filed an antitrust suit on 2026-07-13 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery — a month after the DOJ cleared the deal. The suit alleges Clayton Act violations across three markets: wide-release theatrical distribution, "anticipated top-grossing" theatrical distribution, and basic-cable-channel licensing to distributors — a combined Paramount/WBD would hold ~27% share of wide-release theatrical distribution and control ~30% of anticipated blockbuster films. On Friday 2026-07-17, a federal judge heard 80 minutes of argument on the states' TRO motion and said she'd rule by July 22 — the date Paramount's counsel says the deal will not close by regardless. The EU has its own provisional approval deadline of July 22; the UK CMA has an open investigation. Paramount calls the suit "wrong on both the facts and the law" and argues the combined company is needed to compete with Netflix; Paramount's CEO has committed to 30+ films/year post-close.

The Paramount-WBD Fight Comes Down To One Question: What Counts As A Blockbuster
Output PledgeParamount cited Obsession, made for $750,000 and grossing near $430 million, as proof the market is open; a ticking fee of roughly $650 million per quarter starts Oct. 1 if unclosed.
CEO Summary
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín heard the state AGs' emergency motion against Paramount's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Friday and will rule in writing before July 22, the date of an anticipated EU greenlight and the earliest possible close. The hearing turned on what counts as a blockbuster: Paramount cited the $750K creator film Obsession grossing $430M as proof the market is open; the states answered that five majors make blockbusters consistently. A ticking fee of roughly $650M per quarter starts Oct. 1.
Key Takeaways
  • Output Pledge: Paramount voluntarily offered 30 movies a year at a 45-day window to settle; that is now the studio's own stated view of sustainable output, quotable in any release-commitment negotiation.
  • Antitrust Argument: Studios will cite micro-budget creator hits as proof anyone can reach scale; the counter is the states': breakouts are not capacity, and consistent wide distribution is held by a handful of buyers.
  • Deal Timeline: A TRO freezes the deal; denial clears a near-term close. Any matter whose value depends on which entity survives as an independent buyer has an answer within days.
Why It's Happening
If the court accepts Paramount's framing, studio concentration is legally unremarkable and the deal proceeds; if it accepts the states', going from five majors to four is presumptively illegal. Either way, the states' theory, fewer majors means fewer wide-release slots and less competition for them, is a description of buyer-side leverage, and a court is being asked to rule on whether it is real. The ticking fee is why delay hurts Paramount and why the states asked for proceedings next year.
The Facts
ProceedingFriday hearing before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín (N.D. Cal., Oakland) on the state AGs' emergency motion for a TRO / preliminary injunction against Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery
Ruling timingJudge will issue a written ruling before July 22 — the date of an anticipated EU antitrust greenlight and the earliest the merger could theoretically close
Deal size$110–111B (sources vary); 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta
Markets allegedThree: blockbuster films, wide-release movies, and cable networks
Ticking feeThe controlling shareholders agreed to pay 25 cents cash per share per quarter — roughly $650M per quarter, cited as ~$7.2M/day (Deadline) and ~$6.9M/day (THR) — to WBD shareholders for each day the deal is unclosed starting Oct. 1
Paramount's offerCounsel offered to forgo closing early if the court rules on a preliminary injunction by early September; the AGs asked for proceedings next year
States' share claimCombined company would take more than a quarter of every box office dollar; ~30% share of blockbuster distribution
Rejected remedyParamount pushed to settle pre-filing with behavioral commitments including 30 movies a year at a 45-day theatrical window; the states refused, wanting structural relief (separating a film studio, cable channels, or a news channel)

The hearing's central exchange was definitional. Paramount's counsel cited Obsession — made for $750,000 by a digital creator and grossing close to $430M worldwide via Focus Features — as "undisputed economic evidence" that the majors no longer control blockbuster supply. Counsel for the states answered that breakouts do not define a market: "I'm not saying no one can have a super hit or a breakout, but there are five majors that make blockbusters consistently."

Paramount also pointed to streamers entering theatrical, citing F1 as an Amazon success before correcting that it was an Apple film. The states' retort: Apple made "a successful big movie, but it was distributed by Warner Bros. Apple makes cell phones, not movies."

Divergence flagged: earlier reporting named a different district judge as assigned to the emergency motion; today's Deadline and THR accounts both place Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on the bench for Friday's hearing. This file records Martínez-Olguín per the two same-day accounts, with the earlier attribution unreconciled.

Netflix Brings Back Free Trials, Pulls Back On Viewership Data, And Starts Behaving Like A Challenger Again
Data TransparencyNetflix's granular viewership reporting only began in December 2023, and France's TF1 channels are now being bundled into the service with more partnerships signalled.
CEO Summary
Netflix is reintroducing free trials in some markets, a practice abandoned in 2020, while cutting show-level viewership reporting from twice a year to once annually. Active experiments include YouTube-style shows, video podcasts, live channels and cloud games, and France's TF1 channels are being bundled into the service with more partnerships signalled.
Key Takeaways
  • Data Transparency: A title can now go a full year with no published performance figure; bonus triggers and renewal tests belong on auditable data the platform is contractually obliged to furnish.
  • Subscriber Demand: Reinstating a mechanic abandoned in 2020 suggests acquisition friction, and a platform working harder for subscribers has more need of proven draws.
  • Distribution Model: The TF1 bundling and "help other producers maximize value" framing describe a distribution partner, a different negotiation than an original commission and a possible licensing path for rights holders.
Why It's Happening
The data cut is a governance change dressed as housekeeping. THR is direct about the motive: less data gives Netflix room to take risky bets without analysts asking whether they work, and the same opacity that protects it from analysts protects it from counterparties trying to price a title's performance. A reporting covenant, defined metric, defined window, audit right, is the direct response to voluntary disclosure the platform controls and has now halved.
The Facts
Free trialsNetflix is reintroducing free trials in some markets, a practice it abandoned in 2020; not currently available in the U.S. (first reported by What's On Netflix)

BundlingFrance's TF1 channels are being bundled into Netflix, with more partnerships signalled
Sarandos on method"When we expand into new entertainment offerings, new initiatives, we do it gradually. We do it where we believe we can add more value for our members, and we do it where we believe we have the right to win. And then we look for the positive signals before we invest at material scale."
Peters on partnerships"Whether through licensing or through new partnerships like TF1, we believe that we can help other producers, other services maximize the value, the relevance of the content that they invest in by finding those bigger audiences."

THR's framing is that Netflix has historically reversed itself on ads, live sports and originals, and that the current cluster of moves reads as a deliberate return to disruptor behavior: "Now it needs to disrupt itself."

Paramount-WBD: Emergency Motions, A Showdown Hearing And Next Steps
Output PledgeThe states' theory is modeled on DOJ's Penguin Random House win over author pay; Paramount counters with AT&T-Time Warner, a case the government lost that was unwound three years later.
CEO Summary
Twelve state AGs led by California's Rob Bonta filed for a TRO and preliminary injunction against Paramount's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, with Judge P. Casey Pitts asked to rule before July 22 and a hearing set for Friday. The states' theory rests on a narrow "anticipated top-grossing films" submarket, modeled on DOJ's successful Penguin Random House challenge. The WGA filed a separate labor-market suit the same day.
Key Takeaways
  • Output Pledge: The likely settlement converts Paramount's spoken output pledge into a court-enforceable obligation to keep making theatrical films.
  • Antitrust Theory: The Penguin framework the states chose proved harm to what buyers pay the people who make the work, and that logic invites a compensation argument in film and TV.
  • Market Concentration: Paramount-WBD plus Disney controlling 59% of anticipated top-grossing distribution is the clean citable frame for narrowing tentpole options.
Why It's Happening
The counter-precedent is AT&T/Time Warner, where a judge accepted look-to-the-future arguments and the government lost; the sharp rejoinder is that AT&T-Time Warner was unwound three years later, which is itself evidence the efficiencies never materialized. Ex-FTC chair Kovacic reads the endgame as a settlement hardening the "30 movies a year" pledge into a binding order plus concessions propping up theatrical distribution.

Any overall or first-look at either company is being negotiated against a corporate identity that stays unresolved into 2027, which argues for change-of-control protections over longer commitments until the case resolves.
The Facts
ActionCalifornia AG Rob Bonta + 11 other state AGs filed for emergency relief (TRO + preliminary injunction) against Paramount's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery

Paramount's core argument is that the merger is pro-competitive because a stronger rival is needed against Netflix. The states' theory rests on a narrow submarket — "anticipated top-grossing films" — explicitly modeled on DOJ's successful Penguin Random House/Simon & Schuster challenge, where the market was "anticipated top-selling books" and the harm was to author payments.

  • Director Value: A nearly three-hour literary adaptation with no franchise underneath posting franchise-level previews resets what a director with a proven premium-format audience can ask.
  • Format Value: IMAX 70MM sold out a year in advance and presales concentrated in premium seats mean the value sits in the format, worth pricing explicitly rather than leaving inside a generic gross definition.
  • Comp Timing: The crossover question, premium appointment viewing versus broad conversion, decides whether this is a $100M proposition or a $250M one; both outcomes are live until the 3-day posts.
Why It's Happening
The presales are the more interesting datum than the previews: $30M-$40M is well below Wicked's $60M and Deadpool's $50M, yet previews outperform both per presale dollar. That gap says demand is concentrated in premium formats, appointment viewing booked a year out, rather than broad. Avatar-style films convert because everyone eventually goes; Dune: Part II converted at a lower ceiling. This lands between them.

Paramount-WBD: Emergency Motions, A Showdown Hearing And Next Steps In Challenge To Mega-Merger
Antitrust PrecedentParamount's counsel, Jeff Kessler, told CNBC the company would take the case up to the Supreme Court if it had to; the DOJ closed its own investigation in June with no objection.
CEO Summary
California AG Rob Bonta and 11 other state AGs filed for a TRO and preliminary injunction to halt Paramount's roughly $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, with a hearing set for Friday and a ruling requested before July 22. The states allege the combined company would hold about 30% of the "anticipated top-grossing" theatrical market and, together with Disney, 59% of top-grossing film distribution. The DOJ already closed its own investigation in June with no objection.
Key Takeaways
  • Antitrust Precedent: Antitrust law is starting to treat creator compensation, not ticket prices, as the harm from buyer consolidation.
  • Settlement Outlook: The likely endgame converts the "30 movies a year" pledge into a court-enforced theatrical output floor.
  • Cost Synergies: A settlement on output alone leaves the $6B cost-savings target, and every overhead and first-look deal at both studios, unaddressed.
Why It's Happening
The load-bearing claim is not the 27% wide-release number, which sits under the Supreme Court's 30% marker. It is the "anticipated top-grossing films" submarket, which lands at about 30% and has fresh case law behind it: DOJ beat Penguin Random House/Simon & Schuster by defining a market for anticipated top-selling books and proving harm to author advances, a monopsony theory about what buyers pay talent. If Judge Pitts entertains the same logic, that reasoning ports directly to film and TV compensation.

The decisive question is whether film distribution is defined narrowly (theatres only) or broadly (theatres plus streaming). Narrow, the states have a case; broad, it is in jeopardy. Former FTC chair William Kovacic reads the complaint as strong enough to force concessions and expects a settlement that hardens the output pledge into a binding order. Any position that turns on whether Warner Bros. is still an independent buyer in Q4 gets a concrete answer by July 22, worth holding on rather than guessing before then.

Netflix Shares Fall After Mixed Q2; Company Concedes "Not All Hours Are Equal"
Engagement MetricsRevenue came in at $12.56 billion, a slight miss, while EPS beat by a penny at 80 cents; full-year guidance narrowed to $51 billion to $51.4 billion.
CEO Summary
Netflix reported Q2 revenue of $12.56B, a slight miss, and EPS of 80 cents, a penny beat; shares fell 9% after hours to an 18-month low. First-half viewing grew just 2% to 97 billion hours, and the shareholder letter declared "not all hours are equal." Full-year guidance narrowed to $51B-$51.4B.
Key Takeaways
  • Engagement Metrics: Netflix redefined engagement as quality in the same quarter quantity went flat.
  • Renewal Criteria: Any series in the renewal window is now judged on a rubric the company has not publicly defined; pin the metric down before the option date.
  • Content Durability: A buyer telling Wall Street quality beats volume has supplied the frame for paying up for creators whose second seasons hold.
Why It's Happening
The number that matters is not the revenue miss, a rounding error, but 97 billion hours up 2% on a service that added vertical video, podcasts, live sports and a French broadcast partnership specifically to move that line. Netflix spent a year buying engagement and got 2%. Spend of roughly $20B against 2% engagement growth is the strongest public evidence yet that the marginal hour is getting more expensive, which is the leverage argument for anyone who reliably delivers completion.

With the WBD bid dead and the $2.8B breakup fee collected, the two-year window ahead is one where controllable, outside-owned IP is worth more to Netflix as a buyer than it was while a library deal that size was still live.

Netflix Cuts Viewership Disclosure From Twice A Year To Once, Effective Q1 2027
Reporting CadenceReturning series fell from 7 of the top 10 titles to 3, and Bridgerton season 4 is the first season of that franchise to miss Netflix's all-time list.
CEO Summary
Netflix will cut its What We Watched viewership report from twice a year to once, published each Q1 starting in 2027. The change lands in the same disclosure as a 2% engagement increase and amid reporting on steep second-season dropoffs, which Sarandos denied are material. Netflix remains the only major streamer publishing regular viewing data at all.
Key Takeaways
  • Reporting Cadence: Any bonus, escalator or renewal trigger benchmarked to the public report now settles on a twelve-month lag; a threshold that cannot be verified for a year cannot be enforced for a year.
  • Data Rights: The buyer weakened the public rung and supplied the evidence for defined metrics, delivery dates and audit rights in the contract.
  • Performance Bands: "Well within our bands of expectation" concedes bands exist; the renewal-table question is what the band is, asked while the company is publicly committed to meeting it.
Why It's Happening
The two stated reasons are in tension: publishing less often does not make a metric "clearer," and the decoupling from earnings reads as the real motive. Netflix's own final biannual report substantiates the trend it denies: returning series fell from 7 of the top 10 to 3, and Bridgerton S4 is the first season of that franchise to miss the all-time list. The "we launch so big" defense explains the size of the decline while conceding the decline, and it hands anyone arguing for a weekly or hybrid rollout the buyer's own causal explanation.

Creatives from 'Sharknado' and 'Doctor Who' Are Now Making AI Films
Industry NormsPromise AI is backed by North Road, Google and a16z, and the animated short series Hardcore 94, pairing writer Ivan Rome with AI artist Metapuppet, is already in production.
CEO Summary
Promise AI, an LA startup backed by North Road, Google and a16z, has paired credited working professionals, including a Doctor Who director and the writer who developed Sharknado, with AI filmmakers on named projects, with one animated short series already in production. All financing so far comes from Promise; mainstream distribution remains unsecured.
Key Takeaways
  • Industry Norms: Norms collapse when numerous credentialed mid-tier professionals defect, not when a star endorses; "I don't work on AI projects" becomes a competitive choice within a cycle.
  • Writer Leverage: The scarce input in an AI production is still the script, which reads as writer leverage, not obsolescence.
  • AI Distribution: Until a mainstream streamer or exhibitor takes one of these films, this is a supply-side experiment with no demand proof.
Why It's Happening
Promise's own pitch is that AI filmmaking is weak on writing and development and needs traditional craft, so it is paying for the one input its stack cannot produce and using the credit to buy respectability. The substantive claim underneath is cheap iteration, Pixar-style constant rewriting at a fraction of the cost, which targets development deals and rewrite economics well before it reaches production.

Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' To Begin Epic Journey With Around $200M WW – Box Office Preview
Backend StructureFour European Imax 70mm sites sold out a year in advance, while Moana, opening the same week, managed just a $47.5 million four-day domestic start.
CEO Summary
Universal projects Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey to open at $85M-$100M domestic plus about $110M overseas, a $200M+ global start, with $30M-$40M already in advance sales and no other major studio wide release on the weekend. The benchmark is Oppenheimer: an $82.4M domestic bow that legged to $330M, a 4x multiple.
Key Takeaways
  • Backend Structure: Nolan's scarce-format strategy suppresses openings by design, so backend pegged to full run captures what an opening-weekend trigger misses.
  • Calendar Deference: No studio counter-programmed a filmmaker's name; that calendar deference shows up in every subsequent negotiation.
  • Format Commitment: When a film's value thesis rests on format scarcity booked a year out, that format commitment is a contractual term rather than a marketing decision.
Why It's Happening
Four European Imax 70MM sites sold out a year in advance. When demand wants a specific seat, it queues rather than rushes, which is why a soft-looking Friday would mean little: Oppenheimer legged 4x, Dunkirk 3.75x. The contrast running in the same fortnight is the sharper signal: an auteur original tracking to $200M+ globally while a live-action remake of known animated IP limps to a $47.5M four-day. If both hold, the bankable theatrical asset is the filmmaker, not the pre-awareness, and that is falsifiable by Monday.
