The Video Game IP Boom Is About to Hit the Wall
IP SupplyBorderlands cost more than $110 million and returned just $33 million globally, and Xbox laid off 3,200 workers, a fifth of its staff, after its spending strategy misfired.
CEO Summary
More than half of the 50 best-selling game franchises of all time are already adapted or in development, and the dominant younger-audience titles, Fortnite, Minecraft and Roblox at roughly 40% of playtime, have almost no story to adapt. Gaming's own economics, 7-to-10-year builds, $1B+ budgets and mass layoffs, are not generating replacement franchises.
Key Takeaways
  • IP Supply: The adaptable supply is countable and shrinking, so anything to be won from the game-IP cycle is worth moving on now, not in two years.
  • Emerging Filmmakers: Small, cheap, tonally distinctive titles favor the genre and emerging-filmmaker lane, not the tentpole lane.
  • IP Pricing: Borderlands took $110M+ in and returned $33M; the moment favors selling into this market over buying into it.
  • Market Correction: Netflix, A24, Paramount, Warner Bros., Nintendo and Sony are all committed to the cycle, so a correction reprices the IP class, not one studio.
Why It's Happening
The bull case is an audience-transfer thesis, and the audience being transferred is the wrong one: the games with adaptable narrative are console titles played by older gamers, while younger players have migrated to free-to-play and mobile titles built without story. This is the superhero arc repeating, a dwindling IP pool plus can't-lose sentiment producing late-cycle misses, with one difference: the supply floor is visible in advance.

Marvel Comics Leaves New York For Burbank After 90 Years, With A New Editor-In-Chief
IP OriginationThe move was forced by a Manhattan lease expiring next year, and Marvel has lost its comics market-share lead for the first time this century.
CEO Summary
Marvel's publishing division will leave Manhattan after 90 years, relocating just over 100 employees to Burbank by July 2027, with Stephen Wacker becoming editor-in-chief and outgoing EIC C.B. Cebulski moving to Japan to lead a manga push. Publishing now reports into Brad Winderbaum, head of television, animation, comics and franchise.
Key Takeaways
  • IP Origination: Comics development sits in the same building as the people who greenlight adaptations; the room where the next decade of screen IP originates just moved and got smaller.
  • Content Investment: Against the harvest-only consensus, Disney is investing in the source-material engine with new leadership and a 12-month relocation.
  • Manga Strategy: A former editor-in-chief on the ground in Japan with a live Shonen Jump relationship is a named counterparty for IP that crosses formats.
Why It's Happening
Two facts explain the move: a lease expiring next year, and an audit finding the U.S. creator community is now more Californian than New Yorker. The structural cost is unstated: a publishing arm optimized to feed the screen slate is a different thing than one optimized to sell comics, and Marvel just lost the market-share lead doing the latter. Watch the relocation take-rate; if a meaningful share of 100+ editorial staff decline, a hiring market of experienced comics editors opens over the next 12 months.

WGA Joins The Fight, Federal Judge Sets Friday Hearing: Paramount-WBD Merger Heads For A Pre-July-22 Showdown
Settlement OutlookParamount answered the suit with a pledge of at least 30 movies a year with full 45-day theatrical windows, and hired Daniel Petrocelli, who beat DOJ's 2018 AT&T-Time Warner challenge.
CEO Summary
The Writers Guild of America sued Tuesday in the Northern District of California to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on a labor-monopsony theory, one day after 12 state AGs filed their antitrust suit. Judge P. Casey Pitts hears the states' emergency TRO motion Friday July 17 and is asked to rule before July 22, the window in which Paramount could otherwise close. Paramount responded with a public commitment to at least 30 movies a year with full 45-day theatrical windows.
Key Takeaways
  • Settlement Outlook: The likely endgame is not a clean block or close but a negotiated order that hard-codes Paramount's pledges; those enforceable concessions will reshape talent leverage more than the headline outcome.
  • Output Pledge: Litigation has hard-coded a public output commitment of at least 30 movies a year with full 45-day windows, which converts a merger promise into an enforceable floor on the combined entity's theatrical terms.
  • Leverage Window: A merger tied up in antitrust and labor litigation creates a temporary window in which counterparties can lock better terms with the pre-merger entity; once a ruling lands and a combined buyer can consolidate redundant paper, that leverage closes.
Why It's Happening
The states count the combined company at roughly 27% of wide-release theatrical, 30% of the top-grossing submarket (59% including Disney), and 27-34% of basic cable. Ex-FTC chair William Kovacic calls the complaint strong enough to force a serious fight and predicts a settlement converting executives' verbal promises into a binding order. Paramount filing its 30-film pledge in response to the WGA suit reads as pre-negotiating that settlement in the press.

If Judge Pitts credits "anticipated top-grossing films" as its own market at Friday's hearing, it becomes a reusable argument for tentpole-specific terms like backend, marketing commitments and exhibition minimums, a market-definition precedent worth tracking regardless of how the injunction itself comes out.
The Facts
  • The Writers Guild of America (East + West jointly) sued in the Northern District of California on Tuesday July 14 to block Paramount Skydance's $110B acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one day after 12 state AGs filed their own antitrust suit. The WGA complaint is a labor-market (monopsony) theory: fewer competitors would let the merged entity "lower costs by suppressing writers' wages and reducing output."
  • The state AGs' emergency-relief motion (TRO + preliminary injunction) was assigned to U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts, with a hearing set for Friday July 17 and a ruling asked for before July 22 — the window in which Paramount could otherwise close (the EU is also expected to rule around July 22).
  • The states allege three harmed markets: wide-release theatrical (combined ~27% share at the 600+ theater threshold), "anticipated top-grossing" blockbusters (~30% at the 3,000+ theater threshold; Paramount-WBD + Disney together = 59% of that submarket), and basic cable channel licensing (27% by affiliate fees, 34% by viewership).
  • Paramount's response: it will commit to "at least 30 movies a year, with full 45-day windows," continue commissioning from independent producers, maintain two distinct film studios under independent creative leadership, and argues its true competitive market includes Amazon, Apple and Netflix.
  • Legal teams: Paramount has retained Paul Clement and Jeff Kessler (alongside Daniel Petrocelli, who beat DOJ's AT&T–Time Warner challenge in 2018, and Makan Delrahim, that case's DOJ antitrust chief, now Paramount's CLO).
  • Antitrust read (William Kovacic, ex-FTC chair, GW Law): the states' complaint is "good enough to give Paramount and Warner Brothers a hard time"; the likely endgame is a settlement converting executives' verbal promises into a binding order plus concessions to protect the theatrical channel and possibly a no-workforce-reduction funding commitment (the merger targets $6B in cost savings).

Paramount–WBD Fight Escalates: Ellisons Sued Over Alleged Trump 'Side Deal,' Antitrust Hearing Friday, AG Nominee Grilled
Injunction TimelineThe suit flags $24 billion from Saudi, Qatari and UAE funds set to own 38.5 percent of the combined company, with no CFIUS review since they get no board seats or votes.
CEO Summary
A Paramount shareholder sued David and Larry Ellison in Delaware Chancery Court to block the $111B WBD merger, alleging they promised private benefits to President Trump to clear regulatory barriers; Paramount denies any commitments were made. The suit landed a day after the state AGs' antitrust action and the WGA's labor suit, with Judge Pitts set to hear the emergency injunction motion Friday and rule before July 22. At his Senate confirmation hearing, AG nominee Todd Blanche confirmed he was part of the DOJ's June sign-off decision.
Key Takeaways
  • Injunction Timeline: The pre-July-22 injunction ruling is the first real test of whether the deal can be frozen; expert consensus still sees an eventual close, but late and conditioned.
  • Deal Timing: A counterparty whose decision authority could be frozen or reshaped within weeks argues for papering WB deals now, with downside protection against a $6B cost-savings integration.
  • Market Concentration: Paramount-WBD plus Disney would control 59% of top-grossing theatrical, the buyer-scarcity figure for any big-package conversation, and scarcity value for talent who deliver at that scale.
Why It's Happening
The investor suit and the Blanche testimony do not stop the deal on their own. What they do is harden the narrative the states are running, a politically greased approval that skipped normal scrutiny, which is exactly the public-interest texture a judge weighs on an injunction and that fuels a settlement with conditions: binding CNN and journalism commitments, possibly workforce or theatrical-distribution guardrails against the merger's $6B cost-savings target.

The suit also flags no visible CFIUS review despite $24B from Saudi, Qatari and UAE sovereign funds that would own 38.5% of the combined company (Paramount says no board seats or voting shares means no CFIUS trigger). That structure is a longer-tail risk than the injunction fight itself, the kind a future administration could revisit on multi-year paper inside the combined entity.
The Facts
  • A Paramount shareholder (lead plaintiff Paul Robbins, repped by Thomas Law/Public Integrity Project/Freedom of the Press Foundation) sued David and Larry Ellison in Delaware Chancery Court on Tuesday, seeking to block the $111B WBD merger and unspecified damages. The suit alleges the Ellisons promised "illegal private benefits to President Trump to remove federal regulatory barriers" — including settling Trump's CNN legal claims to "funnel cash" to him and firing CNN anchors Trump dislikes after the takeover. Trump is not named as a defendant.
  • Paramount's response: the suit "recycles allegations already reported and already addressed," and "no commitments from either David or Larry Ellison have been made to any government body… regarding the future of CNN or any other news property." It reiterated the deal "stands on its own merits."
  • The complaint landed a day after 12 Democratic state AGs (led by California's Rob Bonta) filed a federal antitrust suit; the WGA also sued on labor grounds. The AG case was assigned to U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts, who must rule on the states' emergency TRO/preliminary-injunction motion before July 22; a hearing is set for Friday (July 17). A granted TRO would freeze the deal for weeks. (Deadline also reported Paramount sought recusal of an initially-assigned judge, hence the reassignment.)
  • The states' market-share case: the combined entity would hold ~27% of wide-release theatrical (600+ theater threshold) and ~30% of top-grossing theatrical (3,000+ threshold); Paramount-WBD + Disney together would control 59% of the top-grossing market; ~27–34% of basic cable. Antitrust experts (William Kovacic, ex-FTC chair) call the complaint strong enough to force a serious fight and predict a settlement with binding commitments over the spoken CNN/journalism promises, possibly workforce guarantees (vs. the merger's $6B cost-savings target). Paramount's team: Paul Clement and Jeff Kessler.
  • At his Senate confirmation hearing Wednesday, AG nominee Todd Blanche (Trump's former personal lawyer, acting AG) told Sen. Cory Booker "I was part of that decision" on the DOJ's June 12 sign-off but claimed "no idea" whether career Antitrust Division staff recommended closing the probe. The WSJ reported senior leadership closed the investigation before career staffers — who leaned toward challenging the deal — could object. Booker also pressed Blanche on attending an April Paramount dinner honoring Trump while the DOJ probe was open.
  • Separately, the suit flags no visible CFIUS review despite $24B from Saudi, Qatari and UAE sovereign funds that would own 38.5% of the combined company (Paramount says no board seats/voting shares, so no CFIUS trigger).

Lionsgate Studios Draws Takeover Interest From Banijay and Mediawan

CEO Summary
Lionsgate Studios, market value around $3.8B with Hunger Games, John Wick and Twilight in its library, has drawn takeover interest from European groups Banijay and Mediawan, and has engaged an investment bank to assess inbound approaches. Pricing is the obstacle: Lionsgate trades at roughly 26x expected pretax profit, a premium that has already turned away earlier suitors.
Key Takeaways
  • Sale Process: Retaining a bank means the question is price, not appetite, and the Rachesky stake reshuffle into an ex-Elliott-adjacent vehicle is the kind of move that precedes a monetization event.
  • Leverage Window: Sellers greenlight and renew to show a healthy slate, and a new owner arrives needing to prove commitment to the franchises; Lionsgate paper signed now warrants change-of-control protection.
  • Franchise Value: John Wick, Hunger Games and Twilight are where participation, sequel rights and reversion terms carry the most value; downstream upside there becomes a live negotiation if control changes.
Why It's Happening
Mediawan is the more operationally credible of the two suitors: its North Road acquisition already produced A24's Backrooms, now A24's highest-grossing release, so a Mediawan-owned Lionsgate reads as a buyer likely to run the library and franchises rather than hold them passively. Banijay's mostly-unscripted formats business (Big Brother, Survivor) would be adding scripted film/TV IP and a real studio for the first time, and its bid may be delayed by its ongoing All3Media integration.
The Facts
  • Lionsgate Studios (market value ~$3.8B; library includes Hunger Games, John Wick, Twilight, and the $1B+ Michael Jackson biopic Michael) has drawn acquisition interest from European media groups Banijay and Mediawan. The Banijay interest was first reported by Reuters.
  • Lionsgate has engaged an investment bank to assess inbound approaches. No deal is guaranteed; the company could stay independent. Bolloré (Canal+ parent) is not bidding, per Variety.
  • Banijay (Big Brother, Survivor — mostly unscripted formats) is weighing a bid but may be delayed by its ongoing All3Media integration. Lionsgate would add scripted film/TV IP and a real studio/library.
  • Mediawan has been building in English-language markets via Plan B, See-Saw, and its recent North Road acquisition (whose Chernin group produced A24's Backrooms — now A24's highest-grossing release at $368M+ WW). Lionsgate would add mainstream theatrical franchises and library scale onto that U.S. base.
  • Pricing is the obstacle: Lionsgate trades at ~26x expected pretax profit, a premium to comparable studios (LSEG data via Reuters); earlier suitors reportedly walked over the valuation gap.
  • Corporate texture: director/shareholder Mark Rachesky this month moved his ~10% stake into a new fund backed by RenWave Kore — a firm founded in 2024 by ex-Elliott Management PM Cody Kittle, itself backed by Sequoia Heritage. Lionsgate, Banijay declined to comment to Reuters; Mediawan declined to Variety.

  • Remake Strategy: Audiences liked it and still didn't come; a shot-for-shot remake of a title streaming free on Disney's own platform could not manufacture urgency.
  • IP Pipeline: The remake decade's easy layups are used up; what's left needs genuine reinvention or time to earn classic status, which tilts greenlight bias back toward original animation.

Why It's Happening
The tell is the split verdict: an A- CinemaScore and no turnout. Lilo & Stitch's $1B in 2025 proves remakes are not dead, but proximity to the original and a reason to exist now matter more than nostalgia alone. Disney is banking on Mufasa-style legs ($35M open to $722M global), but Mufasa had a clear market for two months; Moana faces Toy Story 5, Minions & Monsters, and The Odyssey taking every premium large-format screen from Thursday.
The Facts
  • Disney's live-action Moana opened to $43M in North America and $95M globally against a $250M production budget plus ~$120M marketing — a start Variety says could lead to a $100M+ theatrical loss unless it legs out.

  • CinemaScore is a solid A- (audiences pleased), but critics called it a shot-for-shot retread. Disney is banking on word-of-mouth legs (the Mufasa path: $35M open → $722M global) — but Mufasa had near-free run of the marketplace through Jan–Feb, while Moana faces Toy Story 5, Universal's Minions & Monsters, and The Odyssey absorbing all premium-large-format screens from Thursday.
  • Analyst reads: Jeff Bock (Exhibitor Relations) — audiences see a remake "as an event or a duplicate. This was the latter. People wanted 'Moana 3,' not a remake of the original." David A. Gross (FranchiseRe) — a property needs time to become a classic, not just prior success; the remake came too soon after the animated sequel.
  • Structural context: Disney pioneered and has largely exhausted the modern live-action-remake playbook (Cinderella, Lion King, Aladdin, Mulan, Dumbo, Little Mermaid, Beauty and the Beast, Lady and the Tramp) and is now reaching for this-century titles. Lilo & Stitch (2025) was still a $1B hit — so remakes aren't dead, but proximity-to-original and "why now" matter more than nostalgia alone.

The FCC signaled it will vote August 6 to repeal the cap barring a single owner from controlling TV stations reaching more than 39% of U.S. markets, replacing it with case-by-case transaction review. Nexstar, blocked by a federal court from acquiring Tegna under the cap, backs the repeal; Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez calls it unlawful, arguing only Congress can change a statutory cap.
Key Takeaways
  • Regulatory Climate: The same regulatory posture behind the Paramount-WBD sign-off is now dismantling broadcast ownership limits, a climate signal that reaches beyond local TV.
  • Station Consolidation: Consolidation concentrates local ad and retransmission leverage and reshapes who buys syndicated and local content, relevant for news-talent and syndication exposure.
  • Litigation Risk: If courts hold that only Congress can change the cap, the thaw stalls; August 6 is a start date, not a finish line.
The Facts
  • The FCC signaled it will vote Aug. 6 to repeal the longstanding cap that bars a single owner from controlling TV stations reaching more than 39% of U.S. markets, replacing it with a case-by-case review of individual transactions.
  • Chairman Brendan Carr (op-ed in Breitbart) argued the cap is obsolete because national programmers already reach 100% of the country via their own streaming services and virtual MVPDs like YouTube TV, and cable/social/Netflix face no equivalent limit.
  • Immediate consequence: Nexstar — a top station owner (also owns the CW network and NewsNation) — has been blocked by a federal court from completing its acquisition of Tegna on grounds it would give Nexstar too much local-TV control. Nexstar backs the repeal.
  • Dissent + legal risk: Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez called it "unlawful," arguing Congress set the 39% cap in federal law and "only Congress" can raise or eliminate it — signaling likely litigation. The NAB (broadcaster trade group) applauded the move.
  • The FCC stressed repeal is not automatic deal approval: transactions exceeding the old 39% cap could still be denied if not in the public interest, or approved if they are.

Music Industry Rolls Out "AI-Generated" vs "AI-Assisted" Labels — With A Data Point That Should Alarm All Of Hollywood
AI Content VolumeDeezer reports 44% of all new music on its platform is AI-generated and Apple Music says more than a third of its tracks are "100% AI," the backdrop for the new voluntary labeling scheme.
CEO Summary
A coalition including the RIAA, IFPI, the Grammys, and SAG-AFTRA introduced two voluntary labels for sound recordings: "AI-Generated" for works where AI is the entirety or primary portion, and "AI-Assisted" for substantially human work with AI elements. The startling data alongside the standard: Deezer reports 44% of all new music on its platform is AI-generated, and Apple Music reports more than a third of its tracks are "100% AI."
Key Takeaways
  • AI Content Volume: 44% of new music on one platform is the first hard quantification of generative AI as a majority-share input in a creative pipeline, and any thesis on AI's pace in film and TV should be recalibrated upward from it.
  • AI Precedent: The "generated vs. assisted" line will become the reference point for AI credit, compensation, and residual clauses within a cycle.
  • Human Authorship: As machine-made saturates, the premium sits on verifiably human work, and the task is turning "human authorship" into a defined, provable, contractible right.
Why It's Happening
The scope carve-out is the tell: the labels do not yet cover lyrics, composition, music videos, or cover art, which means the hardest authorship questions were deferred under commercial pressure. Music hit generative maturity first because audio is cheaper to generate than video; the taxonomy it builds now is a first draft of what film and TV will need.
The Facts
  • A coalition — RIAA, IFPI, the Grammys, SAG-AFTRA, the Human Artistry Campaign (plus A2IM, WIN, IMPALA) — introduced two voluntary labels for sound recordings: "AI-Generated" (AI used for the entirety or primary portion) and "AI-Assisted" (substantially human, AI for some expressive elements).
  • The icons are designed for adoption by digital music services and distributors. They do not yet cover AI use in lyrics, composition, music videos, or cover art.
  • The eye-opening data: Deezer reported 44% of all new music on its platform is AI-generated; Apple Music reported more than one-third of its tracks are "100% AI."
  • IFPI/RIAA leadership: "Fans want to know whether and how generative AI has been used… these labels will provide an immediately understandable and easily scalable approach to transparency."

It is the second opt-out likeness launch after OpenAI's Sora, which was forced to opt-in and then scrapped.
Key Takeaways
  • AI Consent Default: Two platforms in a row shipped likeness tools that put the burden of consent on the individual, a pattern strong enough to treat as the default posture for the next launch, not the exception.
  • Platform Behavior: Shipping opt-out despite the Sora precedent says Instagram's distribution gives Meta the confidence to absorb industry pushback.
  • Likeness Protection: Digital-likeness vaults and deepfake detection are becoming a competitive differentiator among representation businesses, and retained likeness rights, AI carve-outs, and consent-and-compensation clauses are the deal expression of it.
The Facts
  • Meta's Superintelligence Labs rolled out its first AI media tools — Muse Photo and Muse Video — and made all public Instagram profiles opt-out by default: other users can pull in non-opted-out accounts and generate new content using their likeness.
  • A leading talent agency issued a statement calling on Meta to make Muse opt-in: no one's name, image, likeness, voice, or creative work should be used by any third party, including AI models, without clear, documented consent.
  • Agencies point to their own infrastructure — digital-likeness "vaults" for client protection/monetization and early adoption of platform deepfake-detection tools. THR frames Muse as "Sora all over again" — OpenAI's Sora was overrun with likenesses/IP, forced to opt-in, then scrapped; agencies had opted all clients out.
  • Meta's leadership pushed back on the privacy concerns. An opt-out model puts the burden on every high-profile individual to find and disable the setting.

Key Takeaways
  • Regulatory Precedent: State AGs opening a second front after DOJ approval is a precedent, and 60 to 120 days of additional regulatory tail now belongs in any large media M&A thesis.
  • Merger Timeline: Every delay keeps two majors in "wait until the deal closes" limbo on greenlights, slate commitments, and overall-deal renewals.
  • Deal Protection: A counterparty that can wait is better positioned than a studio that can't sign anything material until ownership settles, which argues for short options, walk-away rights, and change-of-control protection on anything papered now.
Why It's Happening
The stated vehicle is antitrust, but the lobbying-records demand, the DOJ's atypical pro-merger statement, and the fixation on CNN control ahead of the midterms make this as much a political-leverage fight as a competition one. It doesn't kill the deal; it injects timing and discovery risk right at the closing window while Paramount also juggles EU and UK regulators.
The Facts
  • Oregon AG Dan Rayfield is asking a Multnomah County judge to delay Paramount's closing of its WBD acquisition by 60 days and to compel document production; a hearing is set for Monday.

  • Paramount objects — calling the requests disproportionate and of "marginal relevance," and citing attorney-client privilege and First Amendment grounds. California AG Rob Bonta and other state AGs are reportedly weighing their own challenge.

The Get-Big-or-Die Era of European TV: Sky Buys ITV for $2.1B
Market ConsolidationSky's £1.6B ITV deal excludes ITV Studios, which spins off separately with a Sky programming commitment of at least £2.1B for 2028-2032; two days later the BBC confirmed its own Channel 4 streaming talks.
CEO Summary
Comcast-owned Sky agreed to acquire ITV's broadcasting and streaming operations for £1.6B ($2.1B), combining Britain's largest pay-TV operator with its largest commercial free-to-air broadcaster; ITV Studios spins off as a standalone listed content business with a ≥£2.1B Sky programming commitment for 2028-2032. Two days later the BBC confirmed talks with Channel 4 about a combined streaming platform, and parallel consolidation is moving in Germany, Italy, and Spain.
Key Takeaways
  • Market Consolidation: European broadcasters are choosing between merging for scale or moving in with a global platform, and regulators who blocked these deals for two decades are now waving them through.
  • International Rights: Near-term the survivors compete to feed scale; longer-term there are simply fewer independent bidders, and both dynamics reprice European windows and output.
  • Capital Allocation: Buying UK scale while selling Sky Deutschland is a capital-allocation tell worth reading alongside its US studio strategy.
Why It's Happening
The alternative model is already live in France: TF1 distributes through Netflix rather than merging, and France Télévisions, M6, and RTVE signed similar carriage deals with Amazon. The broadcaster-inside-a-streamer structure is a genuinely new distribution archetype, and if it spreads it resets how local rights get packaged and valued across Europe.
The Facts
  • Comcast-owned Sky agreed to acquire ITV's broadcasting and streaming operations for £1.6B ($2.1B) — combining Britain's largest pay-TV operator with its largest commercial free-to-air broadcaster. The deal excludes ITV Studios (Coronation Street, Love Island), which spins off as a standalone London-listed content business; Sky committed to ≥£2.1B ($2.8B) in ITV Studios programming spend for 2028–2032.
  • Two days later, the BBC said it is in talks with Channel 4 to combine streaming into a single British "sovereign platform."
  • The wave is Europe-wide: Germany's RTL cleared to buy Comcast's Sky Deutschland; the Berlusconi-family MediaForEurope controls ProSiebenSat.1 plus assets in Spain/Italy/Portugal.
  • The alternative model (France): rather than merge, TF1 struck a carriage deal to distribute through Netflix; France Télévisions and M6 signed similar deals with Amazon Prime Video, and Amazon added RTVE in Spain. Regulators who blocked such tie-ups for two decades are now clearing them, deciding global streamers/ad giants — not domestic TV consolidation — are the primary competitive threat.
